chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: The tales in the Fairy Books are mostly the kind that old women in country villages tell their grandchildren. No one knows how old they are or who told them first. The children of Ham, Shem and Japhet may have heard them in the Ark on rainy days. Hector’s little son may have heard them in Troy, since Homer certainly knew them, and some were written down in Egypt around the time of Moses.

Every country tells them a little differently, yet they are really the same stories, whether the listeners are small Zulus at the Cape or small Eskimos near the North Pole. Only manners and customs change: people wear clothes or go without, and the warm countries have talking lions where the cold ones have talking bears. Fairy tales are full of kings and queens because, long ago, kings were everywhere. In very old Scotland a man who would now be a country squire was a sort of king, and the same was true elsewhere. These old stories, never forgotten, were written down at various times, mostly in this century, in every sort of language. Those ancient tales make up the contents of the Fairy Books.

“The Arabian Nights” (this volume gives some of them, though far from all) are simply fairy tales of the East. The peoples of Asia, Arabia and Persia told them in their own style, and not for children but for grown men and women. Back then there were no novels and, naturally, no printed books, but there were people who made their living entertaining others with stories. They dressed the fairy tales up and turned the characters into good Muslims living in Baghdad or India. The events were often placed in the reign of the great Caliph, the ruler of the Faithful, Haroun al Raschid, who lived in Baghdad from 786 to 808 A.D. The vizier who attends the Caliph was a real person too, from the great family of the Barmecides. The Caliph put him to death in a very cruel way, and nobody ever knew the reason. The stories must have taken their present form a good while after the Caliph died, when nobody remembered clearly what had actually happened. Eventually some storyteller thought of writing the tales down and fitting them into a framework, as though a wife had told them all to a cruel Sultan. They were probably written down around the time Edward I. was fighting Robert Bruce. But they were altered at various times, and much that is dull and stupid was added, along with plenty of verses. This book includes neither the verses nor the dull parts.

France and England knew almost nothing of “The Arabian Nights” until the days of Queen Anne and George I., when Monsieur Galland translated them into French. Grown people then loved fairy tales, and they judged these Arab stories the best they had ever read. They were thrilled by ghouls (who lived among the tombs), by genies, who seemed to be a kind of ogre, by princesses who cast magic spells, and by peris, the fairies of Arabia. Sindbad had adventures that perhaps came from Homer’s Odyssey; indeed the whole East had gathered up its wonders and shipped them to Europe in a single parcel. Young men once made a racket under Monsieur Galland’s windows in the middle of the night and begged him for one of his marvelous tales. Nobody spoke of anything but dervishes and viziers, rocs and peris. The stories were translated from French into every language, and the only complaint came from Bishop Atterbury, who objected that the tales were unlikely to be true and carried no moral. Soon afterwards the bishop was banished for siding with Prince Charlie’s father, and he had plenty of time to regret being so stuffy.

The “Arabian Nights” in this book are translated from Monsieur Galland’s French version. He left out the poetry, and a great deal of what the Arabian authors found funny but which strikes us as tedious. Here the stories are also cut down in places, and passages fit only for Arabs and old gentlemen are left out. The translations are by the authors of the tales in the Fairy Books, and the pictures are by Mr Ford.

I remember reading “The Arabian Nights” at the age of six, in grubby old yellow volumes of small print without a single picture. I hope the children who read them with Mr Ford’s pictures will be as happy in the company of Aladdin and Sindbad the Sailor as I was.

chapters.title: The Arabian Nights
paragraphs: The chronicles of the ancient dynasty of the Sassanidae, which ruled for about four hundred years from Persia to the borders of China and even beyond the great river Ganges, record the praises of one king of this line, who was held to be the finest ruler of his day. His people loved him and his neighbors feared him, and when he died he left his kingdom richer and stronger than any king before him had done.

He left two sons, who were deeply fond of each other. It was a real sorrow to the elder, Schahriar, that the laws of the empire did not let him share his lands with his brother Schahzeman. After ten years of being troubled by this, Schahriar finally cut Great Tartary off from the Persian Empire and made his brother its king.

The Sultan Schahriar had a wife whom he loved above everything in the world, and nothing made him happier than to surround her with splendor and give her the finest gowns and the loveliest jewels. So he was filled with shame and grief when, after some years, he stumbled on proof that she had betrayed him utterly. Her conduct proved so shameful that he felt bound to follow the law of the land and order the grand-vizier to have her put to death. The blow almost unhinged him. He declared that at heart all women were as wicked as the sultana, if only they could be found out, and that the fewer of them in the world the better. So every evening he married a new wife, and every morning he had her strangled in front of the grand-vizier, whose duty it was to supply these unfortunate brides. The poor man hated the task, but there was no way out of it, and each day a girl was married and a wife was dead.

This conduct filled the town with horror, and all one heard was weeping and wailing. In one house a father mourned the loss of his daughter; in another, perhaps, a mother trembled for her child’s fate. The blessings once showered on the Sultan had turned to curses, and the air was thick with them.

The grand-vizier himself had two daughters, the elder named Scheherazade and the younger Dinarzade. Dinarzade had no special gifts to set her apart from other girls, but her sister was extremely clever and brave. Her father had given her the best teachers in philosophy, medicine, history and the fine arts, and on top of all that she was more beautiful than any girl in the kingdom of Persia.
One day the grand-vizier was talking with his elder daughter, who was his joy and pride. Scheherazade said to him, “Father, I have a favor to ask. Will you grant it?”
“I can refuse you nothing,” he answered, “so long as it is fair and reasonable.”
“Then listen,” said Scheherazade. “I have made up my mind to end the Sultan’s barbarous practice, and to save the girls and their mothers from the terrible fate hanging over them.”
“That would be an excellent thing,” said the grand-vizier, “but how do you mean to do it?”
“Father,” Scheherazade replied, “you are the one who has to find the Sultan a new wife every day. By all the love you have for me, I beg you to let the honor fall on me.”
“Have you lost your mind?” cried the grand-vizier, recoiling in horror. “What put such an idea in your head? By now you must know what it means to be the Sultan’s bride!”
“Yes, father, I know it well,” she answered, “and I am not afraid to face it. If I fail, my death will be a glorious one, and if I succeed I will have done my country a great service.”

“It’s no use,” said the grand-vizier. “I will never agree. If the Sultan ordered me to drive a dagger into your heart, I would have to obey. What a task for a father! Ah, if you aren’t afraid of death, then at least be afraid of the anguish you would cause me.”
“Once more, father,” said Scheherazade, “will you give me what I ask?”
“What, are you still so stubborn?” exclaimed the grand-vizier. “Why are you so set on your own destruction?”

But the girl would not listen to a word her father said. In the end, in despair, the grand-vizier had to give in. He went sadly to the palace to tell the Sultan that the next evening he would bring him Scheherazade.
This news left the Sultan utterly astounded.
“How could you bring yourself,” he asked, “to sacrifice your own daughter to me?”
“Sire,” answered the grand-vizier, “it is her own wish. Not even the sad fate awaiting her could hold her back.”
“Make no mistake, vizier,” said the Sultan. “Remember that you will have to take her life yourself. If you refuse, I swear you will pay with your head.”
“Sire,” replied the vizier, “whatever it costs, I will obey you. I am a father, but I am also your subject.” So the Sultan told the grand-vizier he could bring his daughter whenever he liked.

The vizier carried the news back to Scheherazade, who took it as though it were the most pleasant thing in the world. She thanked her father warmly for giving way, and, seeing him still bent with grief, told him she hoped he would never regret letting her marry the Sultan. Then she went to get ready for the wedding, and asked that her sister Dinarzade be sent for so she could speak with her.
When the two were alone, Scheherazade spoke to her like this:

“Dear sister, I need your help in a very important matter. My father is taking me to the palace for my wedding to the Sultan. When his Highness receives me, I will ask him, as a last favor, to let you sleep in our chamber, so that I can have your company on the last night of my life. If he grants my wish, as I hope, make sure you wake me an hour before dawn and say these words to me: ‘Sister, if you are not asleep, please, before the sun rises, tell me one of your charming stories.’ Then I will begin, and I hope in this way to free the people from the terror that rules over them.” Dinarzade answered that she would gladly do as her sister wished.

At the usual hour the grand-vizier led Scheherazade to the palace and left her alone with the Sultan, who told her to lift her veil and was amazed by her beauty. But when he saw that her eyes were full of tears, he asked what was wrong. “Sire,” answered Scheherazade, “I have a sister who loves me as dearly as I love her. Please let her sleep in the same room tonight, since it is the last night we will spend together.” Schahriar agreed to her request, and Dinarzade was sent for.

An hour before daybreak Dinarzade woke and called out, as she had promised, “Dear sister, if you are not asleep, please tell me, before the sun rises, one of your charming stories. It is the last time I will have the pleasure of hearing you.”
Scheherazade did not answer her sister but turned to the Sultan. “Will your highness allow me to do what my sister asks?” she said.
“Gladly,” he answered. So Scheherazade began.

chapters.title: The Story of the Merchant and the Genie
paragraphs: Sire, once upon a time there was a merchant with great wealth in land, goods and ready money. From time to time he had to travel to settle his affairs. One day, with a long journey ahead, he mounted his horse and took along a small wallet holding a few biscuits and dates, since his road crossed a desert where no food could be found. He arrived without trouble, and when his business was done he started for home. On the fourth day of the journey the sun was fierce, so he left the road to rest under some trees. At the foot of a large walnut tree he found a spring of clear, running water. He got down, tied his horse to a branch, and sat by the spring to eat some dates and biscuits from his wallet. When he had finished this plain meal, he washed his face and hands in the spring.
While he was doing this, he saw an enormous genie, white with rage, striding toward him with a scimitar in his hand.
“Get up,” the genie shouted in a terrible voice, “and let me kill you, as you have killed my son!”

As he said this he let out a dreadful yell. The merchant was as terrified by the monster’s hideous face as by his words, and answered with a tremble, “Alas, good sir, what can I have done to deserve death?”
“I will kill you,” the genie said again, “as you killed my son.”
“But how can I have killed your son?” said the merchant. “I don’t know him. I have never even seen him.”
“When you got here, didn’t you sit on the ground?” asked the genie. “And didn’t you take dates from your wallet, and while you ate them, didn’t you toss the stones around?”
“Yes,” said the merchant, “I did.”
“Then,” said the genie, “you have killed my son. While you were flinging those stones about, my son was passing by, and one of them hit him in the eye and killed him. So I will kill you.”
“Ah, sir, forgive me!” cried the merchant.
“I will show you no mercy,” answered the genie.
“But I killed your son quite by accident, so I beg you to spare my life.”
“No,” said the genie, “I will kill you as you killed my son.” With that he seized the merchant by the arm, threw him to the ground, and raised his sabre to cut off his head.

The merchant protested that he was innocent, wept for his wife and children, and pleaded pitifully to be spared. The genie held his scimitar high and waited until he was done, but was not moved in the least.
Just then Scheherazade noticed that daylight had come. She knew the Sultan always got up early for the council, so she broke off her tale.
“Truly, sister,” said Dinarzade, “this is a wonderful story.”
“The rest is even more wonderful,” Scheherazade answered, “as you would agree, if the Sultan would let me live another day and give me leave to tell it to you tomorrow night.”
Schahriar, who had enjoyed listening to Scheherazade, said to himself, “I will wait until tomorrow. I can always have her killed once I have heard the end of her story.”
All this while the grand-vizier was in terrible anxiety. But he was overjoyed when he saw the Sultan enter the council-chamber without giving the dreadful order he was expecting.
Early the next morning, before daybreak, Dinarzade spoke to her sister. “Dear sister, if you’re awake, please go on with your story.”
The Sultan didn’t wait for Scheherazade to ask his permission. “Finish the story of the genie and the merchant,” he said. “I’m eager to hear how it ends.”
So Scheherazade took up the story again. It went this way every morning: the Sultana told a tale, and the Sultan let her live long enough to finish it.

The merchant saw that the genie was set on cutting off his head. “Just one more word, I beg you,” he said. “Give me a little time, only enough to go home, say goodbye to my wife and children, and make my will. Once that is done, I will return here and you can kill me.”
“But if I give you the time you ask for,” said the genie, “I am afraid you will not come back.”
“You have my word of honor,” the merchant answered. “I will come back, without fail.”
“How much time do you need?” the genie asked.
“Give me one year,” the merchant replied. “I promise that a year from tomorrow I will be waiting under these trees, ready to hand myself over to you.”
With that, the genie left him by the fountain and vanished.
Once the merchant had got over his terror, he climbed onto his horse and rode on his way.
At home, his wife and children welcomed him with great joy. But instead of hugging them, he burst into such bitter tears that they quickly guessed something dreadful had happened.
“Please tell us,” said his wife, “what is wrong.”
“Alas,” her husband answered, “I have only one year left to live.”

Then he told them everything that had passed between himself and the genie, and how he had promised to return after a year to be killed. When they heard this sorrowful news, they fell into despair and wept long.

The very next day the merchant began putting his affairs in order, starting with the payment of his debts. He gave gifts to his friends and generous charity to the poor. He freed his slaves and made provision for his wife and children. The year slipped by quickly, and the time came for him to leave. When he tried to say goodbye, grief overwhelmed him, and he could hardly tear himself away. At last he arrived at the spot where he had first met the genie, on exactly the day he had promised. He got off his horse, sat down at the edge of the fountain, and waited for the genie in terrible suspense.

While he sat there, an old man came toward him, leading a hind. The two greeted each other, and then the old man said, “Tell me, brother, what brings you to this deserted place, with so many evil genies around? These lovely trees might make you think someone lived here, but it is a dangerous place to linger.”
The merchant explained why he had to be there. The old man listened in amazement.
“This is a most extraordinary business. I would like to see for myself how your meeting with the genie turns out.” And with that he sat down beside the merchant.

As they talked, a second old man arrived, followed by two black dogs. He greeted them and asked what they were doing in such a place. The old man with the hind told him about the merchant and the genie. No sooner had the second old man heard the story than he too decided to stay and see what would happen. He sat down with the others, and while he was still talking a third old man appeared. He asked why the merchant with them looked so sad. They told him the story as well, and he likewise resolved to watch what would pass between the genie and the merchant, and waited with the rest.

Before long they saw a thick smoke in the distance, like a cloud of dust. It drew closer and closer, and then suddenly it cleared, and there stood the genie. Without a word to them, he walked up to the merchant with a sword in his hand, took him by the arm, and said, “Get up, and let me kill you, as you killed my son.”
The merchant and the three old men began to weep and groan.

Then the old man with the hind threw himself down at the monster’s feet. “O Prince of the Genies,” he said, “I beg you to hold back your rage and listen to me. I will tell you my story and the story of this hind beside me. If you find it more marvelous than the merchant’s story, will you take away a third of the punishment you mean to give him?”
The genie thought for some time, and then said, “Very well. I agree.”

chapters.title: The Story of the First Old Man and of the Hind
paragraphs: Now I will begin my story (said the old man), so listen carefully.
This hind you see with me is my wife. We had no children of our own, so I adopted the son of a slave I was fond of, and made up my mind to leave him everything.

My wife, though, hated both the mother and the child, and she hid it from me until it was too late. When the boy was about ten, I had to go away on a journey. Before leaving, I put the mother and child in my wife’s care and asked her to look after them while I was gone, which turned out to be a whole year. In that time she studied magic, to carry out her wicked plan. Once she had learned enough, she took my son to a faraway place and turned him into a calf. Then she handed him to my steward and told him to take care of a calf she had bought. She also turned the slave into a cow and sent her to the steward too.
When I came home I asked after my slave and the boy. “Your slave is dead,” my wife said, “and as for your son, I haven’t seen him for two months, and I have no idea where he is.”

I was sad to hear that my slave had died, but since my son had only gone missing, I thought I would soon find him. Eight months went by, though, and there was still no word of him. Then the feast of Bairam arrived.

To mark it, I told my steward to bring me a very fat cow to sacrifice. He did. The cow he brought was my poor slave. I tied her up, but just as I was about to kill her, she began to low most pitifully, and I saw her eyes streaming with tears. It struck me as very strange, and, moved by pity, I told the steward to take her away and bring another. My wife was there, and she mocked my softness, which in the end did her malice no good. “What are you doing?” she cried. “Kill this cow. She’s the best we have for the sacrifice.”
To please her, I tried a second time, but again the animal’s lowing and tears disarmed me.
“Take her away,” I told the steward, “and kill her yourself. I can’t.”
The steward killed her, but when he skinned her he found nothing but bones, though she had looked so fat. I was annoyed.
“Keep her for yourself,” I told the steward, “and if you have a fat calf, bring me that instead.”

Soon he brought me a very fat calf, which, though I did not know it, was my son. It struggled hard to break its rope and get to me. It threw itself at my feet with its head on the ground, as if it wanted to win my pity and beg me not to take its life.
This sight surprised and touched me even more than the cow’s tears had done.
“Go,” I told the steward, “take this calf back and look after it well, and at once bring me a different one in its place.”
As soon as my wife heard me say this, she cried out, “What are you doing, husband? Don’t sacrifice any calf but this one.”
“Wife,” I answered, “I will not sacrifice this calf.” And despite all her protests, I stood firm.
I had another calf killed, and this one was led away. On the following day the steward asked if he could talk to me alone.

“I’ve come,” he said, “to bring you some news that I think you’ll be glad to hear. I have a daughter who knows magic. Yesterday, as I was taking back the calf you refused to sacrifice, I noticed her smile, and then straight away start to cry. I asked her why.”

“Father,” she answered, “this calf is our master’s son. I smile from joy at seeing him still alive, and I cry at the thought of his mother, who was sacrificed yesterday as a cow. It was our master’s wife who did this to them, because she hated the mother and her son.”

“When I heard this, O genie,” the old man went on, “you can imagine how astonished I was. I went at once with the steward to speak to his daughter myself. First I went to the stable to see my son, and he answered all my caresses in his own dumb way. When the steward’s daughter came, I asked her whether she could turn my son back into his true shape.”
“Yes, I can,” she replied, “on two conditions. The first is that you give him to me as my husband, and the second is that you let me punish the woman who turned him into a calf.”
“To the first condition,” I answered, “I agree with all my heart, and I will give you a generous dowry. To the second I agree as well. I only beg you to spare her life.”
“I will,” she replied. “I will treat her as she treated your son.”
Then she took a vessel of water and spoke some words over it that I did not understand. When she threw the water over him, he instantly became a young man again.
“My son, my dear son,” I cried, kissing him in a rush of joy. “This kind girl has freed you from a terrible enchantment, and I am sure that out of gratitude you will marry her.”

He agreed happily. But before the wedding, the girl turned my wife into a hind, and that is who stands before you now. I wanted her to have this shape rather than a stranger one, so that we could still see her about the family without disgust.

Since then my son has lost his wife and gone off traveling. I am now searching for him, and since I did not want to leave my wife in other people’s care, I am taking her with me. Is this not a most marvelous tale?
“It is indeed,” said the genie, “and because of it I grant you a third of this merchant’s punishment.”

When the first old man had finished, the second, who was leading the two black dogs, spoke to the genie. “I will tell you what happened to me, and I am sure you will find my story even more astonishing than the one you have just heard. But when I have told it, will you grant me too a third of the merchant’s punishment?”
“Yes,” replied the genie, “as long as your story is better than the hind’s.”
On those terms, the second old man began.

chapters.title: The Story of the Second Old Man, and of the Two Black Dogs
paragraphs: Great prince of the genies, you should know that we are three brothers—these two black dogs and I. When our father died, he left each of us a thousand sequins. With that money we all took up the same trade and became merchants. Soon after we had opened our shops, my eldest brother, one of these two dogs, decided to travel abroad to trade. So he sold everything he owned and bought goods suited to the voyages he planned. He set out and was gone a full year. At the end of it, a beggar came into my shop. “Good day,” I said. “Good day,” he answered. “Is it possible you don’t recognize me?” I looked at him closely and saw that he was my brother. I brought him into my house and asked how his venture had gone.
“Don’t ask me,” he replied. “Look at me, and you see everything I have. It would only renew my pain to tell you all the misfortunes that struck me in a year and brought me to this.”

I closed my shop and did everything for him, taking him to the baths and giving him my finest robes. I went through my accounts and found that I had doubled my capital—that is, I now owned two thousand sequins. I gave my brother half, saying, “Now, brother, you can forget your losses.” He took it gladly, and we lived together as we had before.

Some time later my second brother also wanted to sell his business and travel. My eldest brother and I did everything we could to talk him out of it, but it was no use. He joined a caravan and set out. He came back after a year in the same state as his elder brother. I looked after him, and since I had a thousand sequins to spare, I gave them to him, and he opened his shop again.

One day my two brothers came to me and suggested that we all go on a trading journey. At first I refused. “You traveled,” I said, “and what did you gain?” But they kept coming back to me, and after holding out for five years I finally gave in. But when they had made their preparations and began buying the goods we needed, they found they had spent every piece of the thousand sequins I had given them. I did not reproach them. I divided my six thousand sequins with them, giving a thousand to each, keeping one thousand for myself, and burying the other three in a corner of my house. We bought goods, loaded a ship with them, and sailed off with a favorable wind.

After two months at sea we reached a port, where we went ashore and did a great deal of business. Then we bought the local goods, and were just about to sail again when a woman stopped me on the shore. She was beautiful, though poorly dressed. She came up to me, kissed my hand, and begged me to marry her and take her on board. At first I refused, but she pleaded so hard, and promised to be such a good wife to me, that in the end I agreed. I bought her some lovely dresses, and after I had married her, we boarded the ship and sailed. During the voyage I found so many good qualities in my wife that I loved her more and more. But my brothers grew jealous of my success and started plotting against my life. One night while we slept, they threw my wife and me into the sea. But my wife was a fairy, and she would not let me drown. She carried me to an island. When day broke, she said to me,

“When I saw you on the shore I took a great liking to you, and I wanted to test your goodness, so I came to you in the disguise you saw. Now I have rewarded you by saving your life. But I am very angry with your brothers, and I will not rest until I have taken their lives.”
I was grateful for all she had done, and said so, but I pleaded with her not to take my brothers’ lives.

I calmed her anger, and in an instant she carried me from the island where we stood to the roof of my own house, and then vanished. I went down, unlocked the doors, and dug up the three thousand sequins I had buried. Then I walked to my shop and opened it, and the other merchants welcomed me back and congratulated me. When I got home, two black dogs came to meet me with sad faces. I was greatly surprised, but the fairy appeared again and said to me,
“Don’t be surprised to see these dogs; they are your two brothers. I have sentenced them to keep these shapes for ten years.” Then she told me where I could find news of her, and disappeared.
Those ten years are almost over, and I am on my way to look for her. On the road I met this merchant and the old man with the hind, and I stayed in their company.
That is my story, O prince of genies! Don’t you think it is a most marvelous one?
“Yes, truly,” replied the genie, “and I will give up to you a third of the merchant’s punishment.”

Then the third old man made the same request to the genie that the other two had made, and the genie promised him the last third of the merchant’s punishment if his story proved better than both of the others.
So he told his story to the genie, but I can’t repeat it to you, because I don’t know what it was.

But I do know that it was more marvelous than either of the other two, so much so that the genie was amazed and said to the third old man, “I give up to you the third part of the merchant’s punishment. He should thank all three of you for taking his side. Without you, he would not be here any longer.”

With these words he vanished, to the great delight of everyone present. The merchant did not forget to thank his friends, and then they all went their separate ways. The merchant went back to his wife and children, and spent the rest of his life happily with them.
“But, sire,” Scheherazade added, “fine as these stories are, they cannot compare with the story of the Fisherman.”

chapters.title: The Story of the Fisherman
paragraphs: Sire, once upon a time there was a fisherman so old and so poor that he could barely feed his wife and three children. Every day he went out to fish very early, and he had made it a rule never to cast his nets more than four times a day. One morning he set out by moonlight and reached the seashore. He took off his clothes and cast his nets, and as he hauled them toward the bank he felt a heavy weight. He thought he had caught a big fish, and he was very pleased. But a moment later he saw that he had no fish in his nets at all, only the carcass of an ass, and he was bitterly disappointed.

Annoyed at such a poor catch, he mended his nets, which the dead ass had torn in several places, and cast them a second time. As he pulled them in, he again felt a heavy weight and thought they must be full of fish. But all he found was a big basket of rubbish. He was very irritated.
“O Fortune,” he cried, “don’t play games with me, a poor fisherman who can hardly feed his family!”
With that he threw the rubbish away, and after he had rinsed the dirt from his nets, he cast them for the third time. But all he pulled up was stones, shells and mud. He was close to despair.

Then he cast his nets for the fourth time. Thinking he had a fish this time, he dragged them in with great effort. There was no fish, but he found a yellow pot that felt heavy, as if it were full of something, and he saw that it was closed and sealed with lead, stamped with the mark of a seal. He was delighted. “I’ll sell it to the metal-founder,” he said, “and with the money I get for it, I’ll buy a measure of wheat.”

He turned the jar over and looked at it from every side; he shook it to hear whether anything rattled. He heard nothing, and from the seal and the lid he judged that there must be something valuable inside. To find out, he took his knife and, with some effort, opened it. He tipped it upside down, but nothing came out, which surprised him very much. He set it down in front of him, and while he was studying it closely, a thick smoke poured out, so thick that he had to step back a pace or two. The smoke rose up to the clouds and spread over the sea and the shore, forming a heavy mist, which amazed the fisherman. When all the smoke was out of the jar, it drew itself together into a dense mass, and in it appeared a genie twice as big as the biggest giant. At the sight of such a terrible monster, the fisherman wanted to run, but he was shaking so hard with fear that he could not take a single step.
“Great king of the genies,” cried the monster, “I will never disobey you again!”
When he heard this, the fisherman took heart.
“What are you saying, great genie? Tell me your story, and how you came to be shut up in that vase.”
At this the genie gave the fisherman a proud, hard look. “Speak to me more politely,” he said, “before I kill you.”
“Alas! Why would you kill me?” cried the fisherman. “I have just set you free; have you forgotten that already?”
“No,” answered the genie; “but that will not stop me from killing you; and the only favor I will grant you is to choose how you want to die.”
“But what have I done to you?” asked the fisherman.
“I can’t treat you any differently,” said the genie, “and if you want to know why, listen to my story.

“I rebelled against the king of the genies. To punish me, he locked me inside this copper vase and set his seal on the lead cover, which is enough magic to keep me from getting out. Then he had the vase thrown into the sea. During the first hundred years of my captivity I swore that if anyone freed me before a century had passed, I would make him rich even after his death. But that century went by, and no one freed me. In the second century I swore that I would give all the treasures in the world to my rescuer; but he never came.

“In the third century I promised to make him a king, to stay always at his side, and to grant him three wishes every day; but that century slipped away like the other two, and I stayed in the same plight. At last I grew furious at being a prisoner for so long, and I swore that if anyone released me, I would kill him on the spot, and only let him choose the manner of his death. So you see, since you have freed me today, choose how you will die.”
The fisherman was in misery. “How unlucky I am to have freed you! I beg you, spare my life.”
“I have told you,” said the genie, “that it is impossible. Choose quickly; you are wasting time.”
The fisherman started to think up a trick.
“Since I must die,” he said, “then before I choose how, I ask you, on your honor, to tell me: were you really inside that vase?”
“Yes, I was,” answered the genie.
“I truly can’t believe it,” said the fisherman. “That vase wouldn’t hold even one of your feet, so how could your whole body fit inside? I won’t believe it unless I see you do it.”

Then the genie began to turn himself into smoke, which spread over the sea and the shore as before, and then, gathering itself together, started to flow back into the vase, slowly and steadily, until nothing was left outside. Then a voice came out of the vase and said to the fisherman, “Well, doubting fisherman, here I am in the vase; do you believe me now?”
Instead of answering, the fisherman picked up the lead lid and clamped it quickly down on the vase.

“Now, O genie,” he cried, “it’s your turn to beg my pardon and choose what death you will die! No, it will be better if I throw you back into the sea you came from, and I will build a house on the shore to warn any fishermen who come to cast their nets here against fishing up a wicked genie like you, who swears to kill the man that frees him.”
At these words the genie struggled with all his might to get out, but he could not, because of the magic of the lid.
Then he tried to escape by cunning.
“If you take off the cover,” he said, “I will reward you.”
“No,” answered the fisherman, “if I trust myself to you, I’m afraid you will treat me the way a certain Greek king treated the physician Douban. Listen, and I will tell you.”

chapters.title: The Story of the Greek King and the Physician Douban
paragraphs: In the land of Zouman, in Persia, there lived a Greek king. This king was a leper, and none of his doctors had been able to cure him, until a very skilled physician arrived at his court.
This man was learned in every language, and knew a great deal about herbs and medicines.

As soon as he heard of the king’s illness, he put on his finest robe and came before the king. “Sire,” he said, “I know that no physician has been able to cure Your Majesty, but if you follow my instructions, I promise to heal you without any medicine or ointment.”
The king listened to his proposal.
“If you are clever enough to do this,” he said, “I promise to make you and your descendants rich forever.”
The physician went home and made a polo club, hollowing out the handle and filling it with the drug he meant to use. Then he made a ball, and the next day he took both to the king.

He told the king he wanted him to play polo. So the king mounted his horse and rode out to the field where he played. There the physician came up to him with the club he had made and said, “Take this, sire, and strike the ball until you feel your hand and your whole body glowing. When your hand warms the remedy in the handle of the club, it will spread through your whole body. Then go back to your palace, bathe, and go to sleep, and when you wake tomorrow morning you will be cured.”

The king took the club and spurred his horse after the ball he had thrown. He hit it, and then the courtiers playing with him hit it back. When he was very hot, he stopped playing, returned to the palace, went into the bath, and did everything the physician had told him. The next day when he got up, he found, to his great joy and amazement, that he was completely cured. When he came into his audience chamber, the courtiers, who were eager to see whether the wonderful cure had worked, were overjoyed.
The physician Douban came into the hall and bowed low to the ground. The king saw him, called him over, made him sit at his side, and showed him every sign of honor.
That evening he gave him a long, rich robe of state and presented him with two thousand sequins. The next day he went on heaping favors on him.
Now the king had a grand vizier who was greedy and envious and a thoroughly bad man. He became bitterly jealous of the physician and made up his mind to destroy him.
To do this, he asked to speak to the king in private, saying that he had something very important to tell him.
“What is it?” asked the king.

“Sire,” answered the grand vizier, “it is very dangerous for a monarch to trust a man whose loyalty has not been tested. You don’t know that this physician isn’t a traitor who has come here to murder you.”

“I am sure,” said the king, “that this man is the most loyal and virtuous of men. If he wanted to take my life, why would he have cured me? Stop speaking against him. I see what this is: you are jealous of him; but don’t think you can turn me against him. I remember well what a vizier said to King Sindbad, his master, to keep him from putting his son the prince to death.”
What the Greek king said made the vizier curious, and he said to him, “Sire, I beg Your Majesty to be so kind as to tell me what the vizier said to King Sindbad.”
“This vizier,” the king replied, “told King Sindbad that one should not believe everything a mother-in-law says, and he told him this story.”

chapters.title: The Story of the Husband and the Parrot
paragraphs: There was once a good man with a lovely wife, whom he adored and avoided leaving whenever he could. Pressing business called him away one day, and he went to a market where birds of every kind are sold and bought himself a parrot. It spoke well, but its real gift was that it could repeat everything that had happened in its presence. He carried it home in a cage and asked his wife to keep it in her room and look after it carefully while he was gone. Then he set off. When he returned, he asked the parrot what had gone on in his absence, and what the parrot told him led him to scold his wife.
She guessed that one of her slaves had been carrying tales about her, but they told her the parrot was to blame, and she resolved to get even with it.

The next time her husband went away for a day, she ordered one slave to turn a hand-mill beneath the bird’s cage, another to pour water down from above the cage, and a third to take a mirror and swing it in front of the bird’s eyes, from left to right, by the light of a candle. The slaves did this for part of the night, and did it very well.

When the husband came home the following day, he asked the parrot what it had witnessed. “My good master,” said the bird, “the lightning, the thunder and the rain disturbed me so much all night, and I cannot tell you how much I suffered.”

The husband knew that it had neither rained nor thundered in the night, so he was convinced the parrot was lying. He took it out of the cage and hurled it so hard against the ground that he killed it. But he was sorry afterwards, because he found out that the parrot had told the truth.

“When the Greek king,” the fisherman said to the genie, “had finished the story of the parrot, he said to the vizier, ‘So, vizier, I will not listen to you, and I will look after the physician, in case I regret it the way the husband did after he had killed the parrot.’ But the vizier was determined. ‘Sire,’ he replied, ‘the death of the parrot was nothing. But when a king’s life is at stake, it is better to sacrifice the innocent than to spare the guilty. And this is no uncertain matter. The physician Douban wants to murder you. My loyalty urges me to tell Your Majesty. If I am wrong, I deserve to be punished as a vizier once was.’ ‘What had the vizier done,’ asked the Greek king, ‘to deserve the punishment?’ ‘I will tell Your Majesty, if you will do me the honor of listening,’ answered the vizier.”

chapters.title: The Story of the Vizier Who Was Punished
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a king whose son loved to hunt. The king often let him ride out, but he had ordered his grand vizier to go along every time and never let the prince out of his sight. One day the huntsman flushed a stag, and the prince, assuming the vizier was right behind him, went after it and rode so hard that he ended up alone. He pulled up, and since the stag was gone, he turned back to find the vizier, who had not been attentive enough to keep up. But the prince had lost his way. While he was searching for the road, he noticed a beautiful woman at the roadside, weeping bitterly. He reined in his horse and asked who she was, what she was doing in such a place, and whether she needed help. “I am the daughter of an Indian king,” she replied. “I was riding in the countryside when I fell asleep and slipped from my horse. It bolted, and I have no idea where it has gone.”

The young prince felt sorry for her and offered her a seat behind him on his horse, and she accepted. When they came to a ruined building, the woman climbed down and went inside. The prince got down as well and followed her. To his great shock, he heard her call to someone within, “Rejoice, my children! I have brought you a nice plump young man.” Other voices answered, “Where is he, mamma? Let us eat him right now, we are so hungry!”

The prince saw at once the peril he was in. He understood now that the woman who called herself an Indian king’s daughter was an ogress, one of those creatures that live in lonely places and use a thousand tricks to catch travelers and devour them. Terrified, he threw himself onto his horse. Just then the false princess came out, and seeing that her prey had escaped her, she said, “Don’t be afraid. What do you want?”
“I am lost,” he said, “and I am trying to find the road.”
“Keep going straight,” said the ogress, “and you will come to it.”

The prince could scarcely believe what he had heard, and he galloped away as fast as he could. He found the road and reached his father’s house safe and unharmed, and there he told the king of the danger he had faced because of the grand vizier’s negligence. The king flew into a rage and had the vizier strangled on the spot.

“Sire,” the vizier went on, speaking to the Greek king, “let us come back to the physician Douban. If you are not careful, you will regret trusting him. Who can say that this remedy that cured you will not turn out, in time, to do you harm?”
The Greek king was a weak man by nature. He did not see the vizier’s evil purpose, and he lacked the strength to stand by his first decision.
“Very well, vizier,” he said, “you are right. Perhaps he did come to take my life. He could do it with nothing more than the scent of one of his drugs. I must think what to do.”
“Sire,” said the vizier, “the surest way to protect your life is to summon him now, and have his head cut off the moment he arrives.”
“Yes,” the king answered, “I truly think that is the best course.”
He told one of his ministers to bring the physician, and the physician came at once.
“I have sent for you,” said the king, “so that I can be rid of you by taking your life.”
The physician was utterly astonished to hear that he was to die.
“Your majesty, what crimes have I committed?”
“I have learned,” the king answered, “that you are a spy and mean to kill me. But I will strike first, and kill you. Strike!” he ordered an executioner standing nearby. “Free me from this assassin.”
At this cruel command the physician fell to his knees. “Spare my life,” he cried, “and yours will be spared.”

Here the fisherman broke off to say to the genie, “You see, what happened between the Greek king and the physician has just happened between the two of us. The Greek king,” he continued, “showed him no mercy, and the executioner blindfolded him.”
Everyone in the room begged for the physician’s life, but it was no use.

Bound and kneeling, the physician said to the king, “At least give me time to put my affairs in order and leave my books to people who will make good use of them. There is one I would like to give to your majesty. It is very precious, and should be kept safely in your treasury. It holds many curious things, and the chief of them is this: after my head has been cut off, if your majesty will turn to the sixth leaf and read the third line of the left-hand page, my head will answer any question you care to put to it.”

The king, eager to see so wonderful a thing, postponed the execution until the next day and sent the physician home under heavy guard. There the physician settled his affairs, and the next day a great crowd filled the hall to watch him die and to see what would happen afterward. The physician came to the foot of the throne carrying a large book. He also brought a basin, over which he spread the book’s cover, and offering it to the king, he said, “Sire, take this book. When my head has been cut off, have it set in the basin on the cover of this book. As soon as it is there, the blood will stop flowing. Then open the book, and my head will answer your questions. But sire, I beg you for mercy, because I am innocent.”
“Your pleading is wasted, and even if it were only to hear your head speak after you are dead, you will die.”
With that he took the book from the physician’s hands and told the executioner to do his work.

The head was cut off so skillfully that it dropped right into the basin, and the blood stopped flowing at once. Then, to the king’s great amazement, the eyes opened, and the head said, “Your majesty, open the book.” The king did, and finding that the first leaf was stuck to the second, he put his finger in his mouth to wet it so that it would turn more easily. He did the same for each page until he reached the sixth, and seeing no writing on it, he said, “Physician, there is nothing written here.”

“Turn a few more pages,” the head replied. The king kept turning, wetting his finger in his mouth each time, until the poison that coated every page took hold. His sight failed, and he collapsed at the foot of his throne.
When the physician’s head saw that the poison had done its work and that the king had only a few minutes left, it cried, “Tyrant, see how cruelty and injustice are punished.”
No sooner had it spoken than the king died, and the head lost what little life it had left.
So ends the story of the Greek king, and now we go back to the fisherman and the genie.
“If the Greek king had spared the physician,” said the fisherman, “he would not have died like that. The same goes for you. Now I am going to throw you into the sea.”
“My friend,” said the genie, “don’t do anything so cruel. Do not treat me the way Imma treated Ateca.”
“What did Imma do to Ateca?” the fisherman asked.
“Do you think I can tell you that while I am shut up in here?” replied the genie. “Let me out, and I will make you rich.”
The hope of never being poor again made the fisherman yield.
“If you give me your promise that you will do this, I will take off the lid. I do not think you would dare to go back on your word.”

The genie gave his promise, and the fisherman lifted the lid. The genie rose out in a cloud of smoke, and once he had taken his true shape again, the first thing he did was kick the jar into the sea. This frightened the fisherman, but the genie laughed and said, “Don’t be afraid. I only did that to scare you, and to show you that I mean to keep my word. Take your nets and follow me.”

He set off walking in front, and the fisherman followed him with some misgivings. They passed the town, climbed up a mountain, and then went down into a great plain, where a large lake lay between four hills.
When they reached the lake, the genie said to the fisherman, “Cast your nets and catch some fish.”

The fisherman did as he was told, expecting a good catch, since he could see plenty of fish. How amazed he was to find that there were four entirely different kinds, some white, some red, some blue and some yellow. He caught four, one of each color. He had never seen any like them, so he admired them greatly, and he was delighted to think how much money they would bring.

“Take these fish to the Sultan, and he will pay you more for them than you have ever had in your life. You may come and fish in this lake every day, but take care to cast your nets only once a day, or something bad will happen to you. If you follow my advice closely, you will be glad of it.”
As he said this, he stamped his foot on the ground, and it opened. He vanished into it, and it closed again at once.
The fisherman made up his mind to follow the genie’s orders exactly. He cast his nets only once, then headed into town to sell the fish at the palace.

When the Sultan saw the fish, he was greatly amazed. He looked at them one by one, and when he had admired them long enough, he said to his first vizier, “Take these fish and give them to the skilled cook that the Emperor of the Greeks sent me. I imagine they taste as good as they look.”
The vizier carried them to the cook himself, saying, “Here are four fish that were brought to the Sultan. He wants you to cook them.”

Then he returned to the Sultan, who told him to give the fisherman four hundred gold pieces. The fisherman had never held so much money at one time and could hardly believe his luck. He immediately saw to his family’s needs and put the money to good use.

But now we must go back to the kitchen, where we will find great confusion. When the cook had cleaned the fish, she put them in a pan with oil to fry. When she judged them done on one side, she turned them over. But hardly had she done so when the kitchen wall opened and a beautiful young woman stepped out. She wore Egyptian dress of flowered satin, with earrings, a necklace of white pearls, and gold bracelets set with rubies, and in her hand she held a wand of myrtle.

She walked up to the pan while the cook, astonished, stood frozen at the sight of her. She tapped one of the fish with her wand and said, “Fish, fish, are you doing your duty?” The fish gave no answer. She asked again, and this time they all lifted their heads together and replied, very clearly, “Yes, yes. If you count, we count. If you pay what you owe, so do we. If you run, we win, and we are content.”
When they had spoken, the young woman overturned the pan and went back into the opening in the wall, which closed at once and looked exactly as it had before.
Once the cook got over her fright, she picked the fallen fish out of the ashes. They were burned black as coal, no use to serve the Sultan, and she started to weep.
“Oh no! What will I tell the Sultan? He will be so angry with me, and I know he won’t believe me!”

While she was crying, the grand vizier came in and asked whether the fish were ready. She told him everything that had happened, and he was very surprised. He sent for the fisherman at once, and when the man arrived he said, “Fisherman, bring me four more fish like the ones you brought before, because something has happened to them and they can’t be served to the Sultan.”
The fisherman did not mention what the genie had told him. He excused himself from bringing them that day because of the long distance, and promised to bring them the next day.
That night he went to the lake and cast his nets, and when he pulled them in he found four fish like the others, each a different color.
He went straight back and delivered them to the grand vizier, as he had promised.

The vizier then took them to the kitchen and shut himself in with the cook, who began to cook them just as she had cooked the other four the day before. When she was about to turn them over, the wall opened and the young woman appeared. She spoke the same words to the fish, received the same answer, then overturned the pan and disappeared.
The grand vizier was filled with amazement. “I will tell the Sultan everything that has happened,” he said, and he did.

The Sultan was astounded and wanted to witness this marvel himself. He sent for the fisherman and asked him to get four more fish. The fisherman asked for three days, which were granted, and then he cast his nets in the lake and once more caught four fish of different colors. The Sultan was delighted to have them and again gave him four hundred gold pieces.
As soon as the Sultan had the fish, he had them taken to his own room, together with everything needed to cook them.

Then he shut himself in with the grand vizier, who began to prepare and cook them. When they were done on one side, he turned them over. Then the wall of the room opened, but instead of the young woman, a black slave came out. He was enormously tall and carried a large green staff, with which he touched the fish, saying in a terrible voice, “Fish, fish, are you doing your duty?” At these words the fish raised their heads and replied, “Yes, yes. If you count, we count. If you pay what you owe, so do we. If you run, we win, and we are content.”
The black slave overturned the pan in the middle of the room, and the fish were reduced to cinders. Then, with a proud stride, he went back into the wall, and it closed behind him.
“After seeing that,” said the Sultan, “I cannot rest. These fish point to some mystery that I must get to the bottom of.”
He sent for the fisherman. “Fisherman,” he said, “the fish you brought us have disturbed me. Where did you get them?”
“Sire,” he answered, “I got them from a lake in the middle of four hills, beyond those mountains over there.”
“Do you know this lake?” the Sultan asked the grand vizier.
“No,” said the vizier. “I have hunted around that mountain many times, but I have never heard of it.”
The fisherman said it was only three hours away, so the Sultan ordered his entire court to mount and ride there, with the fisherman leading the way.

They climbed the mountain, and on the far side they saw the lake just as the fisherman had described it. The water was so clear that they could see the four kinds of fish swimming in it. They watched them for a while, and then the Sultan ordered a camp to be set up at the water’s edge.

That night the Sultan summoned his vizier. “I’ve made up my mind to get to the bottom of this mystery,” he said. “I’m going out alone. You stay here in my tent, and when my ministers come tomorrow, tell them I’m unwell and can’t see them. Keep doing that every day until I come back.”

The grand vizier did his best to talk the Sultan out of it, but it was no use. The Sultan took off his robe of state and buckled on his sword, and once he saw that the camp was quiet, he slipped away alone.

He climbed one of the hills and crossed the wide plain beyond it, and at sunrise he saw a huge building far ahead of him. As he drew closer, he could see it was a magnificent palace of polished black marble, plated with steel as smooth as a mirror.
The gate was standing half open. He knocked, and when nobody came, he walked in. He crossed a grand courtyard and still met no one, though he called out several times.

He passed through great halls with silk carpets, with couches and sofas upholstered in tapestry from Mecca, and with hangings of the finest Indian fabrics, woven with gold and silver. Then he came into a splendid chamber with a fountain held up by golden lions. The water that streamed from the lions’ mouths turned into diamonds and pearls, and the jets leapt up until they nearly touched the exquisitely painted dome. Magnificent gardens, small lakes and woods surrounded the palace on three sides. Birds sang in the trees, which were covered with nets so that the birds could never fly away.
Still the Sultan saw nobody, until he heard a mournful cry and a voice saying, “If only I could die! I am too wretched to want to go on living!”

The Sultan looked around to find who was lamenting his fate like this. At last he saw a handsome young man in rich clothes, seated on a throne set a little above the floor. His face was full of sorrow.
The Sultan went up to him and bowed. The young man lowered his head deeply but did not stand.
“Sire,” he said to the Sultan, “I can’t get up and show you the respect I know your rank deserves.”
“Sir,” the Sultan answered, “I’m sure you have good reason. I heard your cry of anguish, and I have come to offer you my help. Whose palace is this, and why is it so empty?”
Instead of replying, the young man raised his robe and showed the Sultan that from the waist down he was a block of black marble.
The Sultan was appalled and asked the young man to tell him what had happened.
“I will gladly tell you my sad story,” said the young man.

chapters.title: The Story of the Young King of the Black Isles
paragraphs: Sire, you should know that my father was Mahmoud, king of this country, the Black Isles. It is called that because of the four small mountains that were once islands, and where the great lake now lies there used to be the capital. My story will explain how all this came about.
My father died at the age of sixty-six, and I took his throne. I married my cousin, whom I loved dearly, and I believed she loved me in return.

But one afternoon, as I lay half asleep while two of her maids fanned me, I heard one of them say to the other, “What a shame that our mistress doesn’t love our master anymore! I think she’d kill him if she could, since she’s an enchantress.”

I watched her and soon saw that the maids were right. Then I gave one of her favorite slaves a mortal wound for a terrible crime, and she asked me to let her build a palace in the garden, where she mourned and wept for him for two years.

In the end I begged her to stop grieving. He could neither speak nor move, I told her, and only her enchantments kept him alive. She turned on me in fury and spoke some magic words over me, and in that instant I became what you see now: half man, half marble.

Then this wicked enchantress turned the capital, a populous and thriving city, into the lake and the barren plain you crossed. The fish of four colors in the lake are the different peoples who lived in the city, and the four hills are the four islands that give my kingdom its name. She told me all this just to add to my misery. And that is not all. Every day she comes and lashes me with a whip of buffalo hide.
When the young king had finished his sad story, he burst into tears again, and the Sultan was deeply moved.
“Tell me,” the Sultan cried, “where is this wicked woman, and where is the wretched creature she loves, the one she barely keeps alive?”
“I don’t know where she lives,” the unhappy prince answered, “but every day at sunrise, after she has beaten me, she goes to see whether the slave can speak to her yet.”
“Unfortunate king,” said the Sultan, “I will do whatever I can to avenge you.”

He and the young king talked over the best way to do it, and they agreed to carry out their plan the following day. The Sultan then rested, and the young king let himself hope for freedom. The next day the Sultan rose and went to the palace in the garden where the black slave lay. He drew his sword and finished off the little life left in him, then threw the body down a well. After that he lay down on the couch where the slave had been and waited for the enchantress.
She went first to the young king and gave him a hundred lashes.
Then she came to the room where she believed her wounded slave was lying, though it was the Sultan on the couch.
She approached the couch and said, “Are you feeling better today, my dear slave? Say just one word to me.”
“How could I feel better,” the Sultan answered, mimicking the speech of the Ethiopians, “when your husband’s cries and groans never let me sleep?”
“What joy to hear you speak!” the queen replied. “Do you want him to have his own shape back?”
“Yes,” said the Sultan. “Hurry and set him free, so I don’t have to hear his cries any longer.”

The queen went out at once, took a cup of water, and spoke some words over it that made it boil as though it stood on a fire. Then she threw it over the prince, who immediately took back his own form. He was overjoyed, but the enchantress said, “Get away from here and never return, or I’ll kill you.”
So he hid, to watch how the Sultan’s plan would end.
Back at the Palace of Tears, the enchantress announced, “It is done, just as you wanted.”

“What you have done,” said the Sultan, “is not enough to heal me. Every night at midnight, all the people you turned into fish raise their heads out of the lake and cry out for vengeance. Go quickly and give them back their proper shapes.”
The enchantress rushed off and spoke some words over the lake.

The fish turned into men, women and children, and the houses and shops filled up again. The Sultan’s attendants, who had camped beside the lake, were astounded to find themselves in the middle of a large and beautiful city.
As soon as she had broken the spell on the city, the queen returned to the palace.
“Are you completely well now?” she asked.
“Come closer,” said the Sultan. “Closer still.”
She did as he said. Then he leapt up and, with a single stroke of his sword, cut her in half.
Then he went to find the prince.
“Rejoice,” he said. “Your cruel enemy is dead.”
The prince thanked him over and over.
“And now,” said the Sultan, “I will go back to my capital, which I’m glad to find is so close to yours.”
“So close to mine!” said the King of the Black Isles.
“Don’t you know it is a full year’s journey from here? You got here in a few hours only because the land was enchanted. But I will go with you on your way.”
“I would be very glad of your company,” said the Sultan, “and since I have no children, I will make you my heir.”
Together the Sultan and the prince started out, the Sultan carrying costly presents given him by the King of the Black Isles.
The day after he reached his capital, the Sultan called his court together and told them everything that had happened to him, and that he meant to adopt the young king as his heir.
Then he gave every man a present suited to his rank.
As for the fisherman, who had been the first cause of the young prince’s rescue, the Sultan gave him a large sum of money and made him and his family prosperous for the rest of their lives.

chapters.title: The Story of the Three Calenders, Sons of Kings, and of Five Ladies of Baghdad
paragraphs: In the reign of Caliph Haroun-al-Raschid, there lived in Baghdad a porter who, humble as his work was, had a sharp mind and good sense. One morning he was sitting in his usual spot with his basket in front of him, waiting for someone to hire him, when a tall young woman in a long muslin veil walked up and said, “Pick up your basket and come with me.” Delighted with her looks and her voice, the porter jumped up at once, hoisted his basket onto his head and followed her, telling himself as he went, “What a happy day! What a lucky meeting!”

Soon the lady stopped at a closed door and knocked. An old man with a long white beard opened it, and without a word she held out some money. The old man seemed to know what she wanted. He disappeared into the house and came back with a large jar of wine, which the porter set in his basket. Then the lady motioned for him to follow, and off they went.

Her next stop was a fruit and flower shop, where she bought a great quantity of apples, apricots, peaches and other fruit, together with lilies, jasmine and all kinds of fragrant plants. From there she went to a butcher, a grocer and a poulterer, until the porter finally cried out in despair, “My good lady, if you’d only told me you meant to buy enough food to supply a town, I’d have brought a horse, or better, a camel.” The lady laughed and told him she wasn’t finished. She picked out a range of perfumes and spices at a druggist’s shop, and then stopped in front of a magnificent palace, where she knocked softly at the door. The porteress who opened it was so beautiful that the man was dazzled, and all the more astonished because he could plainly see she was no slave. The lady who had brought him stood watching him with amusement, until the porteress said, “Why don’t you come in, sister? This poor man is so weighed down he’s about to drop.”

When they were both inside, the door was bolted, and the three of them went into a large courtyard ringed by an open-work gallery. At one end was a platform, and on the platform stood an amber throne held up by four ebony columns and decorated with pearls and diamonds. In the middle of the courtyard was a marble basin, filled with water that flowed from the mouth of a golden lion.

The porter looked around, taking in and admiring everything. But what caught his attention most was a third lady seated on the throne, who was even more beautiful than the other two. From the respect the others showed her, he guessed she was the eldest, and he was right. Her name was Zobeida, the porteress was called Sadie, and the housekeeper was Amina. At a word from Zobeida, Sadie and Amina took the basket from the porter, who was glad to be rid of the weight, and when it was emptied they paid him generously for his trouble. But instead of picking up his basket and leaving, the man hung about, until Zobeida asked what he was waiting for and whether he expected more money. “Oh, madam,” he answered, “you’ve already given me too much, and I’m afraid I was rude not to leave straight away. But if you’ll forgive me for saying so, I was struck dumb at finding such beautiful ladies on their own. A group of women without men, after all, is as dull as a group of men without women.” And after telling a few stories to prove his point, he ended by begging them to let him stay and make a fourth at their dinner.

The ladies found the man’s confident talk rather amusing, and after some discussion they agreed to let him stay, since his company might prove entertaining. “But listen, my friend,” said Zobeida. “We’ll grant your request only on condition that you behave with perfect politeness, and that you keep secret the way we live, which you have found out by chance.” Then they all sat down at the table, which Amina had laid with the dishes she had bought.

After the first few mouthfuls, Amina poured some wine into a golden cup. She drank first, as the Arab custom requires, and then filled it for her sisters. When it was the porter’s turn, he kissed Amina’s hand and sang a song he made up on the spot in praise of the wine. The three ladies liked the song and then sang some themselves, so the meal was a merry one and went on much longer than usual.
At last, seeing that the sun was about to set, Sadie said to the porter, “Get up and go. It’s time for us to part.”

“Oh, madam,” he replied, “how can you expect me to leave you in the state I’m in? Between the wine I’ve drunk and the joy of seeing you, I’d never find my way home. Let me stay here until morning, and when I’ve come to my senses I’ll go whenever you like.”
“Let him stay,” said Amina, who had already shown herself his friend. “It’s only fair, since he has given us so much amusement.”

“If you want it, sister,” Zobeida replied, “but if he stays, I must set a new condition. Porter,” she went on, turning to him, “if you stay, you must promise to ask no questions about anything you see. If you do, you may hear something you won’t like.”

With that settled, Amina brought in supper and lit the hall with a number of sweet-smelling candles. They sat down at the table again and began, with fresh appetite, to eat, drink, sing and recite verses. They were all enjoying themselves enormously when they heard a knock at the outer door, and Sadie got up to answer it. She soon came back to report that three Calenders, all blind in the right eye and all with their heads, faces and eyebrows shaved clean, were begging to be let in, since they had just arrived in Baghdad and night had already fallen. “They seem to have pleasant manners,” she added, “but you can’t imagine how funny they look. I’m sure their company would amuse us.”

Zobeida and Amina were reluctant to admit the newcomers, and Sadie knew why they hesitated. But she pressed her case so strongly that Zobeida finally had to give in. “Bring them in, then,” she said, “but make them understand that they must not comment on matters that are none of their business, and be sure they read the inscription over the door.” For on the door were written, in letters of gold, the words: “Whoever meddles in affairs that are none of his business will hear truths that will not please him.”

The three Calenders came in and bowed low, then thanked the ladies for their kindness and welcome. The ladies answered with warm greetings, and everyone was about to sit down when the Calenders noticed the porter. His clothes were not so very different from their own, except that he still had all the hair nature had given him. “That one,” said one of them, “looks like a fellow Arab of ours who has rebelled against our ruler.”

The porter was half asleep from the wine he had drunk, but he heard this. Without even stirring, he snapped at the Calender, “Sit down and mind your own business. Didn’t you read the inscription over the door? Not everyone has to live the same way.”

“Don’t be so angry, my good man,” the Calender replied. “We would be very sorry to offend you.” With that the quarrel was settled, and supper began in earnest. When the Calenders had eaten their fill, they offered to play for their hostesses if the house had any instruments. The ladies loved the idea. Sadie went to look and came back a few moments later carrying two kinds of flute and a tambourine. Each Calender took the one he liked best and began a well-known tune, while the ladies sang the words. The words were as merry and lively as could be, and every so often the singers had to stop and give way to the laughter that nearly choked them. In the middle of all this noise, there was a knock at the door.

Earlier that evening the Caliph had slipped out of his palace in secret, with his grand vizier Giafar and Mesrour, the chief of the eunuchs. All three were dressed as merchants. As they walked down the street, the Caliph had been drawn by the sound of instruments and laughter, and he had told his vizier to go and knock at the door of the house, because he wanted to go in. The vizier answered that the ladies who lived there seemed to be entertaining friends, and that his master would do well not to intrude. But the Caliph had made up his mind to see for himself, and he insisted on being obeyed.

Sadie answered the knock, holding a taper. The vizier was struck by her beauty and bowed low before her. “Madam,” he said respectfully, “we are three merchants who have just arrived from Moussoul. Because of a mishap that befell us tonight, we reached our inn only to find the doors shut against us until morning. We didn’t know what to do, so we wandered the streets until we happened to pass your house. Seeing lights and hearing voices, we decided to ask you for shelter until dawn. If you grant us this favor, then with your permission we will do everything we can to help you pass the time pleasantly.”

Sadie told the merchant she must first consult her sisters. After talking it over with them, she came back and told him that he and his two friends were welcome to join the party. They came in and bowed politely to the ladies and their guests. Then Zobeida, as the mistress of the house, stepped forward and said gravely, “You are welcome here, but I hope you will let me ask one thing of you. Have as many eyes as you like, but no tongues. Ask no questions about anything you see, however strange it may seem to you.”

“Madam,” the vizier answered, “you will be obeyed. We have plenty here to please and interest us, without troubling ourselves over matters that are none of our concern.” Then they all sat down and drank to the health of the new arrivals.

While Giafar the vizier chatted with the ladies, the Caliph kept wondering who they could be, and why each of the three Calenders had lost his right eye. He was burning to ask the reason behind it all, but Zobeida’s request kept him silent. So he made himself shake it off and join in the conversation, which was very lively; they were discussing the many different kinds of pleasure there are in the world. After a while the Calenders got up and performed some curious dances, which delighted the rest of the company.

When they had finished, Zobeida rose from her seat and took Amina by the hand. “Sister,” she said, “our friends will forgive us if we seem to forget they are here and do our nightly task.” Amina understood what her sister meant. She gathered up the dishes, glasses and musical instruments and carried them away, while Sadie swept the hall and put everything in order. When that was done, Sadie asked the Calenders to sit on a sofa on one side of the room, and the Caliph and his companions to sit opposite them. She asked the porter to come and help her and her sister.

A little later Amina came in carrying a seat, which she set down in the middle of the empty floor. Then she went to the door of a closet and signed to the porter to follow her. He did, and soon came back leading two black dogs on a chain, which he brought to the center of the hall. Zobeida rose from her place between the Calenders and the Caliph and walked slowly over to where the porter stood with the dogs. “We must do our duty,” she said with a deep sigh, pushing back her sleeves. She took a whip from Sadie and told the man, “Take one of those dogs to my sister Amina, and give me the other.”

The porter did as he was told, but as he led the dog to Zobeida it let out piercing howls and looked up at her with pleading eyes. Zobeida paid no attention. She whipped the dog until she was out of breath. Then she took the chain from the porter and lifted the dog onto its hind legs, and the two looked sorrowfully into each other’s eyes until tears began to fall from both. Zobeida took out her handkerchief and gently wiped the dog’s eyes, then kissed it. Putting the chain back into the porter’s hand, she said, “Take it back to the closet and bring me the other.”

The same ritual was repeated with the second dog, and the whole company watched in astonishment. The Caliph in particular could barely hold himself in, and he made signs to the vizier to ask what it all meant. But the vizier pretended not to notice and turned his head away.

Zobeida stayed in the middle of the room for some time, until Sadie went up to her and begged her to sit down, since Sadie too had a part to play. At this, Amina took a lute from a case of yellow satin and handed it to Sadie, who sang several songs to its music. When she grew tired, she said to Amina, “Sister, I can do no more. Please come and take my place.”

Amina struck a few chords and then burst into song. She sang with such passion that she was overcome and sank, gasping, onto a pile of cushions, tearing open her dress to get some air. To everyone’s amazement, her neck was not smooth and white like her face. It was a mass of scars.
The Calenders and the Caliph looked at one another and whispered together, where Zobeida and Sadie, busy tending their fainting sister, could not hear.
“What does it all mean?” asked the Caliph.
“We know no more than you do,” said the Calender he had spoken to.
“What! You don’t belong to the house?”
“My lord,” all the Calenders answered together, “we came here for the first time only an hour before you.”

Then they turned to the porter to see whether he could explain the mystery, but he was no wiser than they were. At last the Caliph could hold back his curiosity no longer. He declared that he would force the ladies to explain their strange behavior. The vizier saw what would come of it. He begged the Caliph to remember the condition their hostesses had set, and added in a whisper that if his Highness would only wait until morning, he could use his power as Caliph to summon the ladies before him. But the Caliph was not used to being contradicted and rejected this advice. After a little more discussion they agreed that the porter should put the question. Just then Zobeida turned round and saw how excited they were. “What is the matter?” she said. “What are you all discussing so earnestly?”

“Madam,” the porter answered, “these gentlemen beg you to tell them why you first whip the dogs and then cry over them, and also how the fainting lady came to be covered with scars. They have asked me, Madam, to speak for them.”
“Is it true, gentlemen,” Zobeida asked, drawing herself up, “that you have told this man to put that question to me?”
“It is,” they all replied, except Giafar, who stayed silent.

“Is this,” Zobeida went on, growing angrier by the moment, “is this how you repay the hospitality I have shown you? Have you forgotten the one condition on which you were allowed into this house? Come quickly,” she added, clapping her hands three times. The words were hardly out of her mouth when seven black slaves, each armed with a sabre, burst in. They stood over the seven men, threw them to the ground, and got ready to cut off their heads at a sign from their mistress.

The seven culprits all thought their last hour had come, and the Caliph bitterly regretted not taking the vizier’s advice. But they resolved to die bravely, all except the porter. He asked Zobeida loudly why he should suffer for other people’s faults. He declared that none of this would have happened if not for the Calenders, who always brought bad luck. He ended by begging Zobeida not to confuse the innocent with the guilty, and to spare his life.

Angry as she was, there was something so comical in the porter’s groans that Zobeida could not help laughing. But she set him aside and spoke to the others again. “Answer me. Who are you? Unless you tell me the truth, you have not another moment to live. I can hardly believe you are men of any standing, whatever country you come from. If you were, you would have shown us more consideration.”

The Caliph was naturally impatient, and he suffered far more than the others at the thought that his life lay at the mercy of a lady he had rightly offended.
