But when he heard her question, he began to breathe more easily, convinced that she had only to learn his name and rank for all danger to vanish. So he whispered hurriedly to the vizier beside him, telling him to reveal their secret. The vizier was wiser than his master and wanted to keep the insult they had received from becoming public. He only answered, “After all, we have got no more than we deserved.”
Meanwhile Zobeida had turned to the three Calenders and asked whether they were brothers, since they were all blind.
“No, madam,” one of them replied, “we are no relations by blood at all, only brothers by the way we live.”
“And you,” she asked, speaking to another, “were you born blind in one eye?”

“No, madam,” he answered, “I lost my eye through a most astonishing adventure, the like of which has probably never happened to anyone. After that I shaved my head and eyebrows and put on the clothes you see me wearing now.”
Zobeida asked the other two Calenders the same thing, and both gave her the same reply.
“But,” added the third, “you may be interested to know, madam, that we are not men of low birth. All three of us are sons of kings, and kings the world holds in high esteem.”

At these words Zobeida’s anger cooled. She turned to her slaves and said, “You may give them a little more freedom, but do not leave the hall. Those who tell us their histories and their reasons for coming here will be allowed to leave unharmed. Those who refuse—” She paused. But the porter understood that all he had to do to be free of this terrible danger was tell his story, and he broke in at once.

“Madam, you already know how I came here, and what I have to say will take no time. Your sister found me this morning in the place where I always stand waiting to be hired. She told me to follow her to various shops, and when my basket was full we came back to this house. You were kind enough to let me stay, and I will be grateful for it forever. That is my story.”
He looked anxiously at Zobeida, who nodded and said, “You may go. And make sure we never meet again.”

“Oh, madam,” cried the porter, “let me stay a little longer. It isn’t fair that the others should have heard my story and I shouldn’t hear theirs.” Without waiting for permission he sat down at the end of the sofa where the ladies were sitting, while the rest crouched on the carpet and the slaves stood against the wall.
Then one of the Calenders turned to Zobeida, as the chief lady, and began his story.

chapters.title: The Story of the First Calender, Son of a King
paragraphs: Madam, to explain how I lost my right eye and came to wear the dress of a Calender, you must first know that I am a king’s son. My father’s only brother ruled the neighboring country. He had two children, a daughter and a son, both my own age.

As I grew up and was given more freedom, I visited my uncle’s court every year and usually stayed about two months. In this way my cousin and I grew very close and became deeply fond of each other. The last time I saw him, he seemed happier to see me than ever and held a great feast in my honor. When we had finished eating, he said to me, “Cousin, you would never guess what I have been doing since your last visit! Right after you left, I put a crowd of men to work on a building of my own design. It is finished now and ready to live in. I would like to show it to you, but first you must swear two things: to be loyal to me, and to keep my secret.”

Of course I never dreamed of refusing him anything, and I gave my promise without a moment’s hesitation. He told me to wait a moment and disappeared. He came back shortly with a richly dressed lady of great beauty. He did not tell me her name, so I thought it best not to ask. The three of us sat down at table and passed the time talking about all sorts of trivial things and drinking each other’s health. Suddenly the prince said to me, “Cousin, we have no time to lose. Please take this lady to a certain spot, where you will find a domed tomb, newly built. You can’t miss it. Go in, both of you, and wait for me. I won’t be long.”

I had given my word, so I got ready to do as I was told. I offered the lady my hand and escorted her by moonlight to the place the prince had described. We had barely arrived when he joined us himself, carrying a small vessel of water, a pickaxe, and a little bag of plaster.

Taking the pickaxe, he set about smashing the empty tomb-chest in the middle of the vault. He lifted the stones out one at a time and stacked them in a corner. Once the whole thing was torn down, he started digging into the ground, and under the spot where the chest had stood I saw a trap-door. He pulled it open, and I could make out the top of a spiral staircase. Then he turned to the lady and said, “Madam, this is the way down to the place I told you about.”

The lady said nothing. She went silently down the stairs, and the prince followed her. At the top, though, he stopped and looked back at me. “Cousin,” he said, “I have no words to thank you for your kindness. Farewell.”
“What are you saying?” I cried. “I don’t understand.”
“Never mind,” he answered. “Go back the way you came.”

He would say nothing more. Completely baffled, I went back to my room in the palace and lay down to sleep. When I woke and thought over what had happened, I decided I must have dreamed it, and I sent a servant to ask whether the prince was up and could see me. But when I heard that he had not slept at home, I was badly frightened and hurried to the cemetery. There, unluckily, the tombs all looked so much alike that I could not tell which one I wanted, though I searched for it four days.

All this while, you should know, the king my uncle was away on a hunting trip, and since nobody could say when he would return, I finally resolved to go home and left the ministers to make my excuses. I was desperate to tell them what had become of the prince, whose fate worried them terribly, but the oath I had sworn kept my mouth shut.

When I reached my father’s capital, I was amazed to see a large body of guards drawn up in front of the palace gate. The moment I walked in, they closed around me. I asked the officers in charge why they were acting so strangely, and to my horror they told me that the army had mutinied, killed the king my father and set the grand vizier on the throne. On his orders, they added, I was under arrest.

This rebel vizier had hated me since I was a boy. Once, while shooting at a bird with a bow, I had accidentally put out his eye. Naturally I had sent a servant straight away to offer him my regrets and apologies, and I had also gone to make them myself. None of it did any good. His hatred of me never faded, and he took every chance to show it. Now that he had me in his power, I knew he would show no mercy, and I was right. Wild with triumph and rage, he came to my prison and tore out my right eye. That is how I lost it.

Even that was not enough for my enemy. He had me shut inside a large chest and ordered his executioner to carry me to a deserted place, cut off my head and leave my body for the birds of prey. So the chest, with me in it, was loaded onto a horse, and the executioner and another man rode out into the countryside until they found a spot that suited their purpose. But their hearts were not as hard as they appeared, and my tears and pleading made them hesitate.

“Leave this kingdom at once,” the executioner finally said, “and never come back. If you do, you will lose your head, and so will we.” I thanked him from my heart, and I tried to comfort myself for my lost eye by thinking of the other disasters I had escaped.

After everything I had been through, and afraid that some enemy might recognize me, I could only move slowly and carefully. Usually I rested by day in some out-of-the-way place and walked as far as I could by night. At last I came to my uncle’s kingdom, where I was sure of his protection.

I found him deeply troubled over the disappearance of his son, who had, he told me, vanished without a trace. Yet his own grief did not stop him from sharing mine. We wept together, since the loss of one of us was a loss to the other, and then I made up my mind that it was my duty to break the solemn oath I had given the prince. So I told my uncle everything I knew without delay, and I noticed that even before I had finished, his sorrow seemed a little lighter.

“My dear nephew,” he said, “what you tell me gives me some hope. I knew my son was having a tomb built, and I think I can find the place. But since he wanted it kept secret, let us go alone and look for it ourselves.”

Then he told me to put on a disguise, and the two of us slipped out through a garden door that opened onto the cemetery. We soon reached the place where the prince had vanished, and we found the tomb I had searched for so fruitlessly before. We went in and found the trap-door over the staircase, but we could hardly lift it, because the prince had sealed it from underneath with the plaster he had brought with him.

My uncle went down first, and I followed. At the foot of the stairs we stepped into a kind of antechamber so thick with smoke that we could barely see. We pushed through it, though, into a large room that at first looked empty. It was brightly lit, and a moment later we noticed a sort of platform at one end. On it lay the bodies of the prince and a lady, both half-burned, as if they had been dragged from a fire before it could finish them off.
The horrible sight made me faint, but to my surprise, what showed in my uncle was not so much shock as anger.

“I knew,” he said, “that my son was deeply in love with this lady, whom he could never possibly marry. I tried to turn his thoughts elsewhere and put the loveliest princesses before him, but he cared for none of them. And now, as you see, a horrible death has joined them together in a tomb underground.” But even as he spoke, his anger melted into tears, and once more I wept with him.

When he had composed himself, he drew me close. “My dear nephew,” he said, putting his arms around me, “you have come to take his place, and I will do my best to forget that I ever had a son who could behave so wickedly.” Then he turned and climbed the stairs.

We got back to the palace without anyone having noticed we were gone. Shortly afterward, the crash of drums and cymbals and the blare of trumpets burst on our startled ears. At the same moment a thick cloud of dust on the horizon showed that a great army was approaching. My heart sank when I saw that its commander was the vizier who had overthrown my father and had now come to seize my uncle’s kingdom.

The capital was in no way ready to withstand a siege, and the city, seeing that resistance was pointless, threw open its gates at once. My uncle fought hard for his life but was soon overwhelmed. When he fell, I escaped through a secret passage and took shelter with an officer I knew I could trust.

Hounded by ill fortune and crushed with grief, I could see only one way to stay safe. I shaved off my beard and eyebrows and put on the clothes of a calender, which let me travel without being recognized. I kept away from towns until I reached the land of the famous and mighty Caliph, Haroun-al-Raschid, where I no longer had any reason to fear my enemies. My plan was to go to Baghdad and throw myself at the feet of His Highness, who I was certain would be moved by my sad story and would give me his help and protection too.

After a journey of some months, I finally arrived at the gates of this city. It was sunset, and I stopped for a while to look around and decide where to go. I was still weighing this up when this other calender came over and greeted me. “You seem to be a stranger, like me,” I said. He told me I was right, and before he could say more, the third calender joined us. He too had just arrived in Baghdad. We were brothers in misfortune, so we agreed to throw in our lot together and share whatever fate had in store for us.

By now it was late, and we had no idea where to spend the night. But our lucky star led us to this door, and we made bold to knock and ask for shelter. It was given to us at once, with the best grace in the world.
That, madam, is my story.
“I am satisfied,” answered Zobeida. “You may leave whenever you like.”
The calender, however, asked permission to stay and hear the stories of his two friends and of the three other people in the company, and this was granted.

chapters.title: The Story of the Second Calender, Son of a King
paragraphs: “Madam,” said the young man, turning to Zobeida, “if you want to know how I lost my right eye, I will have to tell you the story of my whole life.”

I was hardly more than a baby when the king my father, seeing how quick and clever I was for my age, began to think about my education. First I was taught to read and write, and then to learn the Koran, the foundation of our holy religion. To understand it better, I studied the finest commentators on its teaching with my tutors, and I memorised all the traditions about the Prophet that have been gathered from the lips of his companions. I also learned history, and I was schooled in poetry, verse-making, geography, chronology and all the outdoor sports in which every prince ought to excel. But what I loved best of all was writing the Arabic script, and at this I soon outdid my teachers and won a name for it that spread as far as India itself.

Now the Sultan of the Indies was curious to see a young prince with such unusual tastes, and he sent an ambassador to my father with rich gifts and a warm invitation to visit his court. My father badly wanted the friendship of so powerful a ruler, and he also believed that a little travel would improve my manners and broaden my mind. So he accepted gladly, and before long I was on my way to India with the ambassador. Because the journey was long and the roads were bad, I took only a small retinue. But as duty required, I brought ten camels loaded with rich gifts for the Sultan.

We had been traveling about a month when one day we saw a cloud of dust racing toward us. As it drew near, we found that it hid a band of fifty robbers. Our men were barely half that number, and the camels hampered us as well, so there was no point in fighting. We tried to frighten the robbers off by telling them who we were and where we were headed. They only laughed and said that was no concern of theirs, and without another word they attacked us savagely. I defended myself to the end, wounded as I was. But finally I saw that resistance was hopeless and that the ambassador and all our followers had been taken prisoner. I spurred my horse and rode off as fast as I could, until the poor animal dropped dead from a wound in its side. I managed to jump clear unhurt, and I looked around to see whether anyone was chasing me. For the moment I was safe, since the robbers, as I guessed, were all busy quarreling over their loot.

I found myself in a country I had never seen, and I did not dare go back to the main road for fear of falling into the robbers’ hands again. Luckily my wound was only a slight one. I bound it up as well as I could and walked on for the rest of the day until I came to a cave at the foot of a mountain. There I spent the night in peace, making my supper from some fruit I had picked along the way.

For a whole month I wandered with no idea where I was going, until at last I came to the edge of a beautiful city, watered by winding streams, where it was always spring. I was delighted at the prospect of being among people again, but my joy was dampened by the thought of what a wretched sight I must be. My face and hands were burned almost black, my clothes were in rags, and my shoes had fallen into such a state that I had had to throw them away altogether.

I went into the town and stopped at a tailor’s shop to ask where I was. The man could see that I was better than my condition, and he asked me to sit down. In return I told him my whole story. The tailor listened closely, but his answer, far from comforting me, only made my trouble worse.
“Be careful,” he said, “not to tell anyone what you have told me. The prince who rules this kingdom is your father’s worst enemy, and he would be delighted to get you into his power.”
I thanked the tailor for his advice and promised to do as he said. Then, since I was very hungry, I gladly ate the food he set before me, and I accepted his offer of a place to stay in his house.

Within a few days I had fully recovered from my hardships. Then the tailor, who knew that princes of our religion are expected to learn a trade or profession so they can support themselves in hard times, asked if there was anything I could do to earn my living. I answered that I had been trained as a grammarian and a poet, but that my greatest gift was handwriting.

“None of that is any use here,” said the tailor. “Take my advice. Put on a short coat, and since you look tough and strong, go into the woods and cut firewood to sell in the streets. That way you can make a living and wait for better times. The hatchet and the cord will be my gift to you.”

I did not like this advice at all, but I saw that I had no choice but to follow it. So the next morning I set out with a group of poor woodcutters whom the tailor had introduced me to. Even on the first day I cut enough wood to sell for a fair sum, and soon I grew more skilled and had earned enough to pay the tailor back everything he had lent me.

I had been cutting wood for more than a year when, one day, I strayed deeper into the forest than I had ever gone and came out into a lovely green clearing. I started chopping at the root of a tree, and there I saw an iron ring set into a trapdoor made of the same metal. I quickly dug the earth away and lifted the door. Under it was a staircase, and I made up my mind at once to go down, taking my hatchet along for protection. At the bottom I found myself in an enormous palace, lit as brightly as any palace above ground I had ever seen. A long gallery ran through it, its pillars of jasper topped with capitals of gold. A lady came down this gallery to meet me, so beautiful that I forgot everything else and could think of nothing but her.
I wanted to spare her any trouble, so I hurried over to her and bowed low.
“Who are you? Who are you?” she asked. “Are you a man or a genie?”
“A man, madam,” I answered. “I have nothing to do with genies.”
“How did you come to be here?” she asked again, with a sigh. “I have been in this place for twenty-five years, and you are the first man who has ever come to me.”

Her beauty and gentleness gave me courage, and I dared to answer her. “Madam, before I reply to your question, let me tell you how grateful I am for this meeting. It comforts me in my own deep sorrow, and perhaps it may even let me make your lot a happier one.” Then I told her who I was and how I had come there.

“Alas, prince,” she said, sighing more deeply than before, “you have guessed right. I am a prisoner here against my will, in this magnificent place. I am the daughter of the king of the Ebony Isle, whose fame you must surely have heard. At my father’s wish I was married to a prince, who was my own cousin; but on my wedding day a genie snatched me up and carried me here in a faint. For a long time I did nothing but weep, and I would not let the genie come near me. But time teaches us to submit, and now I have grown used to having him here, and if clothes and jewels could content me, I have plenty of them. Every tenth day for twenty-five years he has come to see me. If I need him at any other time, I only have to touch a talisman that stands at the entrance to my chamber. His next visit is still five days away, and I hope that until then you will do me the honor of being my guest.”

Her beauty had dazzled me so much that it never crossed my mind to refuse. The princess had me taken to the bath, and a rich set of clothes fit for my rank was laid out for me. Then a feast of the most delicate dishes was served in a room hung with embroidered Indian cloth.
The next day, as we sat at dinner, I could hold back no longer. I begged the princess to break her chains and come back with me to the world that the sun shines on.

“What you ask is impossible,” she answered. “Stay here with me instead, and we can be happy. All you must do is go to the forest every tenth day, when I expect my master the genie. He is very jealous, as you know, and will not let any man come near me.”

“Princess,” I said, “I see that only fear of the genie makes you talk this way. As for me, I fear him so little that I intend to smash his talisman to pieces! However terrible you think he is, he will feel the weight of my arm, and here and now I swear a solemn oath to wipe out his whole race.”

The princess understood what such recklessness would bring, and she begged me not to touch the talisman. “If you do, we will both be ruined,” she said. “I know genies far better than you.” But the wine I had drunk had clouded my head. I gave the talisman one kick, and it fell into a thousand pieces.

My foot had barely touched the talisman when the air turned black as night, a terrible noise rang out, and the palace shook to its foundations. In an instant I was sober, and I understood what I had done. “Princess!” I cried. “What is happening?”
“Alas!” she cried, forgetting her own terror in her worry for me. “Run, or you are lost!”
I took her advice and bolted up the staircase, leaving my hatchet behind. But I was too late. The palace split open and the genie appeared. He turned angrily on the princess and demanded,
“What is the matter? Why have you called me like this?”
“A pain in my heart,” she answered quickly, “forced me to reach for this little bottle. I felt faint, slipped, and fell against the talisman, and it broke. That is all, truly.”
“You shameless liar!” shouted the genie. “How did this hatchet and these shoes get here?”

“I have never seen them before,” she said. “You came in such a rush that you may have picked them up on the road without noticing.” The genie answered this with nothing but insults and blows. I could hear the princess shrieking and groaning. By now I had taken off my rich clothes and put on the ones I had arrived in the day before. I lifted the trapdoor, found myself in the forest again, and went back to my friend the tailor with a small load of wood and a heart full of shame and sorrow.

The tailor had been worried by my long absence and was glad to see me. I said nothing about my adventure, and as soon as I could I went to my room to mourn my folly in secret. While I was sunk in grief, my host came in and said, “There is an old man downstairs who has brought your hatchet and slippers. He picked them up on the road and wants to give them back to you. One of your fellow workers told him where you lived. You had better come down and talk to him yourself.” When I heard this, I changed color and my legs shook under me. The tailor saw how upset I was and was about to ask why, when the door opened and the old man came in, carrying my hatchet and shoes.

“I am a genie,” he said, “the son of the daughter of Eblis, prince of the genies. Is this hatchet yours? And these shoes?” He did not wait for an answer, and indeed I could hardly have given one, I was so frightened. He seized me and shot up into the air as fast as lightning, then dropped back toward the earth just as fast. When he landed, he struck the ground with his foot. It opened, and we found ourselves in the enchanted palace, in front of the beautiful princess of the Ebony Isle. But how different she looked from when I had last seen her! She was lying stretched out on the ground, covered in blood and weeping bitterly.
“Traitor!” cried the genie. “Isn’t this man your lover?”
She slowly raised her eyes and looked at me sadly. “I have never seen him before,” she said slowly. “I do not know who he is.”
“What!” cried the genie. “All your suffering is his doing, and you dare to say he is a stranger to you!”
“But if he really is a stranger to me,” she answered, “why should I tell a lie and cause his death?”
“Very well,” said the genie, drawing his sword. “Take this and cut off his head.”
“Alas,” said the princess, “I am too weak even to hold the sabre. And if I had the strength, why would I kill an innocent man?”
“By refusing, you condemn yourself,” said the genie. Then he turned to me and added, “And you, do you not know her?”
“How would I?” I answered, determined to match the princess in loyalty. “How could I know her, when I have never seen her before?”
“Then cut her head off,” he said. “If she is a stranger to you, I will believe you are telling the truth, and I will set you free.”

“Certainly,” I said, and took the sabre in my hands. I made a sign to the princess not to be afraid, since it was my own life I meant to give up, not hers. But the grateful look she gave me broke my nerve, and I threw the sabre on the ground.

“I would not deserve to live,” I told the genie, “if I were coward enough to kill a lady who is not only unknown to me but is half dead already. Do with me as you like—I am in your power—but I refuse to carry out your cruel order.”

“I see,” said the genie, “that the two of you have made up your minds to defy me. But I will show you a taste of what to expect.” With that, he swung his sabre once and cut off one of the princess’s hands. She could just manage to lift the other to wave me a last farewell. Then I lost consciousness for several minutes.

When I came to, I begged the genie not to keep me in suspense any longer, but to end my suffering at once. The genie paid no attention to my pleas. “That is how a genie treats a woman who has betrayed him,” he said sternly. “If I wished, I could kill you too. But I will be merciful and be satisfied with turning you into a dog, an ass, a lion or a bird—whichever you prefer.”

I seized on these words, as they gave me a faint hope of softening his anger. “O genie!” I cried. “Since you are willing to spare my life, be generous and spare it completely. Grant my prayer and forgive my crime, as the best man in the world forgave the neighbor who was eaten up with envy of him.” Against my expectation, the genie seemed interested in my words and said he would like to hear the story of the two neighbors. And since I think it may please you, madam, I will tell it to you as well.

chapters.title: The Story of the Envious Man and of Him Who Was Envied
paragraphs: In a town of moderate size, two men lived in neighboring houses. They had not been there long before one of them came to hate the other and envy him so bitterly that the poor man decided to find a new home, hoping that once they no longer met every day his enemy would forget him. So he sold his house and the little furniture in it and moved to the capital of the country, which luckily was not far away. About half a mile from that city he bought a nice little property with a large garden and a fair-sized courtyard, and in the middle of the courtyard stood an old well.

To live more quietly, the good man put on the robe of a dervish. He divided his house into many small cells and soon had a number of other dervishes living there. News of his virtue slowly spread, and many people, some of the highest rank among them, came to visit him and ask for his prayers.

Before long, of course, his reputation reached the man who envied him. This wicked wretch resolved not to rest until he had found some way to harm the dervish he hated. So he left his house and his business to fend for themselves and made his way to the new dervish monastery, where its founder welcomed him as warmly as could be. The excuse he gave was that he had come to consult the chief of the dervishes about a private matter of great importance. “What I have to say must not be overheard,” he whispered. “Please order your dervishes to go to their cells, since night is coming on, and meet me in the courtyard.”

The dervish did as he was asked without delay. As soon as the two were alone, the envious man began a long story, and as they paced back and forth he edged closer and closer to the well. When they were right beside it, he grabbed the dervish and threw him in. Then he ran off in triumph, unseen by anyone, congratulating himself that the man he hated was dead and would never trouble him again.

But he was wrong! The old well had long been home (unknown to ordinary people) to a company of fairies and genies, and they caught the dervish as he fell, so he was not hurt. He could see nothing, but he guessed that something strange had happened, or he would surely have been smashed against the wall of the well and killed. He lay perfectly still, and presently he heard a voice say, “Can you guess who this man is, whom we have saved from death?”
“No,” answered several other voices.

And the first speaker said, “I will tell you. Out of sheer goodness of heart, this man left the town where he lived and came to settle here, hoping to cure one of his neighbors of his envy. But his character soon won everyone’s respect, and the envious man’s hatred only grew, until he came here fully intending to cause his death. And he would have done it, without our help, on the very day before the Sultan is to visit this holy dervish and beg his prayers for the princess, the Sultan’s daughter.”
“But what is wrong with the princess, that she needs the dervish’s prayers?” asked another voice.

“She has fallen into the power of the genie Maimoum, the son of Dimdim,” said the first voice. “But it would be easy for this holy chief of the dervishes to cure her, if only he knew! In his convent there is a black cat with a tiny white tip on its tail. To cure the princess, the dervish must pull out seven of these white hairs, burn three of them, and perfume the princess’s head with the smoke. That will free her so completely that Maimoum, the son of Dimdim, will never dare come near her again.”

The fairies and genies stopped talking, but the dervish remembered every word they had said. When morning came, he noticed a spot in the wall of the well that was broken, where he could easily climb out.

The dervishes, who could not imagine what had become of him, were overjoyed to see him again. He told them how his guest of the day before had tried to kill him, and then went to his cell. Soon the black cat that the voice had spoken of came in to say good morning to its master, as it did every day. He took it on his knee, seized the chance to pull seven white hairs from its tail, and set them aside until they were needed.

The sun had barely risen when the Sultan, who was eager to leave nothing undone that might free the princess, reached the monastery gate with a large retinue. The dervishes received him with deep respect. The Sultan lost no time in telling them why he had come. He took the chief of the dervishes aside and said, “Noble sheikh, perhaps you have guessed what I have come to ask you?”
“Yes, sire,” answered the dervish. “If I am not mistaken, it is the princess’s illness that has brought me this honor.”
“You’re right,” answered the Sultan, “and you’ll give me a new life if your prayers can free my daughter from the strange sickness that has taken hold of her.”
“Your Highness, order her to come here, and I will see what I can do.”

Full of hope, the Sultan immediately ordered the princess to set out as quickly as she could, with her usual household of attendants. She arrived so heavily veiled that the dervish could not see her face. He asked for a brazier to be held above her head, and he laid the seven hairs on the burning coals. The moment they burned away, terrible screams rang out, though nobody could tell where they came from. Only the dervish guessed that they came from Maimoum, son of Dimdim, who could feel the princess slipping out of his grasp.
Until then she had seemed to have no awareness of what she was doing. Now she lifted a hand to her veil and uncovered her face. “Where am I?” she asked, bewildered. “And how did I come to be here?”

The Sultan was so overjoyed at these words that he not only hugged his daughter but kissed the dervish’s hand. Then he turned to the attendants standing around him and asked, “What reward should I give the man who has given me back my daughter?”
With one voice they answered that he deserved to marry the princess.
“I think so too,” said the Sultan, “and from this moment I name him my son-in-law.”

Not long afterwards the grand vizier died, and the dervish was given his office. He did not keep it long, though. The Sultan fell ill and died, and since he had no sons, the soldiers and the priests proclaimed the dervish heir to the throne, to the great delight of the whole people.

One day the dervish, now Sultan, was riding out in royal procession with his court when he noticed the envious man standing in the crowd. He signaled to one of his viziers and whispered in his ear, “Bring me that man standing over there, but be very careful not to alarm him.” The vizier obeyed, and when the envious man was brought before him, the Sultan said, “My friend, I’m delighted to see you again.” Then he turned to an officer and added, “Give him a thousand pieces of gold from my treasury and twenty wagonloads of goods from my private stores, and have an escort of soldiers take him home.” After that he said goodbye to the envious man and rode on.

When I had finished my story, I went on to show the genie how it applied to him. “O genie,” I said, “you see that this Sultan was not satisfied with simply forgiving the envious man for trying to kill him. He showered him with gifts and riches.”

But the genie’s mind was made up, and nothing could soften him. “Don’t think you’re getting off so lightly,” he said. “The most I can do is let you live. You are going to find out what happens to people who meddle with me.”

With these words he grabbed me roughly by the arm. The roof of the palace opened to let us through, and we rose so high into the sky that the earth looked like a small cloud. Then, just as before, he dropped down as fast as lightning, and we landed on a mountaintop.

There he bent down, scooped up a handful of earth, and muttered some words over it. Then he flung the earth in my face and said, “Give up the shape of a man and take the shape of a monkey.” With that he disappeared, and I was left in the body of an ape, in a country I had never seen.

There was no point staying where I was, so I climbed down the mountain and came out on a flat plain that ran down to the sea. I headed toward it, and I was glad to see a ship anchored about half a mile from the shore. The sea was calm, so I broke a branch off a tree and dragged it to the water’s edge. I sat astride it, and using two sticks as oars, I paddled myself out to the ship.

The deck was crowded with people, who watched me come with interest. But when I grabbed a rope and swung myself aboard, I discovered that I had escaped death at the genie’s hands only to die at the sailors’, who feared I would bring bad luck on the ship and the merchants. “Throw him in the sea!” shouted one. “Smash his head with a hammer,” cried another. “Let me shoot him with an arrow,” said a third. Someone would certainly have got his way if I had not thrown myself at the captain’s feet and clung tightly to his clothes. My action seemed to move him. He patted my head and announced that he would take me under his protection and that nobody was to harm me.

After about fifty days we dropped anchor off a large town, and at once the ship was surrounded by crowds of little boats full of people, who had come either to greet friends or just out of curiosity. One of the boats carried several officials, who asked to see the merchants on board. They said the Sultan had sent them as a welcome, and to ask each merchant to write a few lines on a roll of paper. “To explain this odd request,” the officers went on, “you should know that the grand vizier, who died recently, was famous for his beautiful handwriting, and the Sultan wants to find the same talent in his successor. So far the search has failed, but his Highness has not given up hope.”

One after another the merchants wrote a few lines on the roll. When they had all finished, I stepped forward and snatched the paper from the man holding it. At first everyone thought I meant to throw it into the sea, but they calmed down when they saw how carefully I held it. They were greatly surprised when I made signs that I wanted to write something too.

“Let him, if he wants to,” said the captain. “If he only makes a mess of the paper, I promise you I’ll punish him for it. But if he really can write, as I hope, since he’s the cleverest monkey I’ve ever seen, I’ll adopt him as my son. The one I lost had nowhere near as much sense!”

Nothing more was said. I took the pen and wrote in the six kinds of script used among the Arabs, and in each script I wrote an original verse or couplet praising the Sultan. My handwriting did not merely outshine the merchants’; it is hardly too much to say that nobody in that country had ever seen anything so beautiful. When I had finished, the officials took the roll and went back to the Sultan.

As soon as the monarch saw my writing, he did not even glance at the merchants’ samples. He ordered his officials to take the finest, most richly decked horse in his stables and the most magnificent robe they could find, dress the person who had written those lines in it, and bring him to court.

The officials started laughing when they heard the Sultan’s command, and when they could speak again they said, “Your Highness, please forgive our laughter, but those lines were not written by a man. A monkey wrote them.”
“A monkey!” cried the Sultan.
“Yes, sire,” the officials answered. “He wrote them right in front of us.”
“Then bring me the monkey,” he said, “as quickly as you can.”
The Sultan’s officials went back to the ship and showed the captain the royal order.
“He is the master now,” said the good man, and he had me sent for.
They dressed me in the splendid robe and rowed me ashore, where I was set on the horse and led to the palace. There the Sultan was waiting for me in full state, with his court around him.

All the way through the streets I was an object of curiosity to a vast crowd that had packed every doorway and every window, and it was amid their shouting and cheering that I was led into the presence of the Sultan.

I walked up to the throne where he sat, bowed to him three times, and then threw myself on the ground at his feet. Everyone was astonished, since nobody could understand how a monkey could tell a Sultan from other people and show him the respect his rank deserved. Apart from the customary speech, I left out none of the usual formalities of a royal audience.

When it was over, the Sultan sent the whole court away, keeping only the chief of the eunuchs and a young slave. He went into another room and had food brought, and he signed to me to sit at the table and eat with him. I rose from my place, kissed the ground, and sat down at the table, eating, as you can imagine, carefully and with moderation.

Before the dishes were cleared away, I made signs asking for the writing materials that stood in one corner of the room to be set in front of me. Then I took a peach and wrote some verses on it in praise of the Sultan, who was struck dumb with amazement. But when I did the same on a glass I had drunk from, he muttered to himself, “A man who could do this would be more gifted than any other man alive, and this is only a monkey!”

When supper was over, chessmen were brought, and the Sultan signed to ask whether I would play with him. I kissed the ground and put my hand on my head to show I was ready to prove myself worthy of the honor. He won the first game, but I won the second and the third. Seeing that this did not altogether please him, I tossed off a verse to console him.

The Sultan was so delighted with all the talents I had shown that he wanted me to display some of them to others. So he turned to the chief of the eunuchs and said, “Go and ask my daughter, Queen of Beauty, to come here. I’m going to show her something she has never seen before.”

The chief of the eunuchs bowed and left the room. A few moments later he returned with the princess, Queen of Beauty. Her face was uncovered, but the instant she stepped into the room she threw her veil over her head. “Sire,” she said to her father, “what can you be thinking of, calling me like this into the presence of a man?”

“I don’t understand you,” replied the Sultan. “Nobody is here but the eunuch, who is your own servant, the young slave, and myself. Yet you hide behind your veil and blame me for sending for you, as if I had committed a crime.”

“Sire,” answered the princess, “I am right and you are mistaken. This monkey is no monkey at all. He is a young prince who was turned into a monkey by the wicked spells of a genie, the son of Eblis’s daughter.”

As you can imagine, these words took the Sultan by surprise, and he looked at me to see how I would respond to the princess’s claim. Since I could not speak, I put my hand on my head to show that it was true.
“But how do you know this, my daughter?” he asked.

“Sire,” answered Queen of Beauty, “the old woman who looked after me when I was a child was a skilled magician. She taught me seventy rules of her art, and with them I could, in the blink of an eye, move your capital into the middle of the ocean. Her art also teaches me to recognize, at first sight, anyone who is enchanted, and it tells me who cast the spell.”
“My daughter,” said the Sultan, “I had no idea you were so clever.”
“Sire,” answered the princess, “there are many unusual things it is good to know, but one should never boast of them.”
“Well,” said the Sultan, “can you tell me what must be done to free the young prince from the enchantment?”
“Certainly, and I can do it.”
“Then give him back his own shape,” cried the Sultan. “Nothing could please me more, for I want to make him my grand vizier and give him to you as your husband.”
“As Your Highness wishes,” answered the princess.

Queen of Beauty got up and went to her chamber, and came back with a knife that had Hebrew words engraved on its blade. Then she told the Sultan, the chief of the eunuchs, the young slave and me to go down into a secret courtyard of the palace. She placed us under a gallery that ran all the way around it, while she herself stood in the middle of the courtyard. There she drew a large circle and wrote several words inside it in Arabic letters.

When the circle and the writing were done, she stood in the middle of it and recited some verses from the Koran. Slowly the air grew dark, and it felt as if the ground was about to crumble beneath us. Our terror only grew when we saw the genie, the son of Eblis’s daughter, suddenly appear in the form of an enormous lion.
“Dog,” cried the princess as soon as she saw him, “do you think you can frighten me by daring to show yourself to me in this hideous shape?”
“And you,” the lion shot back, “were not afraid to break the treaty in which we solemnly promised never to interfere with each other.”
“Accursed genie!” cried the princess. “You are the one who broke that treaty first.”

“I’ll teach you to cause me so much trouble,” said the lion, and he opened his huge mouth and came forward to swallow her. But the princess had expected something like this and was ready. She leapt aside, grabbed one of the hairs of his mane, and spoke two or three words over it. In an instant it turned into a sword, and with one sharp stroke she cut the lion’s body in two. The pieces vanished, nobody knew where, and only the lion’s head remained, which at once changed into a scorpion. Quick as thought, the princess took the form of a serpent and fought the scorpion. When he found he was losing, he turned himself into an eagle and flew away. But in a moment the serpent had become a still mightier eagle, which soared into the air after him, and then we lost sight of them both.

We all stayed where we were, shaking with fear, when the ground split open in front of us and a black and white cat sprang out, its fur bristling, yowling horribly. A wolf was right behind it and had almost caught it, when the cat turned itself into a worm, bored into a pomegranate that had fallen from a tree, and hid inside the fruit. The pomegranate swelled until it was as big as a pumpkin, rose up to the roof of the gallery, then dropped into the courtyard and smashed to pieces. Meanwhile the wolf had changed himself into a cock and started gulping down the pomegranate seeds as fast as he could. When they were all gone he flew toward us, flapping his wings as though asking whether we could see any more. Then his eye fell on a seed lying at the edge of the little canal that ran through the courtyard. He rushed at it, but before he could touch it the seed rolled into the canal and turned into a fish. The cock plunged in after the fish and became a pike, and for two hours the two of them chased each other back and forth beneath the water, screaming dreadfully, though we could see nothing. At last they rose out of the water in their own shapes again, but they spat such flames from their mouths that we feared the palace would burn down. Soon we had far more to fear, for the genie, having thrown off the princess, flew at us. We would have been finished if the princess, seeing our danger, had not drawn the genie’s attention to herself. Even so, the Sultan’s beard was singed and his face scorched, the chief of the eunuchs was burned to a cinder, and a spark blinded me in one eye. The Sultan and I had both given up all hope of rescue when we heard the princess cry out, “Victory, victory!” and there lay the genie at her feet, a great heap of ashes.

Worn out as she was, the princess at once told the little slave, the only one who had come through unharmed, to bring her a cup of water, and she held it in her hand. She murmured some magic words over it and then splashed it in my face, saying, “If you are a monkey only through enchantment, take back the shape of the man you were before.” In an instant I was standing before her as the same man I had been, except that I had lost the sight of one eye.

I was about to drop to my knees and thank the princess, but she gave me no chance. She turned to the Sultan, her father, and said, “Sire, I have won the battle, but it has cost me dearly. The fire has gone into my heart, and I have only a few moments left. This would not have happened if I had noticed that last pomegranate seed and eaten it like the others. That was the genie’s final stand, and until then I was perfectly safe. But once I had let that chance go by, I had to turn to fire, and for all his experience I showed the genie that I knew more than he did. He is dead and turned to ashes, but my own death is coming fast.” “My daughter,” cried the Sultan, “what a wretched state I am in! I am amazed that I am even alive! The eunuch has been eaten up by the flames, and the prince you have set free has lost an eye.” He could say no more, for sobbing choked his voice, and we all wept together.
Suddenly the princess screamed, “I burn, I burn!” and death came and released her from her agony.

Madam, I cannot tell you what I felt at that terrible sight. I would rather have stayed a monkey for the rest of my life than have my benefactress die in such a dreadful way. The Sultan could not be comforted at all, and his people, who had loved the princess dearly, shared his grief. The whole nation mourned for seven days, and then the princess’s ashes were buried with great ceremony and a magnificent tomb was built over them.

When the Sultan had recovered from the grave illness that struck him after the princess died, he sent for me. He told me plainly, though politely, that the sight of me would always remind him of what he had lost, and he asked me to leave his kingdom at once and never to come back, on pain of death. Naturally I had to obey. I had no idea what would become of me, so I shaved off my beard and eyebrows and put on the clothes of a Calender. I wandered aimlessly through several countries, until I decided to come to Baghdad and ask for an audience with the Commander of the Faithful.
And that, madam, is my story.
Then the other Calender told his story.

chapters.title: The Story of the Third Calender, Son of a King
paragraphs: My story, said the Third Calender, is very different from those of my two friends. Fate took the sight of their right eyes, but I lost mine through my own foolishness.
My name is Agib, and I am the son of a king named Cassib, who ruled a large kingdom whose capital was one of the finest seaports in the world.

When I inherited my father’s throne, the first thing I did was to tour the provinces on the mainland, and then to sail out to the many islands off the coast, to win the hearts of my people. These voyages gave me such a love of sailing that before long I resolved to explore more distant seas, and I ordered a fleet of large ships made ready at once. When they were fully equipped, I set out on my expedition.

For forty days the wind and weather were with us, but on the night after that a terrible storm broke and tossed us about for ten days, until the pilot admitted that he had lost all sense of where we were. So a sailor was sent up the masthead to look for land. He reported that he could see nothing but sea and sky, apart from an enormous patch of blackness behind us.

When he heard this, the pilot turned pale and beat his chest, crying, “Oh, sir, we are lost, lost!” until the crew shook with a fear they could not name. When he had pulled himself together a little and could explain what had frightened him, he answered my question. We had drifted far off our course, he said, and the next day around noon we would come close to that dark mass, which was nothing other than the famous Black Mountain. This mountain is made of adamant, which pulls toward itself every scrap of iron and every nail in your ship. As we are drawn helplessly nearer, the pull grows so strong that the iron and nails will tear loose from the ships and stick to the mountain, and the ships will sink to the bottom with everyone aboard. That, he said, is why the side of the mountain facing the sea looks so deeply black.

“As you can imagine,” the pilot went on, “the sides of the mountain are very rugged, but on the summit stands a brass dome held up by pillars, and on top of it is a brass horse with a rider on its back. The rider wears a lead breastplate engraved with strange signs and figures, and it is said that as long as this statue stays on the dome, ships will go on being destroyed at the foot of the mountain.”
With that, the pilot started weeping again, and the crew, believing their last hour had come, made their wills, each man leaving everything to his comrade.

At noon the next day, just as the pilot had foretold, we came so close to the Black Mountain that we saw every nail and scrap of iron fly out of the ships and hurl itself against the mountain with a horrible din. A moment later the vessels broke apart and sank, and the crews went down with them. I alone managed to seize a floating plank, and the wind drove me ashore without a scratch. How glad I was to find myself at the foot of a stairway cut straight up the mountain, for there was not another inch to the right or left where a man could set his foot. Even the steps themselves were so narrow and steep that the slightest breeze would certainly have blown me into the sea.

When I reached the top I found the brass dome and the statue just as the pilot had described them, but I was too worn out by all I had been through to do more than glance at them. I threw myself down under the dome and fell asleep at once. In my dreams an old man appeared and said to me, “Listen, Agib! As soon as you wake, dig up the ground beneath you, and you will find a bow of brass and three arrows of lead. Shoot the arrows at the statue, and the rider will tumble into the sea, but the horse will fall down beside you, and you must bury him in the place where you took the bow and arrows. When that is done, the sea will rise and cover the mountain, and on it you will see the figure of a metal man sitting in a boat with an oar in each hand. Step aboard and let him take you. But if you want to see your kingdom again, take care never to speak the name of Allah.”

With these words the vision left me, and I woke feeling much comforted. I jumped up and dug the bow and arrows out of the ground, and with the third shot the horseman crashed down into the sea. The sea began to rise at once, so fast that I barely had time to bury the horse before the boat came up to me. I stepped in without a word and sat down, and the metal man pushed off and rowed without stopping for nine days, after which land appeared on the horizon. I was so overjoyed at the sight that I forgot everything the old man had told me, and cried out, “Allah be praised! Allah be praised!”

The words were hardly out of my mouth when the boat and the man sank from under me, and I was left floating on the water. All that day and through the night I alternately swam and floated, making as best I could for the nearest land. At last my strength began to fail and I gave myself up for lost, but then the wind suddenly rose and a huge wave threw me onto a flat shore. Once I was safe, I quickly spread my clothes out to dry in the sun and lay down on the warm ground to rest.

The next morning I dressed and began to look around. I seemed to be alone on the island, which was covered with fruit trees and crossed by streams, but it seemed a long way from the mainland I hoped to reach. Before I had time to lose heart, though, I saw a ship heading straight for the island. Not knowing whether it carried friends or enemies, I hid among the thick branches of a tree.

The sailors steered the ship into a creek, and ten slaves came ashore carrying spades and pickaxes. They stopped in the middle of the island, dug for a while, and then lifted up what looked like a trapdoor. They went back to the vessel two or three times to fetch furniture and provisions, and at last returned with an old man, who was leading a handsome boy of fourteen or fifteen. They all went down through the trapdoor, and after a few minutes below they came up again, but without the boy. They let the trapdoor down and covered it with earth as it had been before. Then they boarded the ship and sailed away.

As soon as they were out of sight, I climbed down from my tree and went to the place where the boy had been buried. I dug away the earth until I reached a large stone with a ring in the middle. When I lifted it, it uncovered a flight of stone steps leading down to a large, richly furnished room lit by candles. The boy was sitting on a heap of cushions covered with tapestry. He looked up, startled and frightened to see a stranger in such a place, and to calm his fears I spoke at once: “Do not be alarmed, sir, whoever you are. I am a king, and a king’s son, and I will do you no harm. On the contrary, perhaps I have been sent here to rescue you from this tomb, where you have been buried alive.”

At my words the young man recovered himself, and when I had finished he said, “Prince, the reasons I have been buried in this place are so strange that they cannot fail to amaze you. My father is a rich merchant with a great deal of land and many ships, and he trades heavily in precious stones, but he never stopped grieving that he had no child to inherit his wealth.

“Then one day he dreamed that the following year a son would be born to him, and when that really happened, he asked all the wise men in the kingdom about the infant’s future. They all said the same thing. I would live happily until I was fifteen, when a terrible danger would threaten me, one I would scarcely escape. But if I did escape it, I would live to a very great age. And they added: when the statue of the brass horse on top of the mountain of adamant is thrown into the sea by Agib, the son of Cassib, then beware, for fifty days later your son will die by his hand!

“This prophecy struck my father’s heart with such grief that he never recovered from it, but that did not stop him from taking great care over my education, until a short while ago I turned fifteen. Only yesterday the news reached him that ten days earlier the brass statue had been thrown into the sea, and he immediately set about hiding me in this underground chamber, which was built for the purpose, promising to come and fetch me out when forty days have passed. As for me, I am not afraid, since Prince Agib is hardly likely to come here looking for me.”

I listened to his story with an inward laugh at the absurdity of my ever wanting to cause the death of this harmless boy, and I hurried to assure him of my friendship and even my protection. In return I begged him to carry me to my own country in his father’s ship. I hardly need say that I took particular care not to tell him I was the Agib he feared.

We spent the day talking about all sorts of subjects, and I found him a youth of quick wit and some learning. I took on the duties of a servant: I held the basin and water for him when he washed, and I cooked the dinner and set it on the table. He soon grew fond of me, and for thirty-nine days we lived as pleasantly as one could expect to underground.

The morning of the fortieth day dawned, and when the young man woke he gave thanks in a burst of joy that the danger was past. “My father may be here at any moment,” he said, “so please heat some water for a bath, so that I can wash and change my clothes and be ready to receive him.”

I brought the water he had asked for, washed him and rubbed him down, and he lay back and slept for a short while. When he woke the second time, he asked me for a melon and a little sugar, so that he could eat something and get his strength back.

I quickly picked a good melon from the ones that were left, but I could not find a knife to cut it. “Look on the ledge above my head,” he said. “I think you’ll find one there.” It was so high up that I had trouble reaching it. As I stretched, my foot caught in the bedcover, I slipped, and I fell straight onto the young man, and the knife went right into his heart.

The horror of it made me scream out in grief and pain. I threw myself on the ground, tore my clothes and pulled at my hair in sorrow. Then, afraid that his unhappy father would punish me as his murderer, I lifted the great stone that sealed the staircase, climbed out of the underground room, and fastened everything again exactly as it had been.

I had barely finished when I looked out over the sea and saw the ship making for the island. I felt it would be pointless to protest that I was innocent, so I hid once more among the branches of a tree close by.

As soon as the ship touched land, the old man and his slaves rowed ashore in a boat and hurried toward the entrance of the underground room. But when they came close enough to see that the ground had been disturbed, they stopped short, and their faces changed color. They all went down in silence and called the young man by name, and for a moment I heard nothing more. Then a terrible scream split the air, and the slaves climbed back up the steps carrying the old man, who had fainted from grief! They laid him at the foot of the very tree where I was hiding and tried hard to bring him round, though it took them a long time. When he finally came to, they left him and dug a grave, then laid the young man’s body in it and shovelled the earth over him.

When that was done, the slaves carried up all the furniture left below and loaded it onto the ship. They broke off some branches and wove a litter, laid the old man on it, and carried him to the vessel, which then spread its sails and put out to sea.

So I was completely alone again, and for a whole month I walked over the island every day, looking for any chance of escape. Then one day it struck me that my prison had become much bigger and that the mainland seemed closer. My heart pounded, because it seemed almost too good to be true. I kept watching, and there was no doubt about it. Before long there was only a narrow stream left to cross.

Even once I was safely across, I still had a long way to go over mud and sand before I reached dry ground. I was very tired when I saw, far ahead of me, a castle of red copper, which at first I took for a fire. I hurried toward it, and after several miles of hard walking I stood in front of it and stared in amazement, because it seemed to me the most wonderful building I had ever seen. While I was still gazing at it, a tall old man came toward me with ten young men, all of them handsome, and all blind in the right eye.

Now, ten men walking together who are all blind in the right eye is as strange a sight as a copper castle, and I was wondering what it could mean when they greeted me warmly and asked what had brought me there. I said that my story was rather long, but that if they would sit down, I would gladly tell it. When I had finished, the young men asked me to come with them to the castle, and I gladly accepted. We passed through what seemed an endless run of rooms and came at last to a large hall. In it stood ten small blue sofas, one for each of the young men, which served as both beds and chairs, and one more sofa in the middle for the old man. Since none of the sofas could hold more than one person, they told me to sit on the carpet, and not to ask any questions about anything I might see.

After a little while the old man got up and brought in supper, and I ate with a good appetite, because I was very hungry. Then one of the young men asked me to tell my story again, which had amazed them all, and when I had finished, the old man was told to “do his duty,” since it was late and they wanted to go to bed. At these words he got up and went to a closet, and brought out ten basins, each covered with blue cloth. He set one in front of each of the young men, along with a lit candle.

When the covers were lifted off the basins, I saw that they were full of ashes, coal dust and lamp-black. The young men mixed it all together and smeared it over their heads and faces. Then they wept and beat their chests, crying, “This is what comes of idleness and of our wicked lives.”
This ritual went on for almost the whole night. When it ended they washed themselves thoroughly, put on clean clothes, and lay down to sleep.

All this time I had held back my questions, though my curiosity felt as if it were burning a hole in me. The next day, when we went out walking, I said to them, “Gentlemen, I have to go against your wishes, because I cannot stay silent any longer. You don’t seem to lack sense, yet you do things that only madmen would do. Whatever happens to me, I can’t help asking: ‘Why do you smear your faces with black, and how is it that you are all blind in one eye?’” But they only replied that such questions were none of my business, and that I would do well to keep quiet.
We talked of other things that day, but when night came and the same ritual was repeated, I begged them as earnestly as I could to tell me what it all meant.

“It is for your own sake,” one of the young men answered, “that we haven’t granted your request. We want to spare you our unhappy fate. But if you truly want to share our destiny, we won’t put it off any longer.”

I told them that whatever the consequences, I wanted my curiosity satisfied, and that I would take the outcome on my own head. He then warned me that even after I had lost my eye, I would not be able to stay with them, because their number was full and could not be increased. I answered that although I would be sorry to part from such honorable gentlemen, that would not turn me from my decision.

When they heard that I was determined, my ten hosts took a sheep and killed it, and handed me a knife, saying I would find it useful before long. “We must sew you into this sheepskin,” they said, “and then leave you. A huge bird called a roc will appear in the sky, and it will take you for a sheep. It will seize you and carry you up into the air, but don’t be afraid, because it will bring you down safely and set you on the top of a mountain. When you are on the ground, slit the skin with the knife and throw it off. As soon as the roc sees you, it will fly away in fright, but you must keep walking until you reach a castle roofed with plates of gold and set with jewels. Go boldly in at the gate, which always stands open. But do not ask us to tell you what we saw or what happened to us there, because you will find that out for yourself. We can say only this: it cost each of us his right eye, and it has put this nightly penance on us.”

Once the young men had gone to the trouble of sewing the sheepskin around me, they left me and went back into the hall. A few minutes later the roc appeared and carried me off to the mountaintop in its huge claws, as easily as if I were a feather. This great white bird is so strong that it has been known to carry even an elephant to its nest in the hills.

The moment my feet touched the ground, I took out my knife and cut the threads that bound me. The sight of me in my ordinary clothes frightened the roc so much that it spread its wings and flew off. Then I set out to look for the castle.

I found it after wandering for half a day, and I could never have imagined anything so magnificent. The gate opened into a square courtyard with a hundred doors around it, ninety-nine of them made of rare woods and one of gold. Through each of these doors I glimpsed splendid gardens or rich storehouses.

I went in through one of the doors that stood open and found myself in a vast hall, where forty young women, richly dressed and perfectly beautiful, were lounging. As soon as they saw me they stood up and welcomed me, and they even insisted that I take a seat higher than their own, though my proper place was at their feet. They did not stop there. One brought me fine clothes, another filled a basin with scented water and poured it over my hands, and the rest busied themselves preparing refreshments. After I had eaten and drunk the most delicate food and the rarest wines, the women gathered around me and asked me to tell them all my adventures.

By the time I finished, night had fallen, and the women lit the castle with so many candles that daylight could hardly have been brighter. Then we sat down to a supper of dried fruits and sweetmeats, after which some of them sang and others danced. I was so well entertained that I never noticed the time passing, until one of the women came up to me and told me it was midnight and that I must be tired, so she would take me to the room made ready for me. Then she wished me good night, and I was left to sleep.

I spent the next thirty-nine days much as I had spent the first. At the end of that time, though, the women came to my room one morning, as they always did, to ask how I had slept, and instead of looking cheerful and smiling, they were in floods of tears. “Prince,” they said, “we have to leave you, and it has never been so hard to part from any friend. We will most likely never see you again, but if you can master yourself, perhaps we may still hope to meet again.”
“Ladies,” I answered, “what is the meaning of these strange words? I beg you, tell me.”

“Then know,” said one of them, “that we are all princesses, each of us a king’s daughter. We live together in this castle in the way you have seen, but at the end of every year secret duties call us away for forty days. That time has now come. Before we go, we will leave you our keys, so that you won’t be without amusement while we are gone. But there is one thing we ask of you. Do not open the Golden Door, as you value your peace and the happiness of your life. Once that door is unlocked, we will have to say goodbye to you forever.”
In tears, I promised them I would be careful, and after they had embraced me tenderly, they went on their way.

Every day I opened two or three new doors, and behind each one were so many remarkable things that I had no chance to feel bored, much as I missed the ladies. Sometimes it was an orchard whose fruit was far bigger than any that grew in my father’s garden. Sometimes it was a courtyard planted with roses, jasmine, daffodils, hyacinths and anemones, and a thousand other flowers whose names I did not know. Or it might be an aviary filled with every kind of songbird, or a treasury piled high with precious stones. Whatever I saw, everything was perfect of its kind.

The thirty-nine days went by faster than I would have thought possible, and the next morning the princesses were due back at the castle. But alas! I had explored every corner except the room behind the Golden Door, and I had nothing left to amuse me. I stood in front of the forbidden door for some time, admiring its beauty. Then a happy thought struck me: just because I unlocked the door, it didn’t follow that I had to go into the room. It would be enough to stand outside and look at whatever hidden wonders were inside.

Arguing against my own conscience like this, I turned the key. A scent rushed out that, pleasant as it was, overpowered me completely, and I fainted across the threshold. Instead of taking this as a warning, as soon as I came to I stepped outside for a few moments to clear my head of the perfume, and then went in boldly. I found myself in a large vaulted room, lit by candles that burned in golden candlesticks and gave off the scent of aloes and ambergris, while gold and silver lamps hung from the ceiling.

Rare and finely made objects lay piled all around me, but I hardly looked at them, because I was so taken with a great black horse standing in one corner, the handsomest and best-formed animal I had ever seen. Its saddle and bridle were of solid gold, intricately worked. One side of its trough was filled with clean barley and sesame, and the other with rose water. I led the horse out into the open air and jumped on its back, shaking the reins, but it did not move, so I touched it lightly with a switch I had picked up in its stable. The instant it felt the blow, it spread wings I had not noticed before and flew straight up into the sky with me. When it had climbed to a tremendous height, it swooped back down and landed on the terrace of a castle, throwing me violently out of the saddle and hitting me with its tail so hard that it knocked out my right eye.

I was half stunned by everything that had happened to me. I got to my feet, thinking of what had befallen the ten young men, and watching the horse as it soared up into the clouds. I left the terrace and wandered on until I came to a hall, which I recognized by the ten blue sofas along the wall as the one the roc had carried me from.

The ten young men weren’t there when I first walked in, but they arrived shortly afterward with the old man. They welcomed me warmly and mourned my misfortune, though they had expected nothing else. “Everything that has happened to you has happened to us too,” they said, “and we would still be living in the same happiness if we hadn’t opened the Golden Door while the princesses were away. You were no wiser than we were, and you have paid the same price. We would gladly take you in to share our penance, but as we’ve already told you, that is impossible. So leave this place and go to the Court of Baghdad, where you will find the man who can decide your fate.” They told me which road to take, and I left them.

Along the way I had my beard and eyebrows shaved off and put on a Calender’s robe. It was a long journey, but I reached the city this evening. At the gate I met my brother Calenders, who were strangers here just as I am. We were amazed to find that all of us were blind in the same eye, but there was no time to talk at length about the troubles we shared. We had only enough time to come here and ask for the kindness you have so generously shown us.
He finished, and then Zobeida spoke. “Go wherever you like,” she told all three of them. “I forgive you all, but you must leave this house at once.”

chapters.title: The Seven Voyages of Sindbad the Sailor
paragraphs: In the days of the Caliph Haroun-al-Raschid, there lived in Baghdad a poor porter named Hindbad. One very hot day he was given a heavy load to carry from one end of the city to the other. He had not covered half the distance when he grew so tired that, seeing a quiet street with rose water sprinkled over the pavement and a cool breeze blowing, he put his burden down and sat in the shade of a grand house to rest. He soon decided he couldn’t have picked a nicer spot. A wonderful scent of aloes wood and incense drifted from the open windows and mingled with the smell of the rose water steaming up from the hot stones. Inside the house he could hear music, many instruments skillfully played, and the sweet warbling of nightingales and other birds. Together with the tempting smell of fine dishes that he also noticed, it told him that a feast and a merry party were under way. He wondered who lived in such a magnificent house, which he had never seen before, since this was a street he rarely had reason to walk down. To satisfy his curiosity, he went over to some splendidly dressed servants standing at the door and asked one of them the name of the house’s owner.
“What?” the servant answered. “You live in Baghdad and you don’t know that this is the home of the noble Sindbad the Sailor, the famous traveler who has sailed every sea the sun shines on?”
The porter had often heard talk of Sindbad’s enormous wealth, and he couldn’t help envying a man whose life seemed as happy as his own was wretched. He looked up at the sky and cried out,

“Look, Mighty Creator of all things, at the difference between Sindbad’s life and mine! Every day I suffer a thousand hardships and misfortunes, and I struggle just to earn enough bad barley bread to keep myself and my family alive, while lucky Sindbad throws money around and lives off the fat of the land! What did he do to earn this pleasant life—and what did I do to deserve such a hard one?”

With that he stamped on the ground, like a man beside himself with misery and despair. Just then a servant came out of the palace, took him by the arm, and said, “Come with me. My master, the noble Sindbad, wants to speak with you.”

Hindbad was more than a little startled by this summons. He feared his careless words had angered Sindbad, so he tried to excuse himself, saying he couldn’t leave the load that had been entrusted to him sitting out in the street. But the servant promised that it would be looked after, and pressed him so firmly to come that in the end the porter had to give in.

He followed the servant into a huge room, where a large company sat around a table piled with every kind of delicacy. In the seat of honor sat a tall, serious man whose long white beard gave him a dignified look. Behind his chair stood a crowd of attendants, ready to meet his every need. This was Sindbad himself. The porter, more alarmed than ever by so much splendor, greeted the distinguished company with a trembling voice. Sindbad signaled him to come closer and had him sit at his right hand. He heaped choice morsels onto the porter’s plate with his own hands and poured him a cup of excellent wine. Then, as the banquet came to an end, he spoke to him in a friendly way and asked his name and trade.
“My lord,” answered the porter, “my name is Hindbad.”

“I’m glad to see you here,” Sindbad went on. “I can promise you that everyone else here is just as pleased. But I want you to tell me what you said a little while ago in the street.” Sindbad had passed the open window before the feast began, had overheard the complaint, and had sent for the man because of it.
At this question Hindbad was thrown into confusion. He hung his head and answered, “My lord, I admit that I was worn out and in a bad mood, and I said foolish things. I beg you to forgive me.”

“Oh,” said Sindbad, “don’t think I’m so unfair as to blame you. On the contrary, I understand your situation and feel for you. But you seem to have the wrong idea about me, and I want to set you straight. No doubt you think I came by all the wealth and comfort you see here without trouble or danger. That is very far from the truth. I reached this happy state only after years of every kind of hardship and peril you can imagine.

“Yes, my noble friends,” he went on, speaking to the whole company, “I assure you that my adventures have been strange enough to put off even the greediest men from crossing the seas in search of riches. You may have heard only muddled accounts of my seven voyages, and of the dangers and marvels I met by sea and land. So now I will give you a full and true account of them, which I think you will enjoy hearing.”

Sindbad was telling his story mainly for the porter’s sake. So before he began, he ordered some of his own servants to carry the load that had been left in the street to the place Hindbad had first been heading for, while Hindbad stayed to listen to the tale.

chapters.title: Sindbad the Sailor: First Voyage
paragraphs: I had inherited a good deal of money from my parents. Being young and foolish, I at first threw it away on every kind of pleasure. Before long I realized that riches fly away quickly when they are managed as badly as I was managing mine, and I remembered that being old and poor is truly miserable. So I began to think about how to make the best of what I had left. I sold all my household goods at a public auction and joined a group of merchants who traded by sea, sailing with them from Balsora in a ship we had fitted out together.

We set sail and made for the East Indies through the Persian Gulf, with the coast of Persia on our left and the shores of Arabia Felix on our right. At first the rocking of the ship made me very ill, but I soon recovered, and I have never suffered from seasickness since.

From time to time we stopped at various islands, where we sold or traded our goods. One day the wind suddenly died, and we found ourselves becalmed close to a small island that looked like a green meadow, barely rising above the water. The sails were furled, and the captain let anyone who wished go ashore for a while to enjoy themselves. I was one of those who did. We wandered around for some time, then lit a fire and sat down to eat the meal we had brought. Suddenly the island began to shake violently, and at the same moment the people left on the ship started shouting at us to come aboard for our lives, because what we had taken for an island was really the back of a sleeping whale. Those nearest the boat threw themselves into it, and others jumped into the sea. But before I could save myself, the whale dived into the depths of the ocean, leaving me hanging on to a piece of the wood we had brought for our fire. Meanwhile a breeze had risen, and in the confusion aboard the ship, as they hoisted the sails and pulled in the people in the boat and those clinging to its sides, nobody noticed I was missing. I was left at the mercy of the waves. All that day I drifted up and down, tossed first one way and then another, and when night fell I gave up hope of living. But, exhausted as I was, I held on to my flimsy piece of wood, and I was overjoyed when the morning light showed that I had drifted up against an island.

The cliffs were high and steep, but luckily for me a few tree roots stuck out here and there, and with their help I finally climbed to the top.
