I stretched out on the grass and lay there, more dead than alive, until the sun was high in the sky. By then I was very hungry. After some searching I found some edible plants and a spring of clear water, and, much refreshed, I set off to explore the island. Soon I came to a great plain where a horse was grazing, tethered there. While I stood looking at it, I heard voices, seemingly from underground, and a moment later a man appeared and asked how I had come to be on the island. I told him my adventures, and he told me in return that he was one of the grooms of Mihrage, the king of the island, and that every year they came to this plain to feed their master’s horses. He took me to a cave where his companions had gathered, and after I had eaten the food they offered me, they told me I was lucky to have found them when I did. They were going back to their master the next day, and without their help I could never have found my way to the inhabited part of the island.

Early the next morning we set out, and when we reached the capital the king received me graciously. I told him my adventures, and he ordered that I be well looked after and given whatever I needed. Since I was a merchant, I looked for men of my own trade, especially those from foreign countries, hoping to hear news of Baghdad and find some way of getting back there. The capital stood on the coast, and ships came to it from all over the world. In the meantime I heard many curious things, and I answered many questions about my own country, for I was happy to talk with anyone who came to me. To pass the time while I waited, I also explored a small island called Cassel, which belonged to King Mihrage and was said to be haunted by a spirit named Deggial. The sailors assured me that at night you could often hear the beating of timbals there. Still, I saw nothing strange on that trip, except some fish fully two hundred cubits long, which luckily were even more afraid of us than we were of them and swam away if we merely banged on a board to scare them. There were also other fish, only a cubit long, with heads like owls.

One day after I got back, I went down to the quay and saw a ship that had just dropped anchor and was unloading its cargo, while the merchants who owned it busily directed the goods to their warehouses. As I came closer, I noticed my own name written on some of the packages. I looked them over carefully and felt sure they were the very ones I had loaded aboard our ship at Balsora. Then I recognized the ship’s captain. Since I was certain he believed I was dead, I went up to him and asked who owned the packages I was looking at.

“I had a merchant from Baghdad on my ship,” he answered, “named Sindbad. One day he and several of my other passengers went ashore on what we took to be an island, but which was really an enormous whale asleep on the waves. The moment it felt the heat of the fire they had lit on its back, it dived into the depths of the sea. Several of the people on it drowned, and among them was this unlucky Sindbad. These goods are his, but I have decided to sell them for the benefit of his family, if I ever happen to meet them.”
“Captain,” I said, “I am the Sindbad you think is dead, and these goods are mine!”

When the captain heard this, he cried out in astonishment, “Good heavens! What is the world coming to? These days you can’t find an honest man anywhere. I saw Sindbad drown with my own eyes, and now you have the nerve to tell me you are him! I took you for an upright man, and yet just to get your hands on what isn’t yours, you’re willing to invent this dreadful lie.”
“Have patience, and do me the favor of hearing my story,” I said.
“Go on, then,” said the captain. “I’m listening.”

So I told him how I had escaped, how I had been lucky enough to meet the king’s grooms, and how kindly I had been welcomed at the palace. Before long I could see I was making an impression on him. Then some of the other merchants arrived and were overjoyed to see me alive again, and he declared that he recognized me too.

He threw his arms around my neck and cried, “Thank heaven you came through such a terrible danger alive! As for your goods, please take them back and do with them whatever you like.” I thanked him and told him how honest he was, and I urged him to accept several bales of merchandise as a token of my gratitude, but he would not take a thing. From the best of my goods I set aside a gift for King Mihrage. He was astonished at first, because he knew I had lost everything. But once I explained how my bales had been restored to me by a miracle, he accepted my gifts graciously and gave me many valuable things in return. Then I said goodbye to him and traded my merchandise for sandalwood, aloes wood, camphor, nutmeg, cloves, pepper and ginger. I boarded the same ship, and my trading on the voyage home went so well that I reached Balsora with roughly one hundred thousand sequins. My family welcomed me with as much joy as I felt at seeing them again. I bought land and slaves and built a great house, where I meant to live happily and, in every pleasure of life, forget all that I had suffered.

At this point Sindbad stopped and ordered the musicians to play again, and the feasting went on until evening. When it was time for the porter to leave, Sindbad handed him a purse with one hundred sequins in it and said, “Take this, Hindbad, and go home. But come back tomorrow, and you will hear more of my adventures.”
The porter went away overwhelmed by such generosity. You can imagine how warmly they greeted him at home, where his wife and children thanked their lucky stars that he had found such a benefactor.

The next day Hindbad put on his best clothes and went back to the voyager’s house, where he was welcomed with open arms. When all the guests had arrived, the banquet began just as before. After they had feasted long and merrily, Sindbad spoke to them like this:
“My friends, please give me your attention while I tell you the adventures of my second voyage, which you will find even more astonishing than the first one.”

chapters.title: Sindbad the Sailor: Second Voyage
paragraphs: As you know, when I came home from my first voyage I had decided to spend the rest of my life quietly in Baghdad. But before long I was bored with such an idle existence, and I longed to be out on the sea again.

So I bought goods that would suit the places I meant to visit, and I set sail for the second time on a good ship, with other merchants I knew to be honorable men. We traveled from island to island and often made excellent bargains. Then one day we landed on a spot that was full of fruit trees and rich in springs of fine water, yet seemed to have no houses and no people. While my companions wandered about picking flowers and fruit, I sat down in a shady place. I ate and drank my fill of the food and wine I had brought along, and then I fell asleep, lulled by the murmur of a clear brook running nearby.

I don’t know how long I slept. When I opened my eyes and jumped to my feet, I saw with horror that I was alone and the ship had gone. I ran back and forth like a madman, crying out in despair. When I finally spotted the vessel far out at sea, under full sail and just vanishing over the horizon, I bitterly wished I had stayed safely at home. But wishing could not help me, so after a while I pulled myself together and looked for some way out. I climbed a tall tree and looked first toward the sea, anxiously, but there was nothing hopeful there. Then I turned to look inland, and my curiosity was caught by something huge and dazzling white, so far away that I could not tell what it was.

I climbed down the tree, quickly gathered what was left of my food, and set off toward it as fast as I could. As I came closer, it looked like an enormous white ball, very large and tall, and when I could finally touch it, I found it wonderfully smooth and soft. There was no foothold, so I could not climb it, and I walked all the way around it looking for an opening. There was none. I counted at least fifty paces around. By now the sun was nearly setting, when suddenly it grew dark. Something like a huge black cloud swept over me, and to my amazement I saw that it was a bird of enormous size, hovering close by. Then I remembered that I had often heard sailors speak of a marvelous bird called the roc, and it came to me that the white object that had puzzled me must be its egg.

Sure enough, the bird slowly settled onto the egg and covered it with its wings to keep it warm. I crouched down close beside the egg, so that one of the bird’s feet, as thick as a tree trunk, lay right in front of me. I took off my turban and used the linen to tie myself firmly to that foot. I hoped that when the roc flew off the next morning, it would carry me away from this deserted island. And that is exactly what happened. At first light the bird rose into the air with me, up and up until I could no longer see the earth, and then it dived so fast that I nearly passed out. When I realized that the roc had landed and I was on solid ground again, I quickly untied my turban from its foot and freed myself, and only just in time. The bird pounced on a huge snake, killed it with a few blows of its powerful beak, snatched it up and flew off again, soon vanishing from sight. When I looked around me, I began to doubt that I had gained anything by leaving the deserted island.

I found myself in a deep, narrow valley, ringed by mountains that rose into the clouds and were so steep and rocky that there was no way to climb them. I wandered about, anxiously looking for a way out of this trap, and I noticed that the ground was littered with diamonds, some of them astonishingly big. The sight pleased me greatly, but my joy faded fast when I saw horrible snakes as well, so long and so thick that even the smallest of them could have swallowed an elephant with ease. Luckily for me, they seemed to hide in caves among the rocks by day and to come out only at night, probably because of their enemy the roc.

I wandered up and down the valley all day. When dusk fell I crept into a little cave and blocked the entrance with a stone. I ate some of my small supply of food and lay down to sleep, but all night long the serpents slid back and forth outside, hissing horribly, and I could hardly close my eyes for fear. I was grateful when morning light came, and when the silence told me the serpents had gone back to their dens, I came out of my cave trembling and wandered the valley again, kicking the diamonds scornfully out of my way, because I felt they were worthless to a man in my position. At last, worn out with weariness, I sat down on a rock. I had barely closed my eyes when something fell to the ground with a thud right beside me and startled me awake.

It was a huge piece of fresh meat. While I stared at it, more pieces tumbled down the cliffs in other places. I had always believed that the sailors’ stories about the famous valley of diamonds, and the clever trick some merchants used to get at the precious stones, were only travelers’ tales made up to entertain listeners. Now I saw that they must be true. These merchants came to the valley at the time when the eagles that nest in the rocks had hatched their young. The merchants threw big lumps of meat down into the valley. They landed so hard on the diamonds that some of the stones were sure to stick to them, and then the eagles swooped on the meat and carried it off to their nests to feed their hungry chicks. Then the merchants scared the parent birds away with shouts and yells and collected their treasure. Until that moment I had looked on the valley as my grave, since I could see no chance of getting out alive. Now I took heart and began to work out a way to escape. First I picked up all the largest diamonds I could find and packed them carefully into the leather bag that had held my food, which I tied firmly to my belt. Then I chose the piece of meat that seemed best for my purpose and used my turban to bind it tightly to my back. That done, I lay down on my face and waited for the eagles. Soon I heard their mighty wings beating above me, and I had the satisfaction of feeling one of them grab my piece of meat, and me with it, and rise slowly toward his nest, where he finally dropped me. Luckily the merchants were watching, and with their usual shouting they rushed to the nest and drove the eagle off. They were amazed to find me there, and also very disappointed, and all together they began to abuse me for robbing them of their usual profit. I turned to the one who seemed the most aggrieved and said, “I’m sure that if you knew everything I have suffered, you would be kinder to me. And as for diamonds, I have enough here, of the very best, for you and me and all your company.” With that, I showed them to him. The others crowded around me, marveling at my adventures and admiring the trick by which I had escaped from the valley. They led me to their camp and examined my diamonds, and they assured me that in all their years in the trade they had never seen stones to equal them in size and beauty.

I learned that each merchant chose one particular nest and took his chances on whatever he found in it. So I asked the man who owned the nest I had been carried to to take as much of my treasure as he liked. He settled for a single stone, and not at all the biggest, and told me that with such a gem his fortune was made and he would never have to work again. I stayed with the merchants for several days, and then, since they were heading home, I gladly went with them. Our road led across high mountains swarming with dreadful serpents, but we were lucky enough to escape them and at last reached the seashore. From there we sailed to the island of Rohat, where the camphor trees grow so huge that a hundred men can shelter under one of them with ease. The sap runs from a cut made high up in the tree into a vessel hung there to catch it, and it soon hardens into what we call camphor, but the tree itself withers and dies after being treated like this.

On this same island we saw the rhinoceros, an animal smaller than the elephant and larger than the buffalo. It has a single horn about a cubit long, which is solid but has a groove running from the base to the tip. The figure of a man is traced on it in white lines. The rhinoceros fights the elephant, spears him with its horn and carries him off on its head. But then the blood of its enemy blinds it, and it falls helpless to the ground. Then the roc comes, clutches them both in its talons and takes them away to feed its young. No doubt this astonishes you, but if you don’t believe my story, go to Rohat and see for yourself. So as not to tire you, I will say nothing of the many other wonderful things we saw on that island. Before we left, I traded one of my diamonds for a great deal of fine merchandise, and I made a large profit from it on our way home. At last we reached Balsora, and from there I hurried to Baghdad. The first thing I did there was to give large sums of money to the poor, and after that I settled down to enjoy in peace the riches I had won through so much toil and pain.

When he had finished telling the story of his second voyage, Sindbad again gave Hindbad a hundred sequins and invited him to come back the next day to hear how he fared on his third. The other guests also went home, but they all returned at the same hour the next day, the porter among them, whose old life of hard work and poverty had already begun to seem to him like a bad dream. Once again, when the feast was over, Sindbad asked his guests for their attention and began the story of his third voyage.

chapters.title: Sindbad the Sailor: Third Voyage
paragraphs: After a very short time, the easy, pleasant life I led made me forget the dangers of my first two voyages. And since I was still in the prime of life, I preferred to be up and doing. So I gathered the rarest and finest merchandise Baghdad had to offer, took it to Balsora, and set sail with other merchants I knew, bound for distant lands. We had called at many ports and made a good deal of profit when, one day on the open sea, a terrible wind caught us and blew us far off our course. It lasted for several days and finally drove us into a harbor on a strange island.

“I would rather have dropped anchor anywhere than here,” our captain said. “This island, and all the ones near it, are inhabited by hairy savages, and they are certain to attack us. Whatever these dwarfs do, we dare not fight back. They swarm like locusts, and if we kill even one of them, the rest will fall on us and finish us off in no time.”

These words threw the whole ship’s company into great alarm, and we soon found out that the captain had told the truth. A vast crowd of hideous savages appeared, no more than two feet tall and covered in reddish fur. They threw themselves into the waves and surrounded our vessel. Chattering all the while in a language we could not understand, they grabbed at ropes and gangways and swarmed up the ship’s side so fast and so nimbly that they almost seemed to fly.

You can imagine the rage and terror that gripped us as we watched them, not daring to stop them and unable to say a word to turn them from their purpose, whatever it was. We were not left in doubt for long. They hoisted the sails and cut the anchor cable, and sailed our ship to another island a little farther off, where they forced us ashore. Then they took the ship and went back to the place they had come from, leaving us helpless on a shore that all sailors avoid in horror, for a reason you will soon learn.

We turned away from the sea and trudged miserably inland. On the way we found herbs and fruits and ate them, feeling that since we had to die we might as well put it off as long as we could, though we had no hope of getting away. After a while, far in the distance, we saw what looked like a magnificent palace, and we dragged our tired feet toward it. When we came up to it, though, we found it was really a castle, tall and solidly built. We pushed open its heavy ebony doors and walked into the courtyard, but at the entrance to the great hall beyond we stopped dead, frozen with horror at what lay before us. On one side was a huge heap of bones—human bones—and on the other were countless spits for roasting! Overcome with despair, we collapsed trembling on the ground and lay there, unable to speak or move. The sun was going down when a loud crash woke us. The door of the hall was flung violently open, and a hideous giant came in. He was as tall as a palm tree and completely black, with a single eye that blazed like a burning coal in the middle of his forehead. His teeth were long and sharp, and they stuck out in a dreadful grin. His lower lip hung down onto his chest, his ears were like an elephant’s and covered his shoulders, and his nails were like the claws of some savage bird.

The sight was so terrible that we lost our senses and lay there like dead men. When we finally came round, the giant was sitting and studying us closely with his fearful eye. After he had looked at us long enough, he came over, reached out his hand and picked me up by the back of the neck. He turned me over this way and that, but when he felt that I was nothing but skin and bone, he put me down again and went on to the next man, and handled him the same way. At last he got to the captain, and since he was the fattest of us all, the giant lifted him in one hand, stuck him on a spit and built up an enormous fire, where he roasted him. When the giant had finished his supper, he lay down to sleep and snored as loud as thunder. We lay shivering with horror all night long, and when day broke he woke up and went out, leaving us in the castle.

When we were sure he had really gone, we jumped up and wailed over our dreadful fate until the hall rang with our cries of despair. There were many of us and only one of him, yet it never crossed our minds to kill him. Even if we had thought of it, it would have been a hard thing to do, and we could not think of any plan to free ourselves. So at last, giving in to our miserable lot, we spent the day wandering about the island, eating whatever fruit we could find, and when night came we went back to the castle, since we had looked everywhere for another shelter and found none. At sunset the giant came back, ate one of our poor companions for supper, slept and snored until dawn, and left us as he had the day before. Our situation seemed so horrible that several of my companions thought it would be better to throw themselves off the cliffs and die in the waves right away than to wait for such a wretched end. But I had a plan of escape, and I now explained it to them, and they agreed at once to try it.

“Listen, my brothers,” I said. “You know there is plenty of driftwood along the shore. Let’s build several rafts and carry them to a good spot. If our plot works, we can wait patiently for a ship to pass and rescue us from this deadly island. If it fails, we’ll have to take to the rafts quickly. Flimsy as they are, we have a better chance of saving our lives on them than we do by staying here.”

They all agreed, and we spent the day building rafts, each big enough for three people. At nightfall we went back to the castle, and soon the giant came in, and one more of us was sacrificed. But the time for our revenge was close! As soon as he had finished his horrible meal he lay down to sleep as before. When we heard him begin to snore, I and nine of the boldest of my comrades got up quietly. Each of us took a spit and heated it red-hot in the fire, and at a signal we all drove them together into the giant’s eye, blinding him completely. He gave a terrible cry and leapt to his feet, grabbing wildly in every direction to catch one of us. But as soon as the deed was done we had all run off different ways and thrown ourselves flat on the ground in corners where he was unlikely to step on us.

After searching in vain, he groped around until he found the door and ran out of it, howling dreadfully. As for us, once he was gone we hurried out of the cursed castle and stationed ourselves beside our rafts to see what would happen. Our thinking was this: if, when the sun rose, there was no sign of the giant and we no longer heard his howls, which were still reaching us faintly through the darkness and growing more and more distant, we would take it that he was dead, and we could safely stay on the island without risking our lives on the flimsy rafts. But alas! In the morning light we saw our enemy coming toward us, held up on each side by a giant almost as huge and terrible as himself, with a crowd more following right behind them. We didn’t hesitate any longer. We scrambled onto our rafts and rowed out to sea with all our strength. The giants saw their prey escaping, so they snatched up enormous chunks of rock, waded into the water and hurled them after us. They aimed so well that every raft except mine was swamped, and the unlucky men on them drowned, with nothing we could do to help. Even I and my two companions had all we could manage to keep our raft out of the giants’ reach, but by rowing hard we finally got out to open sea. There the winds and waves had us at their mercy and tossed us about all that day and night, but the next morning we found ourselves near an island, and we landed gladly.

We found delicious fruit there, and when we had eaten our fill we lay down to rest on the shore. Suddenly a loud rustling woke us. We jumped up and saw that it came from an enormous snake sliding toward us across the sand. It moved so fast that it had caught one of my companions before he could run, and despite his cries and struggles it quickly crushed the life out of him in its powerful coils and began to swallow him. By then my other companion and I were running for our lives, looking for some place safe from this new horror. We saw a tall tree and climbed into it, after first gathering a supply of fruit from the bushes nearby. When night came I fell asleep, only to be woken once more by the terrible snake. It hissed horribly around the tree and at last reared up against it, and finding my sleeping companion perched just below me, it swallowed him too and crawled away, leaving me half dead with terror.

When the sun rose I crept down from the tree. I had hardly any hope of escaping the dreadful fate that had overtaken my comrades, but life is sweet, and I was determined to do everything I could to save myself. All day long I worked in a frantic hurry, gathering heaps of dry brushwood, reeds and thorns and tying them into bundles. I made a ring of them around my tree and piled them firmly one on top of another until I had a sort of tent, where I crouched like a mouse in its hole when it sees the cat coming. You can imagine what a fearful night I spent, for the snake came back, eager to devour me, and slid round and round my flimsy shelter looking for a way in. Every moment I feared it would manage to shove some of the bundles aside, but luckily for me they held together, and when it grew light my enemy slunk back to its den, baffled and hungry. As for me, I was more dead than alive! Shaking with fright and half choked by the monster’s poisonous breath, I came out of my tent and crawled down to the sea. I felt it would be better to jump off the cliffs and end my life at once than to live through another night like that. But then, to my joy and relief, I saw a ship sailing past, and by shouting wildly and waving my turban I managed to catch the attention of her crew.

They sent a boat to pick me up, and soon I was on board, surrounded by a crowd of astonished sailors and merchants, all eager to know how I had come to be on that deserted island. When I had told my story they gave me the best food the ship had to offer, and the captain, seeing that I was in rags, kindly gave me one of his own coats. We sailed on for some time and called at many ports, until at last we came to the island of Salahat, where sandal wood grows in great quantities. We dropped anchor there, and I was standing watching the merchants unload their goods and get ready to sell or trade them, when the captain came up to me and said,

“Brother, I have some merchandise here that belonged to a passenger of mine who died. Would you do me the favor of trading with it? When I meet his heirs I’ll be able to give them the money, though it’s only fair that you should have a share for your trouble.”

I agreed gladly, since I didn’t like standing around doing nothing. He then showed me the bales and sent for the man whose job it was to keep the list of goods on board. When this man arrived, he asked under what name the merchandise should be entered.
“Under the name of Sindbad the Sailor,” the captain answered.

I was greatly startled at this, but when I looked at him carefully I recognized him as the captain of the ship I had sailed on for my second voyage, though he had changed a great deal since then. He believed me to be dead, so it was no wonder that he had not recognized me.
“So, captain,” I said, “the merchant who owned those bales was called Sindbad?”

“Yes,” he replied. “That was his name. He came from Baghdad and joined my ship at Balsora. But by bad luck he got left behind on a desert island where we had put in to fill our water-casks, and it was four hours before anyone noticed he was missing. By then the wind had picked up, and we couldn’t turn back for him.”
“So you think he died?” I asked.
“Alas, yes,” he answered.
“Why, captain!” I cried. “Take a good look at me. I am that Sindbad, who fell asleep on the island and woke to find himself abandoned!”
The captain stared at me in amazement, but before long he was convinced that I was telling the truth, and he was overjoyed that I had escaped.
“At least I can now get that piece of carelessness off my conscience,” he said. “Take your goods, and the profit I’ve made on them for you, and may you do well from now on.”

I took them gratefully, and as we sailed from island to island I bought up supplies of cloves, cinnamon and other spices. In one place I saw a tortoise twenty cubits long and just as wide, and a fish that looked like a cow, with skin so thick that it was used to make shields. I saw another creature that was like a camel in shape and color. So, bit by bit, we made our way back to Balsora, and I went home to Baghdad with so much money that I couldn’t count it myself, besides endless treasures. I gave generously to the poor and bought a lot more land to add to what I already owned, and that was the end of my third voyage.

When Sindbad had finished his story, he gave Hindbad another hundred sequins, and Hindbad left with the other guests. The next day, when they had all gathered again and the banquet was over, their host went on with his adventures.

chapters.title: Sindbad the Sailor: Fourth Voyage
paragraphs: I was rich and happy after my third voyage, but I couldn’t bring myself to stay at home for good. I loved trading, and I enjoyed anything new and strange, so I put my affairs in order and set out on a journey through some of the Persian provinces, having first sent supplies of goods ahead to wait for me in the different places I meant to visit. I boarded a ship at a distant seaport, and for a while all went well. But in the end a violent hurricane struck, and our vessel was wrecked in spite of everything our excellent captain could do to save her, and many of the company drowned. A few of us, myself included, were lucky enough to be washed ashore clinging to pieces of the wreck, for the storm had driven us close to an island. We scrambled up out of the waves’ reach and threw ourselves down, utterly exhausted, to wait for morning.

At daybreak we walked inland and soon saw some huts, and we headed for them. As we came near, their dark-skinned inhabitants poured out in great numbers and surrounded us, and we were led off to their houses and, in a way, shared out among our captors. I and five others were taken into one hut and made to sit on the ground, and we were given some herbs, which the islanders signaled to us to eat. I noticed that they did not touch the herbs themselves, so I was careful only to pretend to taste my share. My companions, though, were very hungry and foolishly ate up everything put in front of them, and very soon I had the horror of watching them go completely mad. They chattered without stopping, but I couldn’t understand a word, and they paid no attention when I spoke to them. Our captors then brought out big bowls of rice cooked in coconut oil, and my crazed companions ate it eagerly, while I tasted only a few grains. I understood perfectly well that our captors meant to fatten us quickly so they could eat us, and that is exactly what happened. My unlucky companions had lost their reason, so they felt no worry or fear and ate greedily everything they were given. Soon they were fat, and that was the end of them. I grew thinner day by day, because I ate very little, and even that little did me no good, for I was so afraid of what lay ahead. But since I was so far from a tempting morsel, I was allowed to wander about freely. One day, when all the islanders had gone off on some expedition and left only an old man to guard me, I managed to slip away from him and dashed into the forest. The more he shouted at me to come back, the faster I ran, until I had left him far behind.

For seven days I hurried on, stopping only when darkness made me, and living mostly on coconuts, which gave me both food and drink. On the eighth day I came out at the seashore, where I saw a party of white men picking pepper, which grew thickly all around. The work they were doing put me at ease, so I walked up to them. They greeted me in Arabic and asked who I was and where I had come from. I was overjoyed to hear a language I knew, and I gladly told them how I had been shipwrecked and then captured by the blacks. “But those savages eat men!” they said. “How did you get away?” I told them what I have just told you, and they were astonished. I stayed with them until they had gathered all the pepper they wanted. Then they took me back to their own country and brought me before their king, who welcomed me generously. I had to tell him my adventures too, and he was amazed by them. When I had finished, he gave orders that I should be given food and clothing and treated with respect.

The island was crowded with people and rich in every kind of good thing, and there was a great deal of trade in the capital, where I soon felt at home and content. The king also favored me especially, and because of this everyone, at court and in the town alike, tried to make my life pleasant. One thing struck me as very odd: from the highest to the lowest, every man rode his horse without a bridle or stirrups. One day I took the liberty of asking his majesty why they did not use them, and he answered, “You speak of things I have never heard of before!” That gave me an idea. I found a skilled craftsman and had him cut out the frame of a saddle to my design. I padded it, covered it with fine leather and decorated it with rich gold embroidery. Then I had a locksmith make a bit and a pair of spurs from a pattern I drew for him. When everything was finished, I presented it all to the king and showed him how to use it. I saddled one of his horses, and he mounted and rode around, delighted with the novelty, and to show his thanks he rewarded me with large gifts. After that I had to make saddles for all the leading officers of the royal household, and since they all gave me rich presents, I soon grew very wealthy and became a person of some importance in the city.

One day the king summoned me and said, “Sindbad, I have a favor to ask of you. My people and I both think highly of you, and we want you to spend the rest of your life among us. So I would like you to marry a rich and beautiful lady whom I will find for you, and to stop thinking about your own country.”

The king’s word was law, so I accepted the lovely bride he gave me, and we lived happily together. All the same, I fully intended to escape at the first chance and return to Baghdad. Things were going well for me like this when the wife of one of my neighbors, a man I had become quite friendly with, fell ill and soon died. I went to his house to comfort him, and found him sunk in grief.
“May Heaven protect you,” I said, “and give you a long life!”
“Alas!” he answered, “what use is it to say that, when I have only one hour left to live!”
“Come, come!” I said, “it surely cannot be as bad as that. I hope you will be spared to me for many years.”

“I hope your own life will be long,” he answered, “but as for me, it is all over. I have put my house in order, and today I will be buried with my wife. This has been the law on our island since the earliest times—when a wife dies, her living husband goes into the grave with her, and when a husband dies, his living wife goes with him. Our fathers did it, and so must we. The law never changes, and everyone must obey it!”

While he spoke, the friends and relatives of the unfortunate couple began to gather. The body, dressed in rich robes and glittering with jewels, was laid on an open bier, and the procession set out for a high mountain some distance from the city. The miserable husband, wrapped from head to foot in a black cloak, followed sadly behind.

When they reached the burial place, the corpse was lowered, just as it was, into a deep pit. Then the husband said goodbye to all his friends and lay down on a second bier, on which were placed seven small loaves of bread and a jug of water. He too was let down, down, down into the depths of that horrible cavern, and a stone was set over the opening. The mourners then trailed back to the city.

You can imagine that I did not watch all this unmoved. To everyone else it was something they had known since childhood, but I was so horrified that I could not keep from telling the king what I felt.

“Sire,” I said, “I cannot tell you how astonished I am at the strange custom in your lands of burying the living with the dead. In all my travels I have never come across so cruel and horrible a law.”
“What can you expect, Sindbad?” he answered. “It is the law for everybody. I would be buried with the Queen myself if she died first.”
“But, your Majesty,” I said, “may I ask whether this law applies to foreigners as well?”
“Why, yes,” answered the king, smiling in what I could only take as a very heartless way, “they are no exception, if they have married in this country.”

When I heard this, I went home deeply downcast, and from then on I never had a moment’s peace. If my wife so much as had an ache in her little finger, I imagined she was about to die, and sure enough, before long she really did fall ill and within a few days she breathed her last. I was in despair, for being buried alive seemed to me an even worse fate than being eaten by cannibals, yet there was no way out. My wife’s body, dressed in her richest robes and hung with all her jewels, was laid on the bier. I walked behind it, and after me came a great procession, led by the king and all his nobles. In this order we reached the fatal mountain, which was part of a high range along the sea.

There I made one more desperate attempt to move the king and the others standing by to pity, hoping to save myself even at the last moment, but it did no good. Nobody spoke to me, and they seemed to hurry through their dreadful task. Before I knew it I was being lowered into the dark pit, with my seven loaves and my jug of water beside me. The stone was rolled into place over my head almost before I reached the bottom, and I was left to my fate. A faint ray of light came into the cavern through some crack, and when I found the courage to look around, I saw that I was in a huge vault, scattered with bones and the bodies of the dead. I even thought I could hear the dying sighs of people who had been brought into this dismal place alive, as I had been. I screamed aloud in rage and despair, all in vain, blaming myself for the greed and love of adventure that had brought me to this, but in the end I grew calmer. I picked up my bread and water, wrapped my cloak around my face, and felt my way along toward the far end of the cavern, where the air was fresher.

I lived there in darkness and misery until my food ran out. Just as I was close to dying of hunger, the rock above was rolled away and I saw a bier being lowered into the cavern, with a man’s corpse on it. In an instant I made up my mind. The woman who came down after him had nothing ahead of her but a slow death, and I would be doing her a kindness if I shortened her suffering. So when she was let down, already senseless with terror, I was waiting with a huge bone in my hand. One blow left her dead, and I took the bread and water that gave me some hope of living. I resorted to this desperate measure several times, and I do not know how long I had been a prisoner when one day I thought I heard something near me, breathing loudly. I turned toward the sound and dimly saw a shadowy shape, which fled as I moved and squeezed itself through a gap in the wall. I chased it as fast as I could and found myself in a narrow crack in the rocks, just wide enough for me to force my way along. I followed it for what felt like many miles, and at last I saw a glimmer of light ahead, which grew brighter with every step, until I came out on the seashore with a joy I cannot describe. When I was sure I was not dreaming, I realized that the creature must have been some small animal that had come into the cavern from the sea and run off when I disturbed it, showing me a way out that I could never have found myself. I quickly looked about and saw that nobody from the town could pursue me here.

The mountains dropped steeply to the sea, and there was no road over them. Once I was sure of that, I went back into the cavern and gathered a rich treasure of diamonds, rubies, emeralds and jewels of every kind, which lay scattered over the ground. I tied them up in bales, stored them in a safe spot on the beach, and then waited hopefully for a ship to pass. I kept watch for two days before a single sail appeared, so I was delighted when at last a vessel came fairly close to the shore, and by waving my arms and shouting I managed to catch the crew’s attention. They sent a boat for me, and when the sailors asked how I had ended up in such a state, I said I had been shipwrecked two days before but had scrambled ashore with the bales, which I pointed out to them. Luckily they believed my story, and without even looking at the place where they had found me, they picked up my bundles and rowed me back to the ship. Once on board, I soon saw that the captain was too busy with the difficulties of navigation to pay me much attention, though he kindly made me welcome, and he would not even take the jewels I offered to pay for my passage. Our voyage went well, and after visiting many lands and buying a great store of fine goods in each, I arrived at last in Baghdad again, with riches beyond anything I had had before. Once more I gave large sums to the poor and endowed all the mosques in the city, and then I gave myself up to my friends and relatives, spending my time with them in feasting and merrymaking.

Here Sindbad stopped, and all his listeners declared that the adventures of his fourth voyage had pleased them more than anything they had heard so far. Then they took their leave, with Hindbad among them, who had once again been given a hundred sequins, and who, like the rest, had been asked to come back the next day to hear the story of the fifth voyage.
When the time came, everyone was in place, and once they had eaten and drunk everything set before them, Sindbad began his tale.

chapters.title: Sindbad the Sailor: Fifth Voyage
paragraphs: Even all I had been through could not make me content with a quiet life. I soon grew tired of its pleasures and longed for change and adventure. So I set out once more, but this time in a ship of my own, which I built and fitted out at the nearest seaport. I wanted to be free to call at any port I liked and to take my time, but since I did not mean to carry enough goods to fill the hold, I invited several merchants of different nations to sail with me. We left with the first favorable wind, and after a long voyage on the open sea we landed on an unknown island, which turned out to be uninhabited. We decided to explore it anyway, but we had not gone far when we found a roc’s egg, as big as the one I had seen before and clearly almost ready to hatch, for the young bird’s beak had already broken through the shell. Whatever I said to stop them, the merchants with me fell on it with their hatchets, smashing the shell and killing the young roc. Then they lit a fire on the ground, hacked pieces off the bird and began to roast them, while I stood by in horror.

They had hardly finished their ill-omened meal when the sky above us was darkened by two huge shadows. The captain of my ship knew from experience what this meant, and he called out to us that the parent birds were coming and urged us to get on board as fast as we could. We did so and the sails were raised, but before we had gone any distance the rocs reached their plundered nest and circled over it, shrieking horribly when they found the mangled remains of their young one. For a moment we lost sight of them and were comforting ourselves that we had got away, when they reappeared and rose into the air right above our ship, and we saw that each one held an enormous rock in its claws, ready to crush us. There was a moment of breathless waiting. Then one bird let go, and the huge block of stone came hurtling through the air, but thanks to the quick thinking of the helmsman, who swung our ship sharply to one side, it fell into the sea right beside us, splitting the water so deep that we could nearly see the bottom. We had barely time to draw a breath of relief before the other rock came down with a mighty crash in the very middle of our unlucky ship, smashing it into a thousand pieces and crushing the passengers and crew or throwing them into the sea. I went down with the rest, but I was lucky enough to come up unhurt, and by holding a piece of driftwood with one hand and swimming with the other I kept myself afloat until the tide washed me up on an island. Its shores were steep and rocky, but I climbed up safely and threw myself down to rest on the green turf.

Once I had got some strength back, I started looking around the place where I had ended up, and it seemed to me a garden of delights. Trees stood everywhere, heavy with flowers and fruit, and a clear stream wound in and out of their shade. At nightfall I slept soundly in a snug hollow. Still, the thought that I was alone in a foreign land kept jolting me awake to stare around in fear, and at those moments I wished with all my heart that I had stayed comfortably at home. But the morning sun gave me back my courage, and I went wandering among the trees again, though always uneasy about what I might come across next. I had gone some way into the island when I saw an old man sitting on the river bank, bent over and frail, and at first I took him for a fellow shipwreck survivor. I went up and greeted him kindly, but all he did was nod. I asked what he was doing there, and he made signs that he wanted to cross the river to pick fruit, and seemed to be begging me to carry him on my back. I felt sorry for his age and weakness, so I lifted him up and waded across the stream. At the far bank I stooped so he could get off easily and told him to climb down. But instead of letting me set him on his feet (even now I laugh to think of it!), this creature who had looked so decrepit sprang lightly onto my shoulders, hooked his legs around my neck and squeezed so tightly that I nearly choked, and I was so terrified that I fell senseless to the ground. When I came to, my enemy was still sitting there, though he had loosened his grip just enough for me to breathe. As soon as he saw me stir, he poked me cleverly, first with one foot and then the other, until I was forced to get up and stagger around under the trees with him on my back while he picked and ate the best of the fruit. This went on all day. Even at night, when I threw myself down half dead from exhaustion, the dreadful old man kept hold of my neck, and at the first glimmer of morning he drummed on me with his heels until I had to wake and drag myself on again, my heart full of rage and bitterness.

One day I walked past a tree with several dry gourds lying beneath it. I picked one up and, to amuse myself, hollowed it out and squeezed into it the juice of several bunches of grapes, which hung from every bush. When it was full I left it wedged in the fork of a tree. A few days later, as I was carrying that hateful old man past the spot, I grabbed my gourd and had the pleasure of drinking some excellent wine, so good and so refreshing that I forgot all about my awful burden and began to sing and dance about.

The old monster quickly noticed what the drink had done to me, and that I was carrying him more lightly than usual. He reached out a bony hand and took the gourd, tasted it carefully at first, and then drained it down to the last drop. The wine was strong and the gourd was large, so he too began to sing, after a fashion, and soon I had the joy of feeling the iron grip of his goblin legs go slack. With one great effort I flung him to the ground, and he never moved again. I was so happy to be finally free of this uncanny old man that I ran leaping and bounding down to the shore. By the greatest good luck, I found some sailors there whose ship was anchored off the island so they could enjoy the delicious fruit and refill their water supply.

They listened to the story of my escape in amazement. “You fell into the hands of the Old Man of the Sea,” they said, “and it is a mercy he did not strangle you, as he has everyone else whose shoulders he has managed to climb onto. This island is famous for his evil deeds, and no merchant or sailor who lands here likes to wander far from his companions.” After we had talked for a while, they took me back with them on board their ship, where the captain welcomed me kindly. We soon set sail, and after several days we reached a large, prosperous-looking town where every house was built of stone. We anchored there, and one of the merchants, who had been very friendly to me during the voyage, took me ashore with him and showed me a lodging kept for foreign merchants. Then he gave me a large sack and pointed out a group of other men who each had one like it.
“Go with them,” he said, “and do what they do. But take care never to lose sight of them, because if you wander off, your life will be in danger.”

He gave me some provisions, said goodbye, and I set off with my new companions. I soon learned that our task was to fill our sacks with coconuts. But when I finally saw the trees, so enormously tall, with slender trunks too smooth to climb, I had no idea how we were going to manage it. The tops of the coconut palms were swarming with monkeys, big and small, leaping from tree to tree with astonishing agility. They seemed curious about us and upset by our arrival. I was surprised, at first, when my companions collected stones and started throwing them at these lively creatures, which looked harmless to me. But I soon saw the reason and joined in eagerly. The monkeys grew angry, and to pay us back in kind they began tearing nuts off the trees and hurling them at us with furious, spiteful gestures. So with very little effort our sacks were full of fruit that we could never have got any other way.

As soon as we had gathered all we could carry, we went back to the town. There my friend bought my share and advised me to keep up the same work until I had earned enough to get home. I did, and before long I had saved a fair amount. Just then I heard that a trading ship was about to sail. I said goodbye to my friend and boarded it, taking a good supply of coconuts with me. We sailed first to the islands where pepper grows, and then to Comari, where the best aloes wood is found and where, by a law that never changes, no one drinks wine. There I traded my coconuts for pepper and good aloes wood, and I went pearl fishing with some of the other merchants. My divers were so lucky that I soon had a huge number of pearls, large and perfect ones. I came back to Baghdad, delighted, with all these treasures, and sold them for large sums of money. As before, I did not forget to give a tenth of it to the poor. After that I rested from my labors and enjoyed every pleasure my wealth could buy.
When Sindbad had finished his story, he ordered that one hundred sequins be given to Hindbad, and the guests left. But after the next day’s feast he began the account of his sixth voyage, like this.

chapters.title: Sindbad the Sailor: Sixth Voyage
paragraphs: You must wonder how, after being shipwrecked five times and meeting with unheard-of dangers, I could tempt fortune again and risk fresh trouble. I am surprised myself when I look back. But it was plainly my fate to wander, and after a year of rest I got ready for a sixth voyage, ignoring the pleading of my friends and relatives, who did everything they could to keep me at home. This time, instead of taking the Persian Gulf, I traveled a long way overland and finally set sail from a distant Indian port, with a captain who planned a long voyage. And long it was, because we met with stormy weather that drove us completely off course. For many days neither the captain nor the pilot knew where we were or where we were heading. When they finally worked out our position, we had little to be glad about. The captain threw his turban down on the deck and tore at his beard, and declared that we were in the most dangerous spot in the whole wide sea, caught in a current that was at that very moment sweeping us to our destruction. It was all too true! Whatever the sailors did, we were swept at terrifying speed toward the foot of a mountain that rose straight out of the sea, and our ship was smashed to pieces on the rocks at its base. But we had managed to scramble ashore first, bringing the most precious of our belongings with us. When we had done that, the captain said to us:
“Now that we are here, we might as well start digging our graves right away, because no shipwrecked sailor has ever returned from this deadly place.”
His words filled us with despair, and we began to weep over our miserable fate.

The mountain made up the seaward edge of a large island, and the narrow strip of rocky shore where we stood was littered with the wreckage of a thousand fine ships. The bones of the unlucky sailors gleamed white in the sun, and we shuddered to think how soon ours would be added to the pile. All around lay huge quantities of the most costly goods, and treasures were heaped in every crack in the rocks, but all of this only made the scene more desolate. One thing struck me as very odd. A river of clear fresh water gushed out of the mountain not far from where we stood, but instead of flowing into the sea, as rivers usually do, it turned sharply aside and flowed out of sight beneath a natural archway of rock. When I went to look more closely, I found that inside the cave the walls were thick with diamonds and rubies and masses of crystal, and the floor was strewn with ambergris. So there on that desolate shore we gave ourselves up to our fate, since there was no way to climb the mountain, and if a ship had appeared it could only have shared our doom. The first thing our captain did was to divide all the food we had equally among us, and after that how long each man lived depended on how long he could make his share last. I myself could live on very little.

Even so, by the time I had buried the last of my companions, my supplies were so low that I hardly thought I would live long enough to dig my own grave, which I started to do. I bitterly regretted the restless nature that was always getting me into such trouble, and I thought longingly of all the comfort and luxury I had left behind. But luckily for me, I took a fancy to stand once more beside the river where it plunged out of sight into the depths of the cavern, and as I stood there an idea came to me. This river, which hid itself underground, surely came out again somewhere far off. Why should I not build a raft and trust myself to its swift current? If I died before I saw daylight again, I would be no worse off than I was now, since death was staring me in the face. And there was always a chance that, being born under a lucky star, I might find myself safe and sound in some pleasant land. At any rate, I decided to take the risk. I quickly built myself a sturdy raft out of driftwood, tied with strong cords, of which there were plenty lying on the beach, more than enough. Then I made up many bundles of rubies, emeralds, rock crystal, ambergris and precious fabrics and tied them onto my raft, taking care to keep it balanced. I sat down on it with two small oars that I had made lying ready at hand, and I untied the rope that held it to the bank. Once in the current, my raft shot swiftly under the gloomy archway, and I found myself in total darkness, carried smoothly along by the rapid river. On I went, for what seemed to me many nights and days. Once the channel grew so narrow that I only just escaped being crushed against the rocky roof, and after that I took care to lie flat on my precious bales. I ate only what I absolutely needed to stay alive, but the moment I had dreaded came all the same. After I swallowed my last scrap of food, I began to wonder whether I must die of hunger after all. Then, worn out with worry and exhaustion, I fell into a deep sleep. When I opened my eyes again I was back in the light of day. A beautiful country lay before me, and my raft was tied to the river bank, surrounded by friendly-looking black men. I stood up and greeted them, and they answered me, but I could not understand a word of their language. I was completely bewildered by this sudden return to life and light, and I murmured to myself in Arabic, “Close your eyes, and while you sleep, Heaven will change your fortune from bad to good.”
One of the natives, who understood this language, then stepped forward and said:

“My brother, do not be surprised to see us. This is our land, and when we came to fetch water from the river we saw your raft floating down it, and one of us swam out and brought you to the shore. We have waited for you to wake. Now tell us where you come from and where you were going by that dangerous route.”

I answered that nothing would please me more than to tell them, but that I was starving and would gladly eat something first. I was soon given everything I needed, and when I had eaten my fill I told them truthfully everything that had happened to me. When my tale was translated for them, they were lost in wonder. They said that such surprising adventures should be told to their king only by the man they had happened to. So they found a horse and set me on it, and we set out, followed by several strong men carrying my raft, just as it was, on their shoulders. In this order we marched into the city of Serendib, where the natives presented me to their king. I greeted him in the Indian fashion, throwing myself at his feet and kissing the ground, but the king told me to rise and sit beside him, and first asked me my name.
“I am Sindbad,” I answered, “and men call me ‘the Sailor’, because I have sailed far upon many seas.”
“And how did you come to be here?” asked the king.
I told him my story and hid nothing, and he was so surprised and delighted that he ordered my adventures to be written in letters of gold and kept in the archives of his kingdom.

Soon my raft was brought in and the bundles were opened in front of him. The king declared that in all his treasury there were no rubies and emeralds like those lying in great heaps before him. Seeing that he looked at them with interest, I took the liberty of saying that I myself and everything I had were at his disposal. But he answered me with a smile:

“No, Sindbad. Heaven forbid that I should want your wealth. I would rather add to it, because I don’t want you to leave my kingdom without some sign of my goodwill.” Then he ordered his officers to find me a comfortable house at his own expense, and sent slaves to serve me and to carry my raft and my bales to my new home. You can imagine how I praised his generosity and thanked him. I went to his audience chamber every day, and the rest of my time I spent seeing everything in the city that was worth a visit. Serendib lies right on the equator, so the days and nights there are the same length. The capital stands at the end of a lovely valley, below the tallest mountain in the world, which rises in the middle of the island. I was curious enough to climb to the very top, since that was the place where Adam was cast out of Paradise. Rubies are found there, along with many other precious things, and rare plants grow in plenty, as well as cedars and coconut palms. Divers hunt for pearls along the shore and at the river mouths, and in some valleys diamonds are common. After many days I asked the king’s permission to go back to my own country, and he kindly agreed. He also piled rich gifts on me, and when I came to say goodbye he gave me a royal present and a letter for the Commander of the Faithful, our sovereign lord, saying, “Please hand these to the Caliph Haroun al Raschid, and tell him I am his friend.”

I accepted the task respectfully, and before long I boarded the ship the king himself had picked out for me. The king’s letter was written in blue letters on a rare and costly skin of a yellowish color, and this is what it said: “From the King of the Indies, who has a thousand elephants walking before him, who lives in a palace whose roof blazes with a hundred thousand rubies, and whose treasury holds twenty thousand diamond crowns, to the Caliph Haroun al Raschid, greetings. The gift we send you is hardly worth your notice, but we ask you to take it as a sign of the respect and friendship we feel for you, which we are glad to show by this token. We ask the same regard from you, if you think us worthy of it. Farewell, brother.”

The gift was a vase carved from a single ruby, six inches tall and as thick as my finger, and filled with the finest pearls, all large and perfectly round and bright. Next came an enormous snake skin, with scales as big as a sequin, which kept anyone who slept on it from falling ill. There were also large quantities of aloes wood, camphor and pistachio nuts, and last of all a beautiful slave girl, whose robes glittered with jewels.

After a long and fortunate voyage we came ashore at Balsora, and I hurried on to Baghdad. I took the king’s letter and went to the palace gate, with the beautiful slave behind me and several of my relatives carrying the treasure.

Once I had said what I had come for, I was taken in to see the Caliph. I bowed low before him and handed over the letter and the king’s gift. When he had looked them over, he asked me whether the Prince of Serendib was really as rich and powerful as he claimed.

“Commander of the Faithful,” I answered, bowing humbly again, “I can assure Your Majesty that he has not exaggerated his wealth and grandeur at all. Nothing compares with the splendor of his palace. When he rides out, his throne is set up on the back of an elephant, and his ministers, his favorites and his courtiers ride on either side of him. An officer sits on the elephant’s neck with a golden lance in his hand, and behind the king stands another, who holds a golden pillar topped with an emerald as long as my hand. A thousand men dressed in cloth of gold, on elephants in rich trappings, go ahead of him. As the procession moves forward, the officer who steers the king’s elephant calls out, ‘Look upon the mighty monarch, the powerful and brave Sultan of the Indies, whose palace is roofed with a hundred thousand rubies, and who owns twenty thousand diamond crowns! Look upon a monarch greater than Solomon and Mihrage in all their glory!’”
“Then the man standing behind the throne replies, ‘This king, so great and powerful, must die, must die, must die!’”
“And the first man takes up the cry again, ‘Praise be to Him who lives for ever.’”
“And one more thing, my lord. In Serendib there is no need for a judge, because the people bring their cases to the king himself.”
The Caliph was very pleased with what I had told him.
“From the king’s letter,” he said, “I took him to be a wise man. It seems he deserves his people, and his people deserve him.”
With that he sent me away with rich presents, and I went home in peace.
When Sindbad finished, his guests left. Hindbad first received a hundred sequins, but they all came back the next day to hear about the seventh voyage, which Sindbad began like this.

chapters.title: Sindbad the Sailor: Seventh and Last Voyage
paragraphs: After my sixth voyage I was fully resolved never to go to sea again. I was old enough now to value a quiet life, and I had taken risks enough. All I wanted was to live out my days in peace. But one day, while I was entertaining a number of friends, I was told that an officer of the Caliph wanted to speak with me. When he was shown in, he told me to follow him to Haroun al Raschid, and I did. After I had greeted him, the Caliph said:
“I sent for you, Sindbad, because I need your help. I have chosen you to carry a letter and a gift to the King of Serendib, in answer to his message of friendship.”
The Caliph’s order struck me like a bolt of lightning.

“Commander of the Faithful,” I answered, “I am ready to do whatever Your Majesty commands. But I humbly beg you to remember that the terrible sufferings I have been through have left me utterly discouraged. In fact, I have sworn never to leave Baghdad again.”
Then I told him at length about some of my strangest adventures, and he listened patiently.

“I grant you,” he said, “that you have had some remarkable experiences. But I don’t see why they should stop you from doing what I ask. All you have to do is go straight to Serendib and deliver my message. After that you are free to come back and live as you please. But you must go. My honor and dignity require it.”

I saw there was no way out, so I said I would obey. The Caliph, delighted to have his way, gave me a thousand sequins for the cost of the journey. I was ready to leave soon enough, and with the letter and the present I boarded a ship at Balsora and sailed swiftly and safely to Serendib. There I explained why I had come, and I was welcomed and taken to the king, who greeted me gladly.
“Welcome, Sindbad,” he cried. “I have often thought of you, and I am glad to see you again.”

I thanked him for the honor he showed me, and then I laid out the Caliph’s gifts. First there was a bed with full hangings, all of cloth of gold, which had cost a thousand sequins, and another like it in crimson. Then fifty richly embroidered robes, and a hundred of the finest white linen, from Cairo, Suez, Cufa and Alexandria. There were more beds of other styles, an agate vase carved with a man shooting an arrow at a lion, and finally an expensive table that had once belonged to King Solomon. The King of Serendib was pleased to hear that the Caliph felt so friendly toward him. My task was done and I was eager to leave, but it was a while before the king would even consider letting me go. At last he sent me off with many presents. I lost no time in boarding a ship, which sailed at once, and for four days all went well. On the fifth day we had the bad luck to run into pirates. They took our ship, killing everyone who resisted and taking prisoner those who were sensible enough to give in at once, and I was one of them. After they had stripped us of everything we owned, they made us put on wretched clothes, sailed to a distant island and sold us there as slaves. I fell into the hands of a rich merchant, who took me home with him and gave me good clothes and food. After a few days he sent for me and asked what I was able to do.
I told him I was a wealthy merchant, taken by pirates, and so had never learned a trade.
“Tell me,” he said, “can you shoot a bow?”
I replied that it had been one of my pastimes when I was young, and that with practice my skill would no doubt return.

So he gave me a bow and arrows, sat me on his own elephant beside him and rode to a huge forest far from the town. When we reached the wildest part, we stopped, and my master said to me, “This forest is full of elephants. Hide in this big tree and shoot at everything that goes by. When you have killed one, come and tell me.”

He gave me a supply of food and went back to the town, and I climbed high into the tree and kept watch. That night I saw nothing, but just after sunrise the next morning a large herd of elephants came crashing and stamping past. I quickly shot several arrows, and in the end one of the great animals dropped dead. The others withdrew, which left me free to climb down from my hiding place and run back to tell my master of my success. He praised me and gave me good things to eat. Then we went back to the forest together and dug a huge pit, in which we buried the elephant I had killed, so that when only the skeleton was left my master could come back and take its tusks.

I hunted like this for two months, and not a day went by without my killing an elephant. Of course, I did not always wait in the same tree, but in one place one day and another place the next. One morning, as I watched the elephants approach, I was surprised to see that instead of walking past my tree as they usually did, they stopped and surrounded it. They trumpeted horribly and shook the ground with their heavy feet. When I saw that all their eyes were fixed on me, I was terrified, and the arrows fell from my trembling hand. I had good reason to be afraid, because a moment later the biggest of them wrapped his trunk around the trunk of my tree and with one huge heave ripped it out by the roots, so that I tumbled to the ground tangled in its branches. I was sure my last hour had come. But the huge creature picked me up, quite gently, and set me on his back, where I clung more dead than alive. Then he turned and, with the whole herd behind him, crashed away into the thick forest. It seemed a long time before the elephant put me down on my feet again. I stood as if in a dream and watched the herd turn and stamp off in another direction, until the undergrowth hid them. Then I pulled myself together and looked around. I was standing on the side of a great hill, and as far as I could see in both directions it was strewn with elephants’ bones and tusks. “This must be where elephants come to die,” I told myself. “They must have brought me here so that I would stop hunting them, since all I want is their tusks, and there are more lying here than I could carry away in a lifetime.”

So I turned and headed for the city as fast as I could, and I did not see a single elephant on the way. That convinced me that they had drawn back deeper into the forest to leave the path to the Ivory Hill open, and I could not admire their wisdom enough. After a day and a night I reached my master’s house, and he welcomed me with joyful surprise.

“Ah, poor Sindbad,” he cried, “I was wondering what had become of you. When I went to the forest, I found the tree freshly uprooted and the arrows lying next to it, and I feared I would never see you again. Please tell me how you escaped with your life.”

I quickly told him everything. Next day the two of us rode to the Ivory Hill, and he was delighted to see that my story was true. We piled as many tusks onto our elephant as it could bear, and while we were heading back to the city, he spoke again:

“My brother—I can no longer treat as a slave a man who has made me so rich—take your freedom, and may Heaven bless you. I will not hide it from you any longer: these wild elephants have killed many of our slaves every year. However much good advice we gave them, sooner or later they were caught. You alone have escaped the tricks of these animals, so you must be under the special protection of Heaven. Now, thanks to you, the whole town will grow rich without losing any more lives. So I will not only give you your freedom, I will also give you a fortune.”
I answered, “Master, I thank you and wish you every success. For myself, I ask only for my freedom to go back to my own country.”
“Very well,” he said. “The monsoon will soon bring the ivory ships here, and then I will send you on your way with something to pay for your passage.”

So I stayed with him until the monsoon came, and every day we added to our stock of ivory until all his warehouses were overflowing. By then the other merchants knew the secret, but there was more than enough for everyone. When the ships finally arrived, my master picked out the one I was to sail on himself and put aboard a large supply of fine provisions for me, along with plenty of ivory and all the most valuable curiosities of the country. I could not thank him enough, and so we parted. I left the ship at the first port we reached, because after everything the sea had done to me I did not feel easy on it. I sold my ivory for a great deal of gold and bought many rare and expensive presents, then loaded my pack animals and joined a caravan of merchants. The journey was long and wearisome, but I put up with it patiently, thinking that at least I no longer had to fear storms, pirates, serpents or any of the other dangers I had suffered before. At last we reached Baghdad. My first duty was to go before the Caliph and report on my mission. He told me my long absence had worried him greatly, but that he had hoped for the best all the same. When he heard of my adventure among the elephants, he was amazed, and said he would not have believed it if he had not known how truthful I was.

The Caliph had his scribes copy down this story and the others I had told him in letters of gold, and ordered them stored among his treasures. I said goodbye to him, well pleased with the honors and gifts he had given me. Since then I have rested from my labors and devoted myself entirely to my family and friends.
So Sindbad finished the tale of his seventh and last voyage. Then he turned to Hindbad and said:

“Well, my friend, what do you think now? Have you ever heard of anyone who suffered more than I have, or came closer to death so many times? Surely it is only right that I should now live in ease and peace?”

Hindbad stepped forward, kissed his hand respectfully, and answered, “Sir, you have indeed been through terrible dangers. My troubles are nothing beside yours. And the generous way you spend your wealth shows that you deserve it. May you live long and happily to enjoy it.”

Sindbad then gave him a hundred sequins and from that day counted him among his friends. He also made him give up his work as a porter and eat at his table every day, so that for the rest of his life Hindbad would remember Sindbad the Sailor.

chapters.title: The Little Hunchback
paragraphs: Long ago, in the kingdom of Kashgar, which as everyone knows lies on the borders of Great Tartary, there lived a tailor and his wife, who were very fond of each other. One day, while the tailor was busy at work, a little hunchback came and sat down at the door of his shop and began to sing and play his tambourine. The tailor found the man’s clowning amusing and thought he would bring him home to entertain his wife. The hunchback agreed, so the tailor shut up his shop and the two of them set off together.

When they got to the house, supper was already laid out, and within minutes the three of them were sitting down to a fine fish that the tailor’s wife had cooked herself. But by bad luck the hunchback swallowed a large bone, and although the tailor and his wife did everything they could to help him, he choked and died on the spot. Besides feeling sorry for the poor man, the couple were badly frightened for themselves, because if the police heard of it, these decent people might be thrown into prison for deliberate murder. To avoid this dreadful disaster, they both started thinking of a plan to throw suspicion onto somebody else, and in the end they decided the best thing was to blame a Jewish doctor who lived nearby. So the tailor took the hunchback by the head, his wife took him by the feet, and they carried him to the doctor’s house. They knocked at the door, which opened straight onto a steep staircase. Before long a servant appeared, feeling her way down the dark stairs, and asked what they wanted.

“Tell your master,” said the tailor, “that we have brought him a very sick man to cure. And,” he added, holding out some money, “give him this in advance, so he won’t think he is wasting his time.” The servant went back up the stairs to give the doctor the message, and the moment she was out of sight, the tailor and his wife hurried up behind her with the body, propped it at the top of the staircase, and ran home as fast as they could go.
Now the doctor was young and did not have many patients, so the news that one had arrived filled him with delight.

“Bring a light,” he called to the servant, “and hurry after me!” He dashed out of his room toward the staircase. There he almost tripped over the hunchback’s body, and without knowing what it was, he kicked it so hard that it rolled all the way to the bottom and nearly pulled the doctor down with it. “A light! A light!” he shouted again, and when it was brought and he saw what he had done, he was nearly out of his mind with terror.

“Holy Moses!” he cried. “Why didn’t I wait for the light? I have killed the sick man they brought me! If the sacred Ass of Esdras doesn’t come to my help, I am lost! It won’t be long before I am dragged off to jail as a murderer.”

Upset as he was, and with good reason, the doctor still remembered to shut the street door so that no passer-by would see what had happened. Then he picked up the corpse and carried it into his wife’s room, almost driving her mad with fright.
“We are finished!” she wailed, “unless we can find some way to get this body out of the house. Once the sun comes up, we can’t hide it any longer! How could you do such a terrible thing?”
“Never mind that,” the doctor answered. “The point is to find a way out.”

The doctor and his wife racked their brains for a long time, but could think of no plan that was good enough. In the end the doctor gave up completely and resigned himself to paying the price of his bad luck.

But his wife, who had twice his wits, suddenly cried out, “I have an idea! Let’s carry the body up to the roof and lower it down the chimney of our neighbor, the Muslim.” This Muslim worked for the Sultan and supplied his table with oil and butter. Part of his house was taken up by a large storeroom, where rats and mice held wild parties.

The doctor seized on his wife’s plan. They picked up the hunchback, passed cords under his arms, and lowered him into the purveyor’s bedroom so gently that he looked as if he were simply leaning against the wall. When they felt his feet touch the ground, they pulled the cords up and left him there.

They had barely got back to their own house when the purveyor came into his room. He had spent the evening at a wedding feast and was carrying a lantern. In the faint light it gave, he was startled to see a man standing in his chimney, but he was a brave man by nature, so he grabbed a stick and went straight for the supposed thief. “Ha!” he shouted. “So it’s you, and not the rats and mice, who has been stealing my butter. I’ll make sure you never want to come back!”

With that he gave him several hard blows. The corpse dropped to the floor, but the man only hit harder, until at last it struck him as odd that the thief lay so still and put up no fight. Then he found that the man was dead, and a cold fear took hold of him. “What a wretch I am,” he said. “I have murdered a man. My revenge has gone too far. Without Allah’s help I am ruined! Curse the goods that have led me to this!” And he could already feel the rope around his neck.

But when the first shock had passed, he began to look for a way out of his trouble. He took the hunchback in his arms, carried him out into the street, and propped him against the wall of a shop. Then he crept back home without once looking behind him.

A few minutes before sunrise, a rich Christian merchant who supplied the palace with all kinds of goods left his house after a night of feasting, on his way to the bath. He was very drunk, but still sober enough to know that dawn was near and that all good Muslims would soon be going to prayer. So he quickened his pace, afraid of meeting someone on the way to the mosque who would see the state he was in and have him sent to prison as a drunkard. In his hurry he bumped into the hunchback, who fell heavily against him, and the merchant, thinking a thief was attacking him, knocked the man down with a single punch. Then he shouted for help, still beating the fallen man all the while.
The chief policeman of the district came running and found a Christian beating a Muslim. “What do you think you’re doing?” he demanded angrily.
“He tried to rob me,” answered the merchant, “and nearly choked me.”
“Well, you have had your revenge,” said the policeman, taking him by the arm. “Come on, get out of here!”
