As he spoke, he reached out a hand to help the hunchback up, but the hunchback did not move. “Aha!” he went on, looking more closely. “So this is how a Christian dares to treat a Muslim!” He gripped the merchant firmly and took him to the inspector of police, who had him thrown into prison until the judge was out of bed and ready to hear the case. All this sobered the merchant, but the more he thought about it, the less he could see how the hunchback could have died merely from the blows he had given him.

The merchant was still turning this over in his mind when he was called before the chief of police and questioned about his crime, which he could not deny. Since the hunchback was one of the Sultan’s own jesters, the chief of police decided to put off the death sentence until he had spoken to his master. He went to the palace, asked for an audience, and told the Sultan the story. The Sultan replied only:
“A Christian who kills a Muslim cannot be pardoned. Do your duty.”
So the chief of police ordered a gallows to be built and sent criers through every street of the city to announce that a Christian would be hanged that day for killing a Muslim.

When everything was ready, the merchant was brought out of prison and led to the foot of the gallows. The executioner pulled the cord tight around the poor man’s neck and was just about to hoist him into the air when the Sultan’s purveyor pushed through the crowd, panting, and shouted to the hangman:
“Stop, stop, don’t be in such a hurry! He is not the one who did the murder. It was I.”

The chief of police, who was there to make sure all was done properly, put several questions to the purveyor, who told him the whole story of the hunchback’s death, and how he had carried the body to the spot where the Christian merchant had found it.

“You are about to put an innocent man to death,” he told the chief of police, “because a man who was already dead cannot possibly have been murdered by him. It is bad enough that I have killed a Muslim, without also having on my conscience an innocent Christian who suffers for my fault.”
The purveyor had spoken loudly, and the whole crowd had heard him, so even if the chief of police had wanted to, he could not have avoided setting the merchant free.
“Take the cord off the Christian’s neck,” he ordered the executioner, “and hang this man instead, since he has confessed that he is the murderer.”

The hangman did as he was told and was tightening the cord when he heard the voice of the Jewish doctor begging him to stop, because he had something very important to say. The doctor fought his way through the crowd and reached the chief of police.

“Honored sir,” he began, “this Muslim you want to hang does not deserve to die. I alone am guilty. Last night a man and a woman I had never seen knocked at my door and brought a patient for me to cure. My servant opened the door, but she had no light and could hardly make out their faces, though she willingly agreed to wake me and hand me the fee for my services. While she was telling me her story, they seem to have carried the sick man to the top of the staircase and left him there. I jumped up in a hurry without waiting for a lantern, and in the darkness I fell against something, which tumbled headlong down the stairs and did not stop until it reached the bottom. When I examined the body, I found that it was quite dead, and that it was the corpse of a hunchbacked Muslim. In terror at what we had done, my wife and I took the body up to the roof and lowered it down the chimney of our neighbor, the purveyor, whom you were just about to hang. The purveyor found him in his room and naturally took him for a thief, and he struck him such a blow that the man fell and lay motionless on the floor. He bent over him, found him stone dead, and supposed the man had died of the blow he gave him. But of course that was a mistake, as my account shows, and I alone am the murderer. I never meant to commit a crime, but I must pay for it all the same, or else carry the blood of two Muslims on my conscience. So send this man away, I beg you, and let me take his place, for I am the guilty one.”

When the chief of police heard the Jewish doctor’s declaration, he ordered the doctor to be led to the gallows and the Sultan’s purveyor to go free. The cord was put around the Jew’s neck, and his feet had already left the ground when the voice of the tailor was heard, begging the executioner to wait one moment and listen to what he had to say.

“Oh, my lord,” he cried to the chief of police, “you have almost brought about the deaths of three innocent people! But if you will only be patient and hear my story, you will learn who the real culprit is. If someone has to suffer, it must be me! Yesterday at dusk I was working in my shop in good spirits when the little hunchback, who was more than half drunk, came and sat in my doorway. He sang me several songs, and then I invited him to spend the rest of the evening at my house. He accepted, and we went off together. At supper I gave him a slice of fish, but as he ate it a bone stuck in his throat, and in spite of everything we did, he died within minutes. We were deeply sorry for his death, but for fear of being held responsible, we carried the corpse to the house of the Jewish doctor. I knocked and asked the servant to tell her master to come down at once and see a sick man we had brought him to cure, and to make him hurry I put a coin in her hand as the doctor’s fee. As soon as she was gone, I dragged the body to the top of the stairs and hurried home with my wife. As he came down the stairs, the doctor knocked the corpse over by accident, and finding it dead, believed he was the murderer. But now you know the truth. Set him free, and let me die in his place.”
The chief of police and the crowd of onlookers were stunned by the strange chain of events that the hunchback’s death had set off.

“Untie the Jewish doctor,” he told the hangman, “and string up the tailor instead, since he has confessed to the crime. Really, one has to admit this is a most extraordinary story, and it deserves to be written down in letters of gold.”

The executioner quickly loosened the ropes that bound the doctor and was fitting the noose around the tailor’s neck, when the Sultan of Kashgar, who had been missing his jester, asked his officers what had become of him.

“Sire,” they answered, “the hunchback drank more than was good for him, slipped out of the palace, and was seen wandering through the town. This morning he was found dead. A man was arrested for causing his death and kept in custody until a gallows could be built. Just as he was about to be punished, one man came forward, then another, each declaring himself the killer. That went on for a long while, and right now the chief of police is questioning a man who swears that he alone is the true murderer.”

As soon as the Sultan of Kashgar heard this, he ordered an usher to go to the chief of police and bring every person involved in the hunchback’s death, along with the corpse, because he wanted to see it once more. The usher hurried off, and he arrived only just in time. The tailor was literally dangling in the air when the usher’s voice cut through the hush of the crowd, telling the hangman to cut the body down. The hangman recognized the usher as one of the king’s servants and cut the tailor down. The usher, seeing the man was safe, found the chief of police and gave him the Sultan’s message. So the chief of police set out for the palace at once, taking the tailor, the doctor, the purveyor and the merchant, who carried the dead hunchback on their shoulders.

When the procession arrived at the palace, the chief of police threw himself down before the Sultan and told him everything he knew about the affair. The Sultan was so struck by what he heard that he commanded his private historian to write out an exact record of what had happened, so that in years to come nobody would forget the miraculous escape of four men who had believed themselves to be murderers.
The Sultan then asked everyone involved in the hunchback’s affair to tell him their stories. One of them was a chattering barber, and his tale about one of his brothers comes next.

chapters.title: The Story of the Barber’s Fifth Brother
paragraphs: While our father was alive, Alnaschar was very lazy. Rather than work for his bread, he felt no shame in begging for it every evening and living the next day on what he had been given the night before. When our father died, worn out with age, all he left us was seven hundred silver drachmas to share out, which came to one hundred for each son. Alnaschar had never had so much money in his life, and he was quite at a loss over what to do with it. After thinking it over for some time, he decided to spend it on glasses, bottles and that sort of ware, which he would buy from a wholesale merchant. Once he had his stock, he looked for a small shop in a good spot. There he sat down by the open door, with his goods heaped in an uncovered basket in front of him, waiting for a customer among the people passing by.

He stayed sitting like that, his eyes on the basket but his thoughts far off. Without realizing it, he started talking aloud, and a tailor whose shop was next to his could hear quite clearly what he was saying.

“This basket,” Alnaschar said to himself, “cost me a hundred drachmas, which is everything I own in the world. Now, if I sell what is in it piece by piece, I will make two hundred. I will spend those two hundred on glass again, and that will bring me four hundred. Little by little I will reach four thousand drachmas, and those will double easily enough. When I have ten thousand, I will give up the glass trade and become a jeweler, and spend all my time dealing in pearls, diamonds and other precious stones. In the end, with all the wealth a heart could wish for, I will buy a fine country house, with horses and slaves, and live merrily and entertain my friends. At my feasts I will send for musicians and dancers from the next town to amuse my guests. Rich as I am, though, I will not give up trade until I have built up a capital of a hundred thousand drachmas. Then, as a man of great standing, I will ask for the grand-vizier’s daughter in marriage. I will make sure to tell her worthy father that I have heard good reports of her beauty and wit, and that on our wedding day I will pay him 3 thousand gold pieces. If the vizier turns down my proposal, which is hardly to be expected, I will grab him by the beard and drag him off to my house.

“Once I have married his daughter, I will give her ten of the best eunuchs to be found, to serve her. Then I will put on my most splendid robes and ride to the grand-vizier’s house on a horse with a saddle of fine gold and trappings blazing with diamonds, with a train of slaves behind me, while the people lower their eyes and bow as I go by. At the foot of the grand-vizier’s staircase I will get down from my horse, and with my servants standing in a row on either side, I will climb the stairs. At the top the grand-vizier will be waiting to welcome me. He will embrace me as his son-in-law, give me his own seat and take a lower one himself. When that is done (as I have every reason to expect), two of my servants will come in, each carrying a purse with a thousand pieces of gold. I will hand one of them to him and say, ‘Here are the thousand gold pieces I offered for your daughter’s hand, and here,’ I will go on, holding out the second purse, ‘are another thousand, to show you that I am a man better than his word.’ After hearing of such generosity, the whole world will talk of nothing else.

“I will go home with the same pomp as I came, and my wife will send an officer to congratulate me on my visit to her father. I will honor the officer with a rich robe and a handsome present. If she sends me a gift, I will refuse it and send the messenger away. I will never let my wife leave her rooms for any reason without my permission, and my visits to her will have all the ceremony needed to inspire respect. No household will be better run than mine, and I will always take care to dress as my position demands. In the evening, when we withdraw to our apartments, I will sit in the place of honor with a grand air, saying little and staring straight ahead. And when my wife, lovely as the full moon, stands humbly before my chair, I will pretend not to see her. Then her women will say to me, ‘Respected lord and master, your wife and slave is standing before you, waiting to be noticed. It hurts her that you never deign to look her way, and she is tired of standing so long. We beg you, tell her to sit down.’ Of course I will show no sign of even hearing this speech, which will annoy them greatly. They will throw themselves at my feet, lamenting, and at last I will lift my head and cast a careless glance at her, and then go back to my former pose. The women will think I am displeased with my wife’s dress and will lead her away to put on a finer one, while I, for my part, will change my own clothes for something even more splendid. They will come back to the attack, but this time it will take much longer to persuade me even to look at my wife. It is best to begin as I mean to go on, and I will begin on my wedding day and keep it up for the rest of our lives.

“The next day she will complain to her mother about the way she has been treated, which will fill my heart with joy. Her mother will come looking for me and, kissing my hands respectfully, she will say, ‘My lord’ (she would not dare risk my anger by calling me son-in-law), ‘my lord, I beg you, do not refuse to look at my daughter or come near her. She lives only to please you and loves you with all her soul.’ But I will pay no more attention to my mother-in-law’s words than I did to the women’s. Again she will plead with me to hear her, this time throwing herself at my feet, but it will do her no good. Then she will put a glass of wine in my wife’s hand and say to her, ‘There, offer it to him yourself. He cannot be so cruel as to reject something offered by such a beautiful hand.’ And my wife will take it and hold it out to me trembling, with tears in her eyes, but I will look the other way. That will make her weep even more, and she will keep holding out the glass, crying, ‘Adorable husband, I will never stop begging until you do me the favor of drinking.’ Sick of her pestering, I will be driven to fury by these words. I will shoot an angry look at her and slap her hard across the cheek, and at the same moment give her a kick so violent that she will stagger across the room and fall onto the sofa.”

“My brother,” the barber went on, “was so lost in his dreams that he really did kick out with his foot, and unluckily it struck the basket of glass. The basket fell into the street and smashed instantly into a thousand pieces.”
His neighbor the tailor, who had been listening to all these fantasies, burst into loud laughter when he saw it happen.

“You wretch!” he cried. “You should die of shame, treating a young wife like that when she has done nothing to you. You must be a brute if her tears and pleading cannot touch your heart. If I were the grand-vizier, I would have you given a hundred blows with a bullock whip, and led around the town with a herald announcing your crimes.”

The accident, so ruinous to all his profits, had brought my brother back to his senses. Seeing that his own unbearable pride had caused the damage, he tore his clothes and pulled out his hair and lamented so loudly that passers-by stopped to listen. It was a Friday, so there were more of them than usual. Some felt sorry for Alnaschar and others only laughed at him, but the vanity that had gone to his head had vanished along with his basket of glass. He was still loudly bewailing his folly when a lady, clearly a person of standing, rode by on a mule. She stopped and asked what was wrong and why the man was weeping. They told her he was a poor man who had spent all his money on this basket of glass, which was now broken. When she heard the reason for the loud wailing, the lady turned to her attendant and said, “Give him whatever you have with you.” The man obeyed and put into my brother’s hands a purse holding five hundred pieces of gold. Alnaschar nearly died of joy when he received it. He blessed the lady a thousand times, and then he closed up the shop, where he now had nothing left to do, and went home.
He was still lost in thoughts of his good luck when someone knocked at his door. He opened it and found an old woman standing outside.
“My son,” she said, “I have a favor to ask you. It is the hour of prayer and I have not yet washed. Please let me come into your house, and give me some water.”

Although the old woman was a stranger to him, my brother did not hesitate to do what she asked. He gave her a vessel of water and then went back to his place and his thoughts. With his mind full of his latest adventure, he put his gold into a long, narrow purse that he could carry easily in his belt. Meanwhile the old woman was busy with her prayers, and when she had finished she came and bowed down to the ground twice before my brother, then stood up and called endless blessings down on his head. Noticing her shabby clothes, my brother decided that her thanks were really a hint that he should give her money for new ones, so he held out two pieces of gold. The old woman drew back in surprise, as if she had been insulted. “Good heavens!” she exclaimed. “What does this mean? Can you possibly take me, my lord, for one of those wretched creatures who push their way into houses to beg for alms? Take your money back. Thank heaven, I do not need it, for I serve a beautiful lady who is very rich and gives me everything I want.”
My brother was not clever enough to see that the old woman had refused the two coins only to get more. Instead he asked whether she could arrange for him to meet this lady.
“Gladly,” she answered. “She will be delighted to marry you and make you master of all her wealth. So pick up your money and follow me.”

My brother was delighted to think he had found a fortune and a beautiful wife so easily. He asked no more questions, hid his purse with the lady’s money in the folds of his clothes, and set off cheerfully with his guide.

They walked for some distance until the old woman stopped at a large house and knocked. A young Greek slave opened the door, and the old woman led my brother across a well-paved courtyard into a well-furnished hall. There she left him to tell her mistress he had arrived. Since the day was hot, he threw himself down on a heap of cushions and took off his heavy turban. A few minutes later a lady came in, and at first glance my brother saw that she was even more beautiful and more richly dressed than he had expected. He rose from his seat, but the lady motioned him to sit down again and took a place beside him. After they had exchanged the usual compliments, she said, “We are not comfortable here. Let us go into another room.” They passed into a smaller chamber that seemed to connect with no other, and there she talked to him for a while. Then she got up quickly and left him, saying, “Stay where you are. I will be back in a moment.”

He waited as he had been told, but instead of the lady, a huge black slave came in with a sword in his hand. He went up to my brother with an angry face and exclaimed, “What are you doing here?” His voice and manner were so terrifying that Alnaschar had no strength to answer, and he let his gold be taken from him, and even let himself be cut with the sabre, without putting up any resistance. When the slave let him go, he sank to the ground, unable to move, though he was still in his senses. Thinking he was dead, the black slave ordered the Greek slave to bring some salt, and between them they rubbed it into his wounds, causing him terrible agony, though he had the presence of mind to give no sign of life. Then they left, and the old woman took their place. She dragged him to a trapdoor and threw him down into a vault full of the bodies of murdered men.

The force of the fall knocked him senseless at first. By luck, though, the salt rubbed into his wounds stung so badly that it kept him alive, and little by little his strength came back. Two days later, during the night, he raised the trapdoor and hid in the courtyard until dawn. Then he watched the old woman leave the house to hunt for more victims. She did not notice him, and as soon as she was out of sight he slipped away from that den of murderers and took shelter in my house.

I bandaged his wounds and nursed him with care, and after a month he was as healthy as ever. He could think of nothing but taking revenge on the wicked old hag. To that end he had a purse made, big enough to hold five hundred gold pieces, and filled it with bits of glass instead. He fastened it around his waist with his sash, dressed himself as an old woman, and hid a sabre under his clothes.

One morning, while he was limping through the streets, he came upon his old enemy, who was out prowling for someone to lure into her trap. He walked up to her and, putting on a woman’s voice, said, “Would you happen to have a set of scales you could lend me? I’ve just arrived from Persia with five hundred gold pieces, and I want to check that they weigh what they should.”

“My good woman,” said the old hag, “you couldn’t have picked a better person to ask. My son is a money-changer, and if you come along with me, he’ll weigh them for you himself. But we must hurry, or he’ll have left for his shop.” With that she led the way to the very same house as before, and the same Greek slave opened the door.

Once more my brother was left waiting in the hall, and once more the pretended son came in, in the shape of the black slave. “Wretched old woman,” he said to my brother, “get up and come with me,” and he turned to lead the way to the place of slaughter. Alnaschar got up as well, pulled the sabre out from under his dress, and struck the black man on the neck so hard that his head flew off his body. My brother picked up the head in one hand, grabbed the body with the other, dragged it to the vault, and threw it in, then tossed the head in after it. The Greek slave, thinking everything had gone as usual, soon arrived with the basin of salt. But when she saw Alnaschar standing there with the sabre in his hand, she dropped the basin and turned to run. My brother was too fast for her, though, and a moment later her head was rolling off her shoulders. The noise brought the old woman hurrying in to see what was happening, and he caught her before she could get away. “Wretch!” he shouted. “Do you know who I am?”
“Who are you, my lord?” she answered, shaking all over. “I’ve never seen you before in my life.”
“I’m the man whose house you came into, to say your false prayers. Do you remember now?”
She threw herself on her knees and begged for mercy, but he cut her into four pieces.

Only the lady was left. She knew nothing of what had been going on around her. He searched the house for her, and when he finally found her, she almost fainted from fear at the sight of him. She begged hard for her life, and he was kind enough to spare her, but he ordered her to tell him how she had come to be partners with the vile creatures he had just killed.

“I used to be the wife of an honest merchant,” she answered, “and that old woman, whose wickedness I knew nothing about, would sometimes visit me. One day she said to me, ‘Madam, we are holding a grand wedding at our house today. If you would honor us by coming, I’m sure you would enjoy yourself.’ I let myself be talked into it, put on my finest dress, and took a purse with a hundred gold pieces. Once I was through the doors, that dreadful black man held me there by force, and it has now been three years that I have been here, to my great sorrow.”
“That horrible black man must have piled up enormous riches,” said my brother.
“So much,” she replied, “that if you can carry it all off, you will be rich for the rest of your life. Come, let’s see how much there is.”
She took Alnaschar into a room full of chests crammed with gold. He stared at it, and could not hide his amazement. “Go,” she said, “and fetch men to carry it away.”

My brother did not need telling twice. He rushed out into the streets and quickly gathered ten men. They all went back to the house, but how astonished he was to find the door standing open and the room with the chests of gold completely bare! The lady had outwitted him and had made good use of her time. Still, he tried to comfort himself by carrying off all the fine furniture, which was worth far more than the five hundred gold pieces he had lost.

Unfortunately, when he left the house he forgot to lock the door. The neighbors saw that the place was empty and told the police, who arrested Alnaschar the next morning as a thief. My brother tried to bribe them to let him go, but they would not listen. They tied his hands and made him walk between them to appear before the judge. When they had explained the charge to the official, he asked Alnaschar where he had got all the furniture that he had taken to his house the day before.
“Sir,” answered Alnaschar, “I am ready to tell you the whole story, but I beg you to give me your word that I will not be punished.”

“I promise,” said the judge. So my brother started at the beginning and told all his adventures, and how he had taken revenge on the people who had betrayed him. As for the furniture, he pleaded with the judge to let him keep at least some of it, to make up for the five hundred gold pieces that had been stolen from him.

The judge, however, would not say a word on that subject, and sent men at once to carry away everything Alnaschar had taken from the house. When it had all been moved under his own roof, he ordered my brother to leave the town and never set foot in it again, on pain of death, for he was afraid that if Alnaschar came back, he might seek justice from the Caliph. Alnaschar obeyed. He was on his way to a nearby city when he ran into a band of robbers, who stripped off his clothes and left him naked beside the road. When I heard what had happened, I hurried after him to comfort him in his misfortunes and put my best robe on him. Then I brought him back to my house in disguise, under cover of night, and there I have looked after him ever since, as carefully as I do my other brothers.

chapters.title: The Story of the Barber’s Sixth Brother
paragraphs: It remains for me to tell you the story of my sixth brother, whose name was Schacabac. Like the rest of us, he inherited a hundred silver drachmas from our father. He thought it a great fortune, but through bad luck he soon lost every coin and was reduced to begging. He had a smooth tongue and good manners, so he did quite well at his new trade. He took particular care to make friends with the servants in great houses, so that he could get in to see their masters.

One day he walked past a magnificent mansion, where a crowd of servants were lounging in the courtyard. From the look of the place, he thought it might bring him a rich reward, so he went in and asked whom it belonged to.

“My good fellow, where are you from?” said one of the servants. “Can’t you see for yourself that it can only belong to a Barmecide?” (The Barmecides were famous for their liberality and generosity.) When my brother heard this, he asked the porters, of whom there were several, whether they would give him alms. They did not refuse, but politely told him to go inside and speak to the master himself.

My brother thanked them for their courtesy and went into the building. It was so big that he needed some time to reach the Barmecide’s rooms. At last, in a room richly decorated with paintings, he saw an old man with a long white beard sitting on a sofa. The old man welcomed him so kindly that my brother felt bold enough to make his request.
“My lord,” he said, “you see before you a poor man who survives only through the help of people as wealthy and as generous as you.”

Before he could say more, he was cut short by the Barmecide’s astonishment. “Is it possible,” he cried, “that a man like you is going hungry while I am in Baghdad? This must be put right at once! No one will ever say that I abandoned you, and I am sure that you, for your part, will never abandon me.”
“My lord,” answered my brother, “I swear I haven’t eaten a bite all day.”

“What, you are dying of hunger?” exclaimed the Barmecide. “Slave, bring water so we can wash our hands before the meal!” No slave appeared, but my brother noticed that the Barmecide rubbed his hands together as if water were being poured over them.

Then he said to my brother, “Why don’t you wash your hands too?” Schacabac thought this must be some joke of the Barmecide’s, though he could not see the point of it. He moved closer and copied the old man’s motions.

Once the Barmecide was done with his hand-rubbing, he called out loudly, “Bring in the meal now, we’re starving.” Nothing came. Still, the Barmecide acted as though he were taking food from a plate and lifting a bite to his lips, and as he did, he said, “Go on, my friend, eat, please. Make yourself as free as you would at your own table! You say you’re starving, yet you hardly eat a thing.”
“Forgive me, my lord,” answered Schacabac, copying his gestures as before, “I am not wasting any time, I assure you, and I am doing full justice to the meal.”
“How do you like this bread?” asked the Barmecide. “I think it is especially good.”
“Oh, my lord,” answered my brother, who could see neither meat nor bread, “I have never tasted anything so delicious.”
“Eat as much as you like,” said the Barmecide. “I paid five hundred gold pieces for the woman who bakes it, so that I would never be without it.”

He ordered a whole series of dishes to be set on the table (none of which ever came) and discussed the merits of each one. Then the Barmecide announced that, having dined so well, they should now move on to the wine. My brother objected at first, saying that wine was forbidden. But the Barmecide insisted that it was out of the question for him to drink alone, and my brother agreed to take a little. The Barmecide pretended to fill their glasses so many times that my brother acted as if the wine had gone to his head, and gave the Barmecide such a blow that he fell to the ground. In fact he raised his hand to strike him a second time, but the Barmecide cried out that he was mad, and my brother held himself back. He apologized and swore that it was all the fault of the wine he had drunk. At this the Barmecide, instead of being angry, started to laugh and gave him a warm embrace. “I have been looking for a man like you for a long time,” he said, “and from now on my house is yours. You had the grace to go along with my humor and to pretend to eat and drink when there was nothing there. Now you shall be rewarded with a really good supper.”

Then he clapped his hands, and all the dishes they had tasted in imagination, both before and during the meal, were brought in, while slaves sang and played on various instruments. Throughout, the Barmecide treated Schacabac as a close friend, and gave him a garment from his own wardrobe to wear.

Twenty years went by, and my brother was still living with the Barmecide, looking after his house and managing his affairs. At the end of that time his generous benefactor died with no heirs, so everything he owned went to the prince. They even stripped my brother of the things that were rightfully his, and he, as poor as he had ever been, decided to join a caravan of pilgrims on their way to Mecca. Sadly, Bedouins attacked and plundered the caravan, and the pilgrims were taken prisoner. My brother became the slave of a man who beat him every day, hoping to force him to offer a ransom, though Schacabac pointed out that the trouble was wasted, since his relations were as poor as he was. In the end the Bedouin grew tired of tormenting him, and sent him on a camel to the top of a high, barren mountain, where he left him to fend for himself. A passing caravan bound for Baghdad told me where he could be found. I rushed to rescue him and brought him back to the city in a pitiful state.
“That,” the barber went on, “is the tale I told the Caliph, and when I finished, he burst into fits of laughter.
“You were well named ‘the Silent,’” he said. “No name was ever better earned. But for reasons of my own, which I need not mention, I want you to leave the town and never come back.”

“I had, of course, no choice but to obey, and I wandered for several years until I heard that the Caliph had died. Then I hurried back to Baghdad, only to find that all my brothers were dead. It was around this time that I did the young cripple the great service you have heard about, and he repaid me with such deep ingratitude that he chose to leave Baghdad rather than risk seeing me. I searched for him from place to place, and only today, when I least expected it, did I run into him, as angry with me as ever—” With these words the tailor went on to tell the story of the lame man and the barber, which has already been told.

“When the barber had finished his tale,” he continued, “we agreed that the young man had been right to accuse him of being a great chatterbox. Still, we wanted to keep him with us and share our feast, and we stayed at table until the hour of afternoon prayer. Then the company broke up, and I went back to work in my shop.

“It was during this interval that the little hunchback, already half drunk, appeared before me, singing and playing on his drum. I took him home to amuse my wife, and she invited him to supper. While he was eating some fish, a bone stuck in his throat, and despite everything we tried, he died almost at once. It happened so suddenly that we lost our heads, and to throw suspicion off ourselves, we carried the body to the house of a Jewish physician. He put it in the room of the purveyor, and the purveyor propped it up in the street, where people thought the merchant had killed it.”
“This, Sire, is the story I was obliged to tell to satisfy your highness. Now it is for you to say whether we deserve mercy or punishment, life or death.”

The Sultan of Kashgar had listened with obvious pleasure, and the tailor and his friends began to feel hopeful. “I have to admit,” he said, “that the stories of the barber and his brothers, and of the lame man, interest me far more than the story of my own jester. But before I let the four of you go home and have the hunchback’s body properly buried, I want to see this barber who won your pardon. Since he is here in town, an usher will go with you right now to find him.”

Before long the usher and the tailor came back with an old man who had to be at least ninety. “O Silent One,” the Sultan said, “I hear you know a great many strange stories. Will you tell me some of them?”
“Never mind my stories for now,” the barber answered. “But would your Highness kindly tell me why this Jew, this Christian and this Muslim are here, and this dead body too?”
“What is that to you?” the Sultan asked, smiling. But he could see the barber had his reasons for asking, so he ordered that the story of the hunchback be told to him.

“It is certainly astonishing,” the barber cried when he had heard all of it, “but I would like to examine the body.” He knelt down, took the head on his knees and studied it closely. All at once he burst into such loud laughter that he toppled over backwards. When he could speak again, he turned to the Sultan. “This man is no more dead than I am,” he said. “Watch.” With that he took a small case of medicines from his pocket and rubbed the hunchback’s neck with an ointment made from balsam. Then he opened the dead man’s mouth and, with a pair of pincers, pulled the bone out of his throat. The hunchback sneezed, stretched, and opened his eyes.

The Sultan and everyone who had watched could not decide what to marvel at more: the toughness of the hunchback, who had seemingly been dead for a whole night and most of a day, or the skill of the barber, whom everyone now regarded as a great man. His Highness ordered the hunchback’s story to be written down and kept in the archives next to the barber’s, so that the two would be linked in memory for all time. Nor did he stop there. To wipe out the memory of all they had been through, he commanded that the tailor, the doctor, the purveyor and the merchant each be given a robe from his own wardrobe, put on in his presence, before they went home. The barber he rewarded with a generous pension and kept at his side.

chapters.title: The Adventures of Prince Camaralzaman and the Princess Badoura
paragraphs: About twenty days’ sail from the coast of Persia lies the island of the children of Khaledan. It is divided into several provinces, each with large, thriving towns, and together they make up an important kingdom. In the old days it was ruled by a king named Schahzaman, who had good reason to think himself one of the most peaceful, prosperous and fortunate monarchs on earth. He had only one complaint: none of his four wives had given him an heir.

This troubled him so much that one day he told his grief to the grand-vizier, a wise counselor, who answered: “No human power can fix such a matter. Only Allah can grant what you want. I would advise you, sire, to send generous gifts to the holy men who spend their lives in prayer and ask them to plead for you. Who knows, their prayers may well be answered!”
The king followed his vizier’s advice, and all those prayers for an heir had their result: the next year a son was born to him.

Schahzaman sent splendid gifts to every mosque and religious house in thanks, and there were great celebrations for the birth of the little prince. He was so beautiful that he was named Camaralzaman, which means “Moon of the Century.”

Prince Camaralzaman was raised with great care by an excellent governor and the cleverest teachers, and he did them so much credit that by the time he was grown, no young man could be found more charming or accomplished. While the prince was still a youth, the king, who loved him dearly, began to think of giving up the throne to him. As usual he talked his plans over with his grand-vizier. The vizier did not approve of the idea, but he held back some of his objections.

“Sire,” he said, “the prince is still very young to carry the burdens of state. Your Majesty fears he will grow idle and careless, and no doubt you are right. But what if he were to marry first? That would tie him to his home, and you could give him a place in your councils, so that little by little he would learn how to wear a crown. You can hand it over to him whenever you judge him ready to wear it.”
Once again the king found the vizier’s advice sound. He sent for his son, who came at once, stood respectfully before him with eyes lowered, and asked what he wished.
“I sent for you,” said the king, “because I want you to marry. What do you say to that?”

The words overwhelmed the prince, and for a while he said nothing. At last he spoke. “Sire, forgive me if I cannot answer as you would like. I certainly never expected such a proposal, since I am still so young, and I admit that the thought of marriage is very unpleasant to me. Perhaps I will not always feel this way, but I know it will take me some time to bring myself to take the step your Majesty wants.”

The answer pained the king deeply, for he was truly grieved by his son’s dislike of marriage. Still, he did not want to resort to harsh measures. “I don’t wish to force you,” he said. “I will give you time to think it over. But remember that this step is necessary for a prince like you, who will one day be called to rule a great kingdom.”
From then on Prince Camaralzaman sat in the royal council, and the king showed him every sign of favor.
After a year had passed, the king took his son aside. “Well, my son,” he said, “have you changed your mind about marriage, or do you still refuse to do as I ask?”
This time the prince was less surprised but just as firm as before. He begged his father not to raise the subject again and added that pressing him any further was pointless.
The king was greatly distressed by this reply, and once more he took his trouble to his vizier.
“I did what you advised,” he said, “but Camaralzaman still refuses to marry, and he is more stubborn than ever.”

“Sire,” the vizier answered, “patience gains a great deal, and your Majesty might regret using force. Why not wait one more year, and then tell the prince, in front of the whole assembled council, that the good of the state requires him to marry? He cannot possibly refuse again before so distinguished a gathering, with all of us looking on.”

The Sultan longed to see his son married right away, but the vizier’s arguments won him over and he decided to wait. Then he went to the prince’s mother. He told her of his disappointment and of the extra time he had given their son, and he added: “I know Camaralzaman trusts you more than he trusts me. Please speak to him very seriously about this. Make him understand that he will anger me deeply if he stays obstinate, and that he will surely regret the measures I will be forced to take to have my way.”

So the first time the Sultana Fatima saw her son, she told him she had heard he refused to marry and said how upset she was that he had vexed his father so much. She asked him what reasons he could have for refusing to obey.

“Mother,” the prince replied, “I have no doubt that there are as many good, virtuous, sweet and lovable women as there are women who are the opposite. If only all of them were like you! But what disgusts me is the thought of marrying a woman I know nothing about. My father will ask for the hand of some neighboring sovereign’s daughter, and that sovereign will agree to the match. Whether she is beautiful or hideous, clever or stupid, good or bad, I must marry her, with no choice in the matter. How can I know she won’t be proud, hot-tempered, scornful and wildly extravagant, or that her nature will suit mine at all?”
“But, my son,” Fatima urged, “surely you don’t want to be the last of a line that has ruled this kingdom for so long and with such glory?”
“Mother,” said the prince, “I have no wish to outlive the king my father. But if I do, I will try to rule in a way that is worthy of those who came before me.”
Conversations like these showed the Sultan that arguing with his son was useless, and the year went by without any change in the prince’s views.

Finally the day came when the Sultan called his son before the council and told him there that not only his own wishes but the good of the empire required him to marry. He ordered the prince to give his answer in front of the assembled ministers.

Camaralzaman grew so angry at this, and spoke so hotly, that the king, naturally irritated at being defied by his son before the whole council, had the prince arrested and locked in an old tower. There he was given only a little furniture, a few books, and one slave to attend him.
Camaralzaman was glad to be free to enjoy his books, and he took his sentence very lightly.
When night fell he washed, said his prayers, read a few pages of the Koran, and lay down on a couch. He left the lamp burning beside him and was soon asleep.

Now, the tower where Prince Camaralzaman was imprisoned had a deep well, and this well was a favorite haunt of the fairy Maimoune, daughter of Damriat, chief of a legion of genies. Around midnight Maimoune drifted lightly up out of the well, meaning, as she often did, to wander the world above wherever curiosity or chance led her.

The light in the prince’s room surprised her. Without waking the slave, who was sleeping across the threshold, she went in, and when she reached the bed she was even more astonished to find someone lying in it.
The prince lay with his face half covered by the blanket. Maimoune raised it a little and saw the most beautiful young man she had ever seen.
“How wonderfully handsome he must be when his eyes are open!” she thought. “What can he have done to be treated like this?”
She could not stop gazing at Camaralzaman. At last she softly kissed his forehead and each cheek, pulled the blanket back over him, and flew off again through the air.

As she reached the middle region of the sky, she heard the beating of great wings coming toward her, and soon met one of the wicked genies. This genie, named Danhasch, recognized Maimoune with terror, for he knew that her goodness gave her power over him. He would gladly have avoided her altogether, but they were so close that he had to choose between fighting her and giving way. So he quickly spoke to her in a placating tone.
“Good Maimoune, swear to me by Allah that you will do me no harm, and I promise in return not to harm you.”
“Accursed genie!” Maimoune answered. “What harm could you do me? But I’ll grant that you have some power, and I’ll give the promise you ask. Now tell me what you have seen and done tonight.”

“Fair lady,” said Danhasch, “you’ve met me at just the right moment to hear something truly interesting. I come from the farthest end of China, one of the largest and mightiest kingdoms in the world. The present king has one daughter, and she is so perfectly lovely that neither you nor I nor any other creature could find words to do justice to her charms. Picture the most perfect features, with a radiant, delicate complexion and a bewitching expression, and even then your imagination will fall short of the truth.

“The king, her father, has carefully kept this treasure away from common eyes and has taken every precaution so that no one sees her except the lucky man he may choose as her husband. To give her some variety in her confinement, though, he has built her seven palaces unlike any ever seen. The first is made entirely of rock crystal, the second of bronze, the third of fine steel, the fourth of another, more precious kind of bronze, the fifth of touchstone, the sixth of silver, and the seventh of solid gold. All are lavishly furnished, and the gardens around them are laid out with exquisite taste. No trouble or expense has been spared to make this retreat pleasant for the princess. News of her wonderful beauty has spread far and wide, and many powerful kings have sent embassies to ask for her hand. The king always receives these embassies graciously, but he says he will never force the princess to marry against her will. She turns down every new proposal, and so the envoys have gone home as disappointed in their missions as they were delighted by their magnificent welcomes.

“‘Sire,’ the princess said to her father, ‘you want me to marry, and I know you wish to please me, for which I am very grateful. But truly, I have no desire to change my way of life. Where could I find so happy a life, among so many beautiful and delightful things? I feel I could never be as happy with any husband as I am here, and I beg you not to press one on me.’

“At last an embassy came from a king so rich and powerful that the King of China felt bound to urge the match on his daughter. He told her how important such an alliance would be and pressed her to agree. In fact he pressed her so stubbornly that the princess finally lost her temper and forgot the respect she owed her father. ‘Sire,’ she cried angrily, ‘do not speak of this or any other marriage again, or I will drive this dagger into my breast and escape all these demands.’

“The king of China was furious with his daughter. ‘You have lost your senses,’ he answered, ‘and you must be treated as someone who has.’ So he had her shut up in one suite of rooms in one of her palaces and allowed her only ten old women to serve and keep her company, with her nurse at their head. Then he wrote to all the kings who had sought the princess’s hand and asked them to give up thinking of her, since she was quite mad. He told his envoys to announce everywhere that whoever could cure her would have her as his wife.

“Fair Maimoune,” Danhasch went on, “that is how things stand now. Not a day goes by that I don’t go to gaze at this incomparable beauty. I am sure that if you would only come with me, you would find the sight well worth the trouble, and you would admit you had never seen such loveliness.”

The fairy answered only with a peal of laughter. When she could finally speak again, she cried, “Oh, come now, you’re making fun of me! I thought you had something truly interesting to tell me, and all you do is rave about some girl nobody has heard of. What would you say if you saw the prince I’ve just been looking at, whose beauty is beyond anything? Now that is worth talking about. You would lose your head completely.”
“Charming Maimoune,” said Danhasch, “may I ask who this prince is, and what sort of man?”

“Listen,” said Maimoune. “He is in much the same position as your princess. His father the king wanted to force him to marry, and when the prince refused, the king had him shut up in an old tower. That is where I have just seen him.”
“I hate to contradict a lady,” said Danhasch, “but you will have to allow me to doubt that any mortal can be as beautiful as my princess.”
“Be quiet,” cried Maimoune. “I tell you again, that is impossible.”
“Well, I don’t want to seem stubborn,” answered Danhasch. “The best way to prove what I say is true would be for you to let me carry you to see the princess with your own eyes.”

“That isn’t necessary,” Maimoune shot back. “We can settle it another way. Bring your princess here and lay her down next to my prince. Then we can compare the two at our leisure and decide which of us is right.”
Danhasch gladly agreed. He had Maimoune point out the tower where the prince was held, and they made a wager on the outcome of the comparison. Then he flew off to China to fetch the princess.
Danhasch was back in no time at all, carrying the sleeping princess. Maimoune took him to the prince’s room, and the rival beauty was laid down beside him.
So there lay the prince and princess side by side, and a lively quarrel broke out between the fairy and the genie over which of them was lovelier. Danhasch began by saying:
“There, you can see that my princess is more beautiful than your prince. Can you still doubt it?”

“Doubt it? Of course I do!” cried Maimoune. “You must be blind not to see how far my prince outshines your princess. I won’t deny that your princess is very pretty, but just look, and you will have to admit I’m right.”
“I don’t need to look any longer,” said Danhasch. “My first impression stands. But still, charming Maimoune, I am ready to give way to you if you insist.”
“Certainly not,” answered Maimoune. “I have no intention of being in debt to an accursed genie like you. I refer the question to a judge, and I expect you to submit to his verdict.”

Danhasch agreed at once. Maimoune stamped on the floor, and it split open. Out came a hideous genie, hunchbacked, lame and squint-eyed, with six horns on his head and hands like claws. The moment he saw Maimoune he threw himself at her feet and asked what she commanded.

“Get up, Caschcasch,” she said. “I called you to judge between Danhasch and me. Look at that couch, and tell me honestly, without taking sides, which you think is more beautiful, the young man or the girl lying there.”
Caschcasch looked at the prince and the princess, plainly astonished and full of admiration. He gazed for a long time and could not reach a decision. At last he said:

“Madam, I have to admit that I would be deceiving you if I claimed that either one is handsomer than the other. I can see only one way to settle it. Wake them one after the other, and see which of the two shows the greater admiration for the other.”

Maimoune and Danhasch liked this advice. The fairy immediately changed herself into a gnat, settled on Camaralzaman’s throat, and stung him so hard that he woke up. His eyes fell on the Princess of China. Startled to find a lady so close to him, he propped himself up on one arm to look at her. Her youth and beauty stirred a feeling in him that his heart had never known before, and he could not hold back his delight.
“What loveliness! What charms! Oh, my heart, my soul!” he cried, and he kissed her forehead, her eyes and her mouth. Surely he would have woken her, had the genie’s enchantments not kept her asleep.
“What, fair lady!” he cried. “You don’t wake at the sign of Camaralzaman’s love? Whoever you are, he is not unworthy of you.”

Then it suddenly struck him that she might be the bride his father had chosen for him, and that the king had probably had her put in this room to see how long Camaralzaman’s dislike of marriage would hold out against her charms.
“In any case,” he thought, “I will take this ring to remember her by.”
With that he pulled a fine ring off the princess’s finger and put one of his own in its place. Then he lay down again and was soon fast asleep.
Then it was Danhasch’s turn. He too took the shape of a gnat and bit the princess on the lip.
She sat bolt upright and was greatly surprised to see a young man beside her. Her surprise soon turned to admiration, and then to delight, as she saw how handsome and captivating he was.

“Why,” she cried, “was it you my father wanted me to marry? What bad luck that I didn’t know sooner! I would not have made him so angry. But wake up! Wake up! I know I will love you with all my heart.”
With that she shook Camaralzaman so hard that only Maimoune’s spells could have kept him from waking.

“Oh!” cried the princess. “Why are you so sleepy?” She took his hand, and noticed her own ring on his finger, which made her wonder even more. But he still slept deeply, so she kissed him on the cheek and soon fell fast asleep herself.
Then Maimoune turned to the genie and said, “Well, are you convinced that my prince is better than your princess? Next time, please believe me when I tell you something.”
Then she turned to Caschcasch. “Thank you. Now you and Danhasch carry the princess back to her own home.”
The two genies hurried to obey, and Maimoune went back to her well.

When Prince Camaralzaman woke next morning, the first thing he did was look around for the lovely lady he had seen in the night. The second was to question the slave who attended him about her. But the slave insisted so firmly that he knew nothing of any lady, and even less about how she could have got into the tower, that the prince ran out of patience. He gave the man a good beating, tied a rope around him, and dunked him in the well until the poor wretch cried out that he would tell everything. Then the prince hauled him up, dripping wet. The slave begged leave to change his clothes first, and the moment the prince agreed, he ran off to the palace just as he was. There he found the king telling the grand vizier how worried his son had made him. The slave was let in at once and cried:

“Alas, Sire! I bring sad news to your Majesty. There is no doubt that the prince has lost his mind completely. He swears he saw a lady sleeping on his couch last night, and the state I’m in shows how violently he flies out when he is contradicted.” Then he gave a detailed account of everything the prince had said and done.

The king, deeply troubled, asked the vizier to look into this new misfortune. The vizier went straight to the tower, where he found the prince calmly reading a book. After they had exchanged greetings, the vizier said:
“I am really very angry with your slave for alarming his Majesty with the news he brought.”
“What news?” asked the prince.
“Ah,” said the vizier, “something ridiculous, I’m sure, judging by how I find you.”
“Very likely,” said the prince. “But now that you’re here, I’m glad of the chance to ask you where the lady is who slept in this room last night.”
The grand vizier was thrown into a panic by this question.

“Prince!” he exclaimed. “How could any man, let alone a woman, get into this room at night without stepping over your slave in the doorway? Please think it over, and you will see that a dream has made a deep impression on you.”

But the prince angrily demanded to know who the lady was and where she was. All the vizier’s denials could not convince him that the whole thing was not a plot of the vizier’s own making. At last, losing his patience, he seized the vizier by the beard and rained blows on him.
“Stop, Prince,” cried the miserable vizier. “Wait, and hear what I have to say.”
The prince, whose arm was growing tired, stopped.

“I admit, Prince,” said the vizier, “that there is something to what you say. But you know very well that a minister must carry out his master’s orders. Let me go, and I will take the king any message you wish to send.”
“Very well,” said the prince. “Then go and tell him that I agree to marry the lady he sent or brought here last night. Hurry, and bring me back his answer.”
The vizier bowed low and rushed out of the room and the tower.
“Well?” asked the king as soon as he appeared. “How did you find my son?”
“Alas, sire,” came the answer, “the slave’s report is only too true!”

He then gave an exact account of his meeting with Camaralzaman: the prince’s fury when told that no lady could possibly have entered his room, and the way he himself had been treated. The king, greatly distressed, decided to get to the bottom of it himself. He ordered the vizier to follow him and set out to visit his son.

The prince received his father with deep respect. The king sat him down beside him and asked him several questions, and Camaralzaman answered them all sensibly. At last the king said, “My son, please tell me about the lady who, they say, was in your room last night.”

“Sire,” answered the prince, “please do not add to my distress over this. Make me happy instead, and give her to me in marriage. However much I objected to marriage before, the sight of this lovely girl has swept all my objections away, and I will gladly accept her from your hands.”

The king was almost speechless at his son’s words. After a while he solemnly assured him that he knew nothing at all about the lady, and that he had had no hand in bringing her there. Then he asked the prince to tell him the whole story.
Camaralzaman did so at great length. He showed the ring, and begged his father to help him find the bride he longed for so passionately.

“After all you’ve told me,” said the king, “I can no longer doubt your word. But how the lady came, where she came from, or why she stayed so short a time, I cannot imagine. The whole affair is truly a mystery. Come, my dear son, let us wait together for happier days.”

With that the king took Camaralzaman by the hand and led him back to the palace. There the prince took to his bed and gave himself up to despair, and the king shut himself away with his son and neglected the business of the kingdom altogether.

The prime minister was the only person allowed in. In the end he felt it was his duty to tell the king how much the court and all the people were complaining about his seclusion, and how harmful it was for the country. He urged the sultan to move with the prince to a pretty little island nearby. From there the king could easily attend public audiences, and the lovely scenery and fresh air would do the sick prince so much good that he could bear his father’s occasional absences.

The king approved the plan. As soon as the castle on the island was ready to receive them, he and the prince moved in. Schahzaman never left his son except for the public audiences required twice a week.

While all this was going on in Schahzaman’s capital, the two genies had carefully carried the Princess of China back to her own palace and put her in her bed again. When she woke next morning, she turned from one side to the other, and then, finding herself alone, called loudly for her women.
“Tell me,” she cried, “where is the young man I love so dearly, who slept beside me last night?”
“Princess,” exclaimed the nurse, “we can’t tell what you mean without more explanation.”
“Why,” the princess went on, “the most charming and beautiful young man was sleeping next to me last night. I did everything I could to wake him, but it was no use.”
“Your Royal Highness is making fun of us,” said the nurse. “Would you like to get up?”
“I am completely serious,” the princess insisted, “and I want to know where he is.”
“But Princess,” the nurse protested, “we left you quite alone last night, and we have seen no one come into your room since.”
At this the princess lost all patience. She seized the nurse by the hair and boxed her ears soundly, shouting, “You will tell me, you old witch, or I’ll kill you.”
The nurse had great trouble getting away. She hurried to the queen and told her the whole story, with tears in her eyes.
“You see, madam,” she finished, “the princess must be out of her mind. If you will only come and see her, you can judge for yourself.”
The queen rushed to her daughter’s rooms. After embracing her tenderly, she asked why she had treated her nurse so badly.

“Madam,” said the princess, “I see that your Majesty wants to make fun of me. But I assure you that I will never marry anyone except the charming young man I saw last night. You must know where he is, so please send for him.”

The queen was very surprised by these words. But when she said she knew nothing at all about it, the princess forgot her respect and answered that if she were not allowed to marry as she wished, she would kill herself. The queen tried in vain to calm her and bring her to reason.

The king himself came to hear the truth of the matter, but the princess only stuck to her story, and as proof she showed the ring on her finger. The king hardly knew what to make of it all, but ended by thinking his daughter was crazier than ever. Without further argument he had her confined even more closely, with only her nurse to attend her and a strong guard at the door.
Then he called his council together, told them the sad state of affairs, and added, “If any of you can cure the princess, I will give her to him in marriage, and he shall be my heir.”
An elderly emir who was present, fired by the wish to have a young and lovely wife and to rule a great kingdom, offered to try the magic arts he knew.
“You are welcome to try,” said the king, “but I set one condition: if you fail, you will lose your life.”
The emir accepted the condition, and the king took him to the princess. She veiled her face and said, “I am surprised, sire, that you would bring a strange man into my presence.”
“Don’t be shocked,” said the king. “This is one of my emirs, and he asks for your hand in marriage.”
“Sire,” answered the princess, “this is not the man you gave me before, the one whose ring I wear. Allow me to say that I can accept no other.”

The emir had expected the princess to talk nonsense. When he found her calm and sensible instead, he told the king he could not risk attempting a cure, and offered his head to His Majesty. The king, justly angry, had it cut off at once.
He was the first of many suitors for the princess, and every one of them paid with his life for failing to cure her.

Some time went on like this. Then the nurse’s son Marzavan came home from his travels. He had visited many countries and learned many things, astrology among them. Naturally, one of the first things his mother told him was how badly the princess, his foster-sister, was faring. Marzavan asked whether she could arrange for him to see the princess without the king knowing.
His mother thought it over and agreed. She even talked the eunuch on guard into letting Marzavan enter the royal rooms.
The princess was delighted to see her foster-brother again. After they had talked for a while, she told him her whole story and why she was shut away.
Marzavan listened closely, with his eyes lowered. When she had finished, he said,

“If all this is true, Princess, I don’t despair of bringing you comfort. Be patient a little longer. I will leave right now to search other countries, and when you hear that I am back, you can be sure the man you long for is close at hand.” With that he said goodbye, and the next morning he set out.

Marzavan went from city to city, and from island to island and province to province. Everywhere he went, he heard people telling the strange story of Princess Badoura, which was the name of the Princess of China.

After four months he arrived at a big, crowded seaport called Torf. There he heard nothing more of Princess Badoura, but a great deal about Prince Camaralzaman, who was said to be ill, and whose story sounded very much like hers.

Marzavan was overjoyed and headed straight for Prince Camaralzaman’s home. The voyage went well until his ship came within sight of the capital of King Schahzaman. Then, just as she was about to enter the harbor, she hit a rock and sank, in full view of the palace where the prince lived with his father and the grand vizier.

Marzavan was a strong swimmer. He threw himself into the sea and made it ashore near the palace, where he was given a kind welcome and a change of clothes, and was then brought before the grand vizier. The vizier took to the young man at once, struck by his fine bearing and his intelligent talk. Seeing that he had learned a great deal on his travels, he said, “Ah, if only you had learned some secret that could cure an illness that has kept this court in grief for so long!”
Marzavan answered that if he knew what the illness was, he might be able to suggest a remedy. The vizier then told him the whole history of Prince Camaralzaman.
Hearing it, Marzavan was glad at heart, for he was sure he had found the man Princess Badoura was so infatuated with. But he said nothing, and only asked to be allowed to see the prince.

When he went into the royal apartment, the first thing he noticed was the prince himself, lying on his bed with his eyes shut. The king was sitting beside him, but Marzavan paid no attention to him and cried out, “Heavens! What a striking likeness!” And in fact Camaralzaman’s features did bear a good deal of resemblance to those of the Princess of China.

At these words the prince opened his eyes, listlessly curious. Marzavan took the moment to greet him respectfully, and at the same time managed to describe the Princess of China’s condition in words that meant nothing to the Sultan and his vizier, but left the prince certain that this visitor had welcome news for him.

The prince asked his father for the favor of a private talk with Marzavan. The king was only too glad to see his son interested in anyone or anything. As soon as they were alone, Marzavan told the prince the story of Princess Badoura and what she had suffered. He added, “I am convinced that you alone can cure her. But before you set out on such a long journey you must be fit and strong, so do all you can to get well as quickly as possible.”

These words had a powerful effect on the prince. The hope they gave him cheered him so much that he said he felt well enough to get up and dress. The king was overjoyed at what Marzavan’s visit had done, and ordered public celebrations for the prince’s recovery.
Before long the prince had returned to his old health entirely. As soon as he felt truly strong, he took Marzavan aside and said to him,

“Now is the time to keep your promise. I am so eager to see my beloved princess again that I’m sure I will fall ill once more if we don’t leave soon. The only obstacle is my father’s anxious care for me, because, as you may have noticed, he can’t bear to have me out of his sight.”

“Prince,” answered Marzavan, “I have already thought about this, and here is what seems the best plan. You haven’t been outdoors since I arrived. Ask the king’s permission to go hunting with me for two or three days, and once he agrees, order two good horses to be kept ready for each of us. Leave everything else to me.”

The next day the prince found a good moment to make his request. The king gladly agreed, on the condition that they spend only one night away, so that he would not tire himself too much after such a long illness.

The following morning Prince Camaralzaman and Marzavan rode out very early, with two grooms leading the two spare horses. They hunted a little along the way, but took care to get as far from any towns as they could. At nightfall they came to an inn, where they ate supper and slept until midnight. Then Marzavan woke and roused the prince without disturbing anyone else. He asked the prince to give him the coat he had been wearing and to put on another that they had brought along. They mounted their second horses, and Marzavan led one of the grooms’ horses by the bridle.

At daybreak the travelers reached a place in the middle of the forest where four roads crossed. Here Marzavan asked the prince to wait for him. He led the groom’s horse into a thick part of the wood and cut its throat, dipped the prince’s coat in its blood, then came back to the prince and threw the coat on the ground where the roads divided.

Camaralzaman asked why he had done this. Marzavan answered that their only chance of finishing the journey was to throw people off the scent by making them believe the prince was dead. “Your father will surely be sunk in grief,” he went on, “but his joy when you come back will be all the greater.”

The prince and his companion now traveled on, by land and by sea. They had brought plenty of money for their expenses, so nothing held them up for long. At last they reached the capital of China, where they rested for three days in a decent lodging to recover from the journey.

During this time Marzavan had an astrologer’s outfit made for the prince. Then they went to the baths, and afterwards the prince put on the astrologer’s robe. Marzavan took him to a spot within sight of the king’s palace, left him there, and went to consult his mother, the princess’s nurse.
Meanwhile the prince, following Marzavan’s instructions, walked up close to the palace gates and called out in a loud voice,

“I am an astrologer, and I have come to restore the health of Princess Badoura, daughter of the mighty King of China, on the terms His Majesty has set: that I marry her if I succeed, and lose my life if I fail.”

It had been a while since anyone had come forward to take the terrible risk of trying to cure the princess, and a crowd soon gathered around the prince. When they saw how young he was, how handsome, and how nobly he carried himself, everyone felt sorry for him.

“What are you thinking, sir?” some cried. “Why throw yourself into certain death? Aren’t the heads you can see on the city wall warning enough? For pity’s sake, give up this mad idea and leave while you still can.”
But the prince did not waver. He simply called out again, even more confidently, to the horror of the crowd.
“He is determined to die!” they cried. “May heaven have mercy on him!”
Camaralzaman called out a third time, and at last the grand vizier himself came out and brought him in.

The prime minister led the prince to the king. The king was much struck by this new adventurer’s noble look, and felt so sorry for the fate that clearly awaited him that he tried to talk the young man out of his plan.
But Camaralzaman, polite and firm, stuck to his purpose. In the end the king ordered the eunuch who guarded the princess’s apartments to take the astrologer to her.

The eunuch led the way down long corridors, with Camaralzaman hurrying after him, impatient to reach the one he longed for. At last they came to a large hall, the antechamber of the princess’s room, and there Camaralzaman said to the eunuch,
“Now it is for you to choose. Shall I cure the princess in her own presence, or from this spot, without seeing her at all?”
All along the way the eunuch had scornfully doubted the newcomer’s powers. Now he was very surprised, and said,
“If you really can cure her, it makes no difference when you do it. Your fame will be just as great.”

“Very well,” said the prince. “Then, eager as I am to see the princess, I will work the cure right here where I stand, so that you will believe in my power all the more.” He took out his writing case and wrote the following: “Adorable princess! Camaralzaman, who loves you, has never forgotten the moment when he gazed at your beauty as you slept and gave you his heart. Since he could not then have the happiness of speaking with you, he dared to give you his ring as a token of his love and to take yours in exchange, which he now encloses in this letter. If you will agree to return it to him, he will be the happiest of men. If not, he will accept death gladly, since he dies for love of you. He waits for your answer in your antechamber.”
When he had finished the note, the prince carefully sealed the ring inside it without letting the eunuch see, and handed him the letter, saying,
“Take this to your mistress, my friend. If she is not cured at once when she has read it and seen what is inside, you may call me a shameless fraud.”
The eunuch went straight into the princess’s room, handed her the letter and said,
“Madam, a new astrologer has come, and he says you will be cured as soon as you have read this letter and seen what is in it.”

The princess took the note and opened it listlessly, without interest. But the instant she saw her ring, she barely glanced at the writing. She jumped up, crossed to the doorway in a single bound and pushed aside the hangings. There she and the prince recognized each other, and in a moment they were in each other’s arms, embracing tenderly and marveling that they had finally met after being parted so long. The nurse, who had hurried after her charge, drew them back into the inner room, where the princess gave her ring back to Camaralzaman.
“Take it back,” she said. “I couldn’t keep it without returning yours, and I mean to wear that one for as long as I live.”

Meanwhile the eunuch had rushed back to the king. “Sire,” he cried, “all the earlier doctors and astrologers were frauds. This man has cured the princess without even seeing her.” Then he told the king everything. The king, overjoyed, hurried to his daughter’s rooms. There he embraced her, then placed her hand in the prince’s and said,
“Fortunate stranger, I keep my promise and give you my daughter as your wife, whoever you are. But unless I am badly mistaken, you are of higher rank than you appear.”

The prince thanked the king in the warmest and most respectful words, and added, “As for who I am, Your Majesty has guessed rightly that I am not an astrologer. It was only a disguise, which I put on to earn the honor of joining your illustrious family. I am a prince myself. My name is Camaralzaman, and my father is Schahzaman, King of the Isles of the Children of Khaledan.” Then he told his whole story, including the extraordinary way he had first seen Princess Badoura and fallen in love with her.
When he had finished, the king exclaimed, “A story this remarkable must not be lost to future generations. It will be written down in the archives of my kingdom and made known far and wide.”
The wedding took place the next day with great splendor and celebration. Marzavan was not forgotten. He was given a well-paid position at court, with a promise of further promotion.
The prince and princess were now completely happy, and the months slipped by unnoticed as they enjoyed each other’s company.

One night, though, Prince Camaralzaman dreamed that he saw his father lying at the point of death and saying, “Alas! My son, whom I loved so tenderly, has abandoned me, and now he is causing my death.”
The prince woke with a groan so loud that it startled the princess, who asked what was wrong.
“Ah!” cried the prince. “At this very moment my father may be dead!” And he told her his dream.
The princess said little at the time, but the next morning she went to the king, kissed his hand, and said,
“I have a favor to ask of Your Majesty, and I beg you to believe that my husband has not put me up to it. I ask that you let us both go and visit my father-in-law, King Schahzaman.”

The king was sorry to think of parting with his daughter, but her request seemed so reasonable that he could not refuse. He made only one condition: that she spend just one year at King Schahzaman’s court. He suggested that from then on the young couple should visit their parents in turn.
The princess carried the happy news to her husband. He thanked her warmly, moved that she should care for him so much.

Preparations for the journey were now rushed forward. When everything was ready, the king went with the travelers for some days. Then he said an affectionate goodbye to his daughter, told the prince to take every care of her, and returned to his capital.

The prince and princess traveled on, and after a month they came to a huge meadow dotted with clumps of tall trees that cast a pleasant shade. The heat was great, so Camaralzaman thought it best to make camp in this cool spot. The tents were pitched. While the prince was still giving further orders, the princess went into hers, took off her girdle and set it down beside her, told her women to leave her, lay down, and was soon asleep.

Once the camp was fully set up, the prince went into the tent. The princess was asleep, so he sat down close beside her without a word. His eye fell on her girdle, and he picked it up. As he looked over the precious stones set into it, he noticed a little pouch sewn onto the girdle and held shut by a loop. He pressed it and felt something hard inside. Curious what it could be, he opened the pouch and found a cornelian engraved with various figures and strange characters.
“This cornelian must be very precious,” he thought, “or my wife would not carry it on her so carefully.”
It was in fact a talisman. The Queen of China had given it to her daughter and told her that it would bring her happiness for as long as she kept it with her.

To see the stone better, the prince walked over to the open entrance of the tent. He was standing there with it lying on the flat of his palm when a bird suddenly dived down, snatched the stone in its beak and flew off with it.
Imagine the prince’s dismay at losing something his wife clearly valued so highly!

With its prize in its beak, the bird flew a short way and landed on the ground. Prince Camaralzaman walked toward it, hoping it would let the talisman fall, but each time he came near, the thief hopped or fluttered a little farther off. He kept after it until the bird suddenly swallowed the stone and flew off much farther than before. The prince then thought of killing it with a thrown stone, but the harder he chased, the farther the bird flew.
So he was drawn on over hill and valley for the whole day. When night came, the maddening creature settled for the night at the top of a very tall tree, where it could rest safely.

The prince was in despair over all this wasted effort, and he began to wonder whether he should go back to the camp. “But how would I find the way?” he thought. “Do I go uphill or downhill? Even if my strength lasted, I would surely get lost in the dark.” Worn out by hunger, thirst, tiredness and the need for sleep, he ended up spending the night at the foot of the tree.

The next morning Camaralzaman woke before the bird had left its perch, and the moment it took off, he went after it again, with no more luck than the day before. He stopped only to eat some herbs and fruit he came across on the way. He spent ten days like this, following the bird all day and sleeping at the foot of a tree while it roosted on the highest branch. On the eleventh day the bird and the prince came to a large town.
