The Sultan saw him arrive and stepped down from the throne to embrace him. He led him into a hall where a banquet waited, planning to see him wed to the princess before the day was out.
But Aladdin refused. “I must first build a palace worthy of her,” he said, and took his leave.

Back home he said to the genie: “Build me a palace of the finest marble, inlaid with jasper, agate and other precious stones. In the middle, build me a great hall with a dome, its four walls of solid gold and silver, with six windows on each side. The lattices of these windows must be set with diamonds and rubies, all except one, which is to be left unfinished. There must be stables, horses, grooms and slaves. Go and see to it!”

By the next day the palace was finished. The genie carried Aladdin there and showed him that all his orders had been faithfully carried out, even to the velvet carpet laid from Aladdin’s palace to the Sultan’s. Aladdin’s mother then dressed with care and walked to the palace with her slaves, while Aladdin followed on horseback. The Sultan sent musicians with trumpets and cymbals to meet them, so that the air rang with music and cheering. She was taken to the princess, who greeted her and treated her with great honor. That night the princess said goodbye to her father and set out along the carpet to Aladdin’s palace, with his mother beside her and the hundred slaves following. She was delighted when she saw Aladdin, who ran to welcome her.
“Princess,” he said, “if I have offended you, blame your beauty for my boldness.”

She told him that now that she had seen him, she was glad to obey her father in this matter. After the wedding, Aladdin led her into the hall, where a feast was laid out, and she dined with him. Afterward they danced until midnight.
The next day Aladdin invited the Sultan to see the palace. As he entered the hall with the twenty-four windows, with their rubies, diamonds and emeralds, he exclaimed:
“It is a wonder of the world! Only one thing puzzles me. Was it by accident that one window was left unfinished?”
“No, sir, it was on purpose,” Aladdin answered. “I wanted Your Majesty to have the glory of finishing this palace.”
This delighted the Sultan. He summoned the finest jewelers in the city, pointed out the window that was not yet done, and ordered them to decorate it to match the rest.
“Sir,” their spokesman answered, “we cannot find enough jewels.”

The Sultan had his own jewels brought, and the jewelers soon used them up, but it did no good, because after a month the work was not even half done. Aladdin knew their effort was useless, so he told them to undo their work and take the jewels back, and at his command the genie finished the window. The Sultan was amazed to get his jewels back, and he came to see Aladdin, who showed him the finished window. The Sultan embraced him, while the envious vizier hinted that it was the work of enchantment.

Aladdin had won the people’s hearts with his gentle manners. He was made captain of the Sultan’s armies and won several battles for him, yet he stayed as modest and courteous as ever, and lived this way, peaceful and content, for several years.

But far away in Africa the magician remembered Aladdin. By his magic arts he found out that Aladdin had not died miserably in the cave after all, but had escaped, married a princess, and was living in great honor and wealth. He knew the poor tailor’s son could only have done this by means of the lamp, and he traveled day and night until he reached the capital of China, determined to ruin Aladdin. As he passed through the town, he heard people everywhere talking about a marvelous palace.
“Forgive my ignorance,” he asked, “but what is this palace you are talking about?”
“Haven’t you heard of Prince Aladdin’s palace?” was the answer. “It is the greatest wonder in the world! I can show you the way if you would like to see it.”

The magician thanked the man who had spoken, and when he saw the palace he knew that the genie of the lamp had raised it, and he was nearly mad with rage. He made up his mind to get hold of the lamp and throw Aladdin back into the deepest poverty.

As bad luck would have it, Aladdin had gone hunting for eight days, which gave the magician plenty of time. He bought a dozen copper lamps, put them in a basket, and went to the palace, calling out: “New lamps for old!” A jeering crowd followed him.

The princess was seated in the hall of the twenty-four windows. She sent a slave out to learn the reason for the commotion, and the slave returned laughing, which earned her a scolding from the princess.
“Madam,” the slave answered, “how can anyone help laughing at an old fool offering to trade fine new lamps for old ones?”
Another slave heard this and said: “There is an old one up on the ledge there that he can have.”

Now that was the magic lamp, which Aladdin had left there because he could not take it hunting with him. The princess did not know its value, and told the slave, laughing, to go and make the exchange.
The slave went to the magician and said: “Give me a new lamp for this one.”

He snatched it from her and told her to take her pick, while the crowd jeered. He did not care. He stopped crying his lamps, left the city through the gates, and found a lonely spot where he stayed until nightfall. Then he took out the lamp and rubbed it. The genie appeared, and at the magician’s command carried him to a lonely place in Africa, together with the palace and the princess inside it.

The next morning the Sultan looked out of his window toward Aladdin’s palace and rubbed his eyes, because it was gone. He sent for the vizier and asked what had become of the palace. The vizier looked out too, and stood speechless with astonishment. Once more he blamed enchantment, and this time the Sultan believed him, and sent thirty men on horseback to bring Aladdin back in chains. They met him riding home, tied him up, and forced him to walk along with them. But the people, who loved him, followed with weapons to make sure no harm came to him. He was brought before the Sultan, who ordered the executioner to cut off his head. The executioner made Aladdin kneel, blindfolded him, and raised his scimitar to strike.

At that moment the vizier saw that the crowd had forced its way into the courtyard and was climbing the walls to rescue Aladdin, and he called out to the executioner to hold back. The people looked so threatening, indeed, that the Sultan gave in. He ordered Aladdin to be untied, and pardoned him in front of the crowd.
Aladdin now begged to be told what he had done.
“You lying wretch!” said the Sultan. “Come here.” He led Aladdin to the window and showed him the empty ground where his palace had stood.
Aladdin was so stunned that he could not utter a single word.
“Where is my palace? Where is my daughter?” the Sultan demanded. “The palace matters less to me, but I will have my daughter back, and you will find her for me or lose your head.”

Aladdin asked for forty days to search for her. If he failed, he promised, he would come back and accept death at the Sultan’s pleasure. The Sultan granted his plea, and Aladdin left the royal presence in sorrow. For three days he roamed about like a madman, asking everyone he met what had happened to his palace, but they only laughed at him and pitied him. At last he reached the bank of a river and knelt down to say his prayers before throwing himself in. As he did so, he rubbed the magic ring that he still wore.
The genie he had seen in the cave appeared before him and asked what he wished.
“Save my life, genie,” said Aladdin, “and bring my palace back.”
“That is beyond my power,” said the genie. “I am only the slave of the ring. You must ask the slave of the lamp.”

“Then at least,” said Aladdin, “you can take me to the palace and set me down beneath my dear wife’s window.” In an instant he was in Africa, under the princess’s window, and out of sheer exhaustion he fell asleep.
The singing of the birds woke him, and his heart felt lighter. He saw clearly that all his misfortunes came from losing the lamp, and he wondered in vain who had stolen it from him.

That morning the princess got up earlier than she had done since the magician had carried her off to Africa. She was forced to endure his company once a day, but she treated him so harshly that he did not dare to live in the palace full time. While she was dressing, one of her women looked out and saw Aladdin. The princess ran and threw open the window, and Aladdin looked up at the sound. She called him to come to her, and the two lovers were overjoyed to see each other again.

After he had kissed her, Aladdin said: “Princess, I beg you in God’s name, for your sake and for mine, before we say anything else, tell me what became of an old lamp I left on the cornice in the hall of twenty-four windows when I went hunting.”
“Alas!” she said. “I am the innocent cause of all our sorrows.” And she told him how the lamp had been exchanged.
“Now I understand,” cried Aladdin, “that we have the African magician to thank for this! Where is the lamp?”

“He keeps it on him,” said the princess. “I know, because he pulled it out of his robe to show me. He wants me to break my faith with you and marry him, and he tells me my father had you beheaded. He is always speaking ill of you, but I answer him only with tears. If I keep refusing, I have no doubt he will use force.”

Aladdin comforted her and left her for a while. He swapped clothes with the first person he met in the town, bought a certain powder, and went back to the princess, who let him in through a small side door.

“Put on your most beautiful dress,” he told her, “and welcome the magician with smiles, so that he believes you have forgotten me. Invite him to dine with you, and say you would like to taste the wine of his country. He will go to fetch some, and while he is away I will tell you what to do.”

She listened closely to Aladdin, and when he had gone she dressed herself in splendor for the first time since leaving China. She put on a belt and a head-dress of diamonds, and when she saw in a mirror that she looked lovelier than ever, she received the magician. To his great amazement she said: “I have made up my mind that Aladdin is dead and that all my tears will never bring him back to me. So I have resolved to mourn no more, and I have invited you to dine with me. But I am tired of the wines of China, and I would like to taste those of Africa.”

The magician hurried to his cellar, and the princess poured the powder Aladdin had given her into her cup. When he came back, she asked him to drink her health in the wine of Africa. As a sign that she had made peace with him, she handed him her cup in exchange for his.
Before drinking, the magician made her a speech praising her beauty, but the princess cut him short.
“Let me drink first,” she said. “You can say what you like afterwards.” She put her cup to her lips and held it there, while the magician drained his to the last drop and fell back dead.

The princess then opened the door to Aladdin and threw her arms around his neck, but Aladdin pushed her away and told her to leave him, because he still had work to do. He went to the dead magician, took the lamp out of his robe, and ordered the genie to carry the palace and everything in it back to China. It was done, and in her chamber the princess felt only two slight shocks, never guessing that she was home again.

The Sultan was sitting in his private room, mourning his lost daughter, when he happened to glance up. He rubbed his eyes, because the palace stood there just as before! He hurried over, and Aladdin received him in the hall of twenty-four windows, with the princess beside him. Aladdin told him what had happened and showed him the magician’s dead body so that he would believe it. A feast of ten days was proclaimed, and it seemed that Aladdin could now live out the rest of his life in peace. But it was not to be.

The African magician had a younger brother who was, if possible, even more wicked and cunning than he was. This brother traveled to China to avenge the magician’s death, and he went to see a pious woman named Fatima, thinking she might be useful to him. He entered her cell, held a dagger to her chest, and ordered her to get up and do as he said or die. He swapped clothes with her, stained his face to look like hers, put on her veil, and murdered her so that she could not tell anyone. Then he set off toward Aladdin’s palace. Everyone took him for the holy woman and crowded around him, kissing his hands and begging for his blessing. When he reached the palace, the noise around him was so great that the princess told her slave to look out of the window and find out what was going on. The slave said it was the holy woman, who cured people of their ailments with her touch. The princess had wanted to see Fatima for a long time, so she sent for her. When he came before the princess, the magician offered a prayer for her health and prosperity. When he had finished, the princess had him sit beside her and begged him to stay with her always. The false Fatima, who wanted nothing better, agreed, but kept his veil down for fear of being found out. The princess showed him the hall and asked what he thought of it.
“It is truly beautiful,” said the false Fatima. “But in my opinion it lacks just one thing.”
“And what is that?” asked the princess.
“If a roc’s egg were hung from the middle of this dome,” he answered, “it would be the wonder of the world.”

After that the princess could think of nothing but a roc’s egg. When Aladdin came home from hunting, he found her in a very bad mood. He asked what was wrong, and she told him that all her pleasure in the hall was spoiled because there was no roc’s egg hanging from the dome.
“If that is all,” said Aladdin, “you will soon be happy.”
Aladdin left her, rubbed the lamp, and when the genie rose up he ordered him to fetch a roc’s egg. The genie gave a shriek so loud and terrible that the whole hall trembled.

“Wretch!” he cried. “Isn’t it enough that I have done everything for you? Now you order me to bring my own master and hang him in the middle of this dome? You, your wife and your palace deserve to be burned to ashes. But this request did not come from you. It comes from the brother of the African magician whom you destroyed. He is in your palace right now, disguised as the holy woman—the one he murdered. He is the one who put that wish into your wife’s head. Watch yourself, because he means to kill you.” With those words the genie vanished.

Aladdin went back to the princess, complaining that his head ached and asking for the holy Fatima to be fetched to lay her hands on it. But as the magician came near, Aladdin seized his dagger and stabbed him through the heart.
“What have you done?” cried the princess. “You have killed the holy woman!”
“No,” replied Aladdin, “only a wicked magician.” And he told her how she had been deceived.
From then on Aladdin and his wife lived in peace. He became ruler when the Sultan died, held the throne for many years, and left a long line of kings after him.

chapters.title: The Adventures of Haroun-al-Raschid, Caliph of Baghdad
paragraphs: The Caliph Haroun-al-Raschid sat in his palace, wondering whether anything was left in the world that could give him even a few hours of amusement, when his old and trusted friend Giafar, the grand vizier, suddenly appeared before him. Giafar bowed low and waited, as was his duty, for his master to speak. But Haroun-al-Raschid only turned his head to look at him, and sank back into his earlier weary slump.
Giafar, however, had something important to tell the Caliph and had no intention of being put off by silence. So he bowed low again in front of the throne and began to speak.

“Commander of the Faithful,” he said, “I have taken it upon myself to remind your Highness that you have undertaken to observe in secret how justice is done and order is kept throughout the city. Today is the day you set aside for this purpose, and perhaps in carrying out this duty you may find some relief from the melancholy that, to my sorrow, I see has taken hold of you.”
“You are right,” answered the Caliph. “I had forgotten all about it. Go and change your coat, and I will change mine.”

A few moments later they both came back into the hall dressed as foreign merchants, and they slipped through a secret door and out into the open country. From there they turned toward the Euphrates, crossed the river in a small boat, and walked through the part of the town on the far bank, without seeing anything that called for their interference. The Caliph and his vizier were pleased with the peace and good order of the city. They made their way to a bridge that led straight back to the palace, and they had already crossed it when an old blind man stopped them, begging for alms.
The Caliph gave him a coin and started to walk on, but the blind man grabbed his hand and held him tight.
“Kind sir,” he said, “whoever you may be, grant me one more favor. Strike me, I beg you, one blow. I have richly deserved it, and even a harsher punishment.”

The Caliph was very surprised at this request, and he answered gently: “My good man, what you ask is impossible. What use would my charity be if I treated you so badly?” As he spoke, he tried to pull free of the blind beggar’s grip.

“My lord,” the man answered, “forgive my boldness and my insistence. Either take back your money or give me the blow I ask for. I have sworn a solemn oath never to accept anything without being punished for it, and if you knew everything, you would see that the punishment is not even a tenth of what I deserve.”

The Caliph was moved by these words, and perhaps even more by the fact that he had other business to attend to. He gave in and struck the man lightly on the shoulder. Then he went on his way, followed by the blind man’s blessing. When they were out of earshot, he said to the vizier, “There must be something very strange behind that man’s behavior—I would like to find out the reason. Go back to him, tell him who I am, and order him to come to the palace tomorrow, after the hour of evening prayer, without fail.”
So the grand vizier returned to the bridge. He handed the blind beggar a coin and then a blow, gave him the Caliph’s message, and went back to join his master.

They continued toward the palace, but as they crossed a square they came upon a crowd watching a young, well-dressed man who was driving a horse at full speed around the open space. He used his spurs and whip so mercilessly that the animal was covered in foam and blood. The Caliph was astonished at this and asked a passer-by what it meant, but nobody could tell him anything except that the same thing happened every day at the same hour.
He walked on, still puzzled, and for now could only tell the vizier to summon the horseman too, to appear before him at the same hour as the blind man.

The next day, after evening prayer, the Caliph entered the hall, and the vizier followed him with the two men we have spoken of, and a third, who has nothing to do with our story. They all bowed low before the throne. Then the Caliph told them to rise and asked the blind man his name.
“Baba-Abdalla, your Highness,” he said.

“Baba-Abdalla,” said the Caliph, “your way of asking for alms yesterday seemed so strange to me that I almost ordered you on the spot to stop causing such a public scandal. But I have sent for you to ask what made you take such a curious vow. Once I know the reason, I can judge whether you should be allowed to go on with it, because I cannot help thinking it sets a very bad example for others. So tell me the whole truth, and hide nothing.”

These words troubled Baba-Abdalla, and he threw himself down at the Caliph’s feet. Then he rose and answered: “Commander of the Faithful, I humbly beg your pardon for pressing your Highness to do something that seems, on the face of it, to have no meaning. In the eyes of men it may well have none. But I regard it as a small payment for a terrible sin I have committed, and if your Highness will be kind enough to hear my story, you will see that no punishment could atone for my crime.”

chapters.title: The Story of the Blind Baba-Abdalla
paragraphs: Commander of the Faithful, I was born in Baghdad, and I was left an orphan while I was still very young, because my parents died within a few days of each other. They left me a small fortune, and I worked hard day and night to increase it, until I finally owned eighty camels. I hired these out to traveling merchants, often going along with them on their journeys, and I always came home with large profits.

One day I was returning from Balsora, where I had taken a load of goods meant for India, and at noon I stopped in a lonely spot that promised rich grazing for my camels. I was resting in the shade of a tree when a dervish, who was walking toward Balsora, sat down beside me. I asked him where he had come from and where he was going. We soon became friends, and after we had asked each other the usual questions, we took out the food we had with us and ate until we were full.

As we ate, the dervish mentioned that very close to where we were sitting a treasure lay hidden, so enormous that if my eighty camels were loaded until they could carry no more, the hiding place would still look as full as if no one had ever touched it.

When I heard this I nearly lost my head with joy and greed. I threw my arms around the dervish’s neck and cried out: “Good dervish, it’s plain that the riches of this world mean nothing to you, so what use is it to you to know about this treasure? On foot and alone, you could carry off no more than a handful. Tell me where it is, and I will load my eighty camels with it and give you one of them as a token of my thanks.”

I know my offer was hardly a generous one, but it seemed large to me, because at his words a wave of covetousness had swept through my heart, and I felt as though the seventy-nine camels I would keep were nothing by comparison.
The dervish saw perfectly well what was going on in my mind, but he gave no sign of what he thought of my proposal.

“My brother,” he said calmly, “you know as well as I do that you are treating me unfairly. I could have kept my secret and saved the treasure for myself. But the fact that I told you about it shows that I trusted you, and that I hoped to win your lasting gratitude by making your fortune along with mine. Before I show you the secret of the treasure, though, you must swear that once we have loaded the camels with all they can carry, you will give half of them to me and we will go our separate ways. I think you will agree this is fair, because if you give me forty camels, I in return will give you the means to buy a thousand more.”

Of course I couldn’t deny that what the dervish said was entirely reasonable. Even so, I couldn’t stand the thought of him being as rich as I would be. But there was no point in arguing; I had to accept his terms or mourn the loss of an immense fortune for the rest of my life. So I gathered my camels and we set off together, with the dervish leading the way. After walking for some time we came to what seemed to be a valley, though its entrance was so narrow that my camels could only pass through one at a time. This little valley, or open space, was closed in by two mountains whose sides were sheer cliffs that no human being could climb.
When we stood exactly between the two mountains, the dervish stopped.
“Make your camels lie down here in the open,” he said, “so that we can load them easily. Then we will go to the treasure.”

I did as I was told and went back to the dervish, who was trying to start a fire with some dry wood. As soon as it was burning, he tossed a handful of perfumes onto it and spoke a few words I didn’t understand, and at once a thick column of smoke rose high into the air. He split the smoke into two columns, and then I saw a rock that stood like a pillar between the two mountains slowly open, and a magnificent palace appeared inside it.

But, Commander of the Faithful, the love of gold had such a hold on my heart that I couldn’t even stop to look at the riches around me. I threw myself on the first heap of gold within reach and began shoveling it into a sack I had brought with me.

The dervish set to work as well, but I soon noticed that he took only precious stones, and I decided it would be wise to copy him. At last the camels were loaded with all they could carry, and all that remained was to seal up the treasure and go our ways.

Before that, though, the dervish walked over to a great golden vase, beautifully engraved, and took out of it a small wooden box, which he tucked inside his robe, saying only that it held a special kind of ointment. Then he lit the fire again, threw on the perfume and muttered the same unknown spell, and the rock closed and stood whole as before.

Next we divided the camels and loaded them with the treasure. Then each of us took charge of his own animals and led them out of the valley, until we reached the spot on the high road where the routes part. There we separated, the dervish heading for Balsora and I for Baghdad. We embraced warmly, and I poured out my thanks for the honor he had done me by choosing me for this great fortune. Then, after a hearty farewell, we turned our backs on each other and hurried after our camels.

I had barely caught up with mine when the demon of envy took hold of my soul. “What does a dervish want with riches like that?” I said to myself. “He alone knows the secret of the treasure, and he can always get as much as he likes.” So I stopped my camels at the roadside and ran back after him.

I was a fast runner, and it didn’t take me long to catch him. “My brother,” I cried, as soon as I had breath to speak, “just as we were saying goodbye, a thought struck me that may be new to you. You are a dervish by calling and lead a very quiet life, caring only to do good and not at all for the things of this world. You don’t realize what a burden you are taking on by gathering so much wealth into your hands, not to mention that nobody who hasn’t been used to camels since birth can ever manage such stubborn animals. If you are wise, you won’t saddle yourself with more than thirty, and you will find even those trouble enough.”
“You are right,” said the dervish, who understood me perfectly but didn’t want to quarrel. “I confess I hadn’t thought of it. Pick any ten you like and drive them ahead of you.”

I chose ten of the best camels, and we walked along the road to where I had left the others. I had got what I wanted, but the dervish had proved so easy to deal with that I almost regretted not asking for ten more. I looked back. He had gone only a few paces, and I called after him.

“My brother,” I said, “I don’t want to leave you without pointing out something I don’t think you fully grasp: anyone who means to keep a herd of thirty together needs a great deal of experience driving camels. For your own sake, I’m sure you would be much happier if you handed ten more over to me, because with my practice it makes no difference to me whether I handle two or a hundred.”
Once again the dervish raised no objection, and I drove off my ten camels in triumph, leaving him only twenty for his share. I now had sixty, and anyone would have thought I should be satisfied.

But, Commander of the Faithful, there is a saying that goes, “The more one has, the more one wants.” That was how it was with me. I couldn’t rest while a single camel remained with the dervish. I went back to him and redoubled my pleas and embraces and promises of eternal gratitude, until the last twenty were in my hands.
“Use them well, my brother,” said the holy man. “Remember that riches can sprout wings if we hoard them for ourselves, and that the poor are at our gates precisely so that we can help them.”

Gold had so blinded me that I paid no attention to his wise advice and only looked around for something else to grab. Suddenly I remembered the little box of ointment the dervish had hidden, which most likely held a treasure more precious than all the rest. I gave him one last embrace and then said, as if it had just occurred to me, “What are you going to do with that little box of ointment? It hardly seems worth taking along; you might as well let me have it. And really, a dervish who has renounced the world has no need of ointment!”

Oh, if only he had refused! But even then I would have taken it from him by force, such was the madness that had seized me. Instead, far from refusing, the dervish held it out at once, saying graciously, “Take it, my friend, and if there is anything else I can do to make you happy, you only have to tell me.”
The moment the box was in my hands I tore off the lid. “Since you are so kind,” I said, “please tell me what this ointment can do.”

“Its powers are strange and remarkable,” the dervish replied. “If you put a little on your left eye, you will see at once all the treasures hidden in the depths of the earth. But take care not to touch your right eye with it, or you will lose your sight forever.”

His words roused my curiosity to the highest pitch. “Try it on me, I beg you,” I cried, holding the box out to the dervish. “You will know how to do it better than I! I am burning to find out what it can do.”

The dervish took the box I held out to him and told me to close my left eye, then touched it gently with the ointment. When I opened it again, I saw spread out before me treasures of every kind, without number. But all this while I had had to keep my right eye shut, which was very tiring, so I asked the dervish to put the ointment on that eye too.
“If you insist, I will do it,” the dervish answered, “but remember what I told you a moment ago: if it touches your right eye, you will go blind on the spot.”

Unluckily, although the dervish’s words had proved true again and again, I was firmly convinced that he was hiding from me some secret and precious power of the ointment. So I would not listen to a word he said.
“My brother,” I replied with a smile, “I can see you are joking. It isn’t natural for the same ointment to have two such completely opposite effects.”
“It is true all the same,” said the dervish, “and it would be better for you if you took my word for it.”

But I refused to believe him. Dazzled by greed, I figured that if one eye could show me riches, the other might teach me how to take possession of them. So I kept pressing the dervish to anoint my right eye, and he kept firmly refusing.
“After doing you so much good,” he said, “I am truly reluctant to do you such harm. Think what it is to be blind, and don’t make me do something you will regret as long as you live.”

It was no use. “My brother,” I said firmly, “please say no more and do what I ask. You have been most generous in granting my wishes until now; don’t spoil my memory of you over a matter of such little importance. Whatever happens, I take it on my own head and will never reproach you.”

“Since you are set on it,” he answered with a sigh, “there is no use talking.” He took the ointment and put some on my right eye, which I was holding tightly shut. When I tried to open it, thick clouds of darkness swam before me. I was as blind as you see me now!

“Wretched dervish!” I screamed. “So it was true after all! What a bottomless pit my lust for gold has thrown me into! Ah, now that my eyes are closed they are truly open. I know that I alone have caused all my suffering! But good brother, you who are so kind and charitable and know the secrets of such vast learning, do you have nothing that can give me back my sight?”

“Unhappy man,” replied the dervish, “it is not my fault that this has happened to you; it is a just punishment. The blindness of your heart has brought about the blindness of your body. Yes, I do have secrets; you have seen that in the short time we have known each other. But I have none that can restore your sight. You have shown yourself unworthy of the riches you were given. Now they have passed into my hands, and from there they will flow to others who are less greedy and ungrateful than you.”

Without another word the dervish walked away. I was left mute with shame and bewilderment, and so crushed that I stayed frozen where I stood while he rounded up the eighty camels and set off toward Balsora. I begged him not to abandon me, or at least to lead me to where the next caravan would pass, but he ignored my pleas and my cries. I would soon have starved to death in my misery if some merchants had not happened along the track the following day and kindly carried me back to Baghdad.

In a single moment I had gone from a rich man to a beggar, and to this day I have lived only on the alms people have given me. But to atone for the sin of greed that ruined me, I make every passer-by give me a blow.
This, Commander of the Faithful, is my story.

When the blind man had finished, the Caliph spoke to him: “Baba-Abdalla, your sin is truly great, but you have suffered enough. From now on, repent in private, for I will see to it that you are given enough money every day to meet all your needs.”
At these words Baba-Abdalla threw himself at the Caliph’s feet and prayed that honor and happiness would be his for all time.

chapters.title: The Story of Sidi-Nouman
paragraphs: The Caliph, Haroun-al-Raschid, was greatly pleased with the tale of the blind man and the dervish. When it was over, he turned to the young man who had mistreated his horse and asked his name as well. The young man answered that he was called Sidi-Nouman.

“Sidi-Nouman,” said the Caliph, “I have watched horses being broken all my life, and I have broken them myself, but I have never seen a horse broken as savagely as you did it yesterday. Everyone who watched was outraged and blamed you loudly. I myself was so angry that I very nearly revealed who I was and put a stop to it on the spot. Still, you don’t look like a cruel man, and I would like to believe you didn’t act this way without a reason. I am told it was not the first time, and that every day you can be seen whipping and spurring your horse, so I want to get to the bottom of the matter. Tell me the whole truth, and hide nothing.”

Sidi-Nouman changed color when he heard this, and he grew flustered, but he saw clearly that there was no escape. So he threw himself down before the Caliph’s throne and tried to obey, but the words stuck in his throat and he stayed silent.

The Caliph, though used to being obeyed at once, guessed something of what was going on in the young man’s mind and tried to put him at ease. “Sidi-Nouman,” he said, “don’t think of me as the Caliph, but only as a friend who would like to hear your story. If there is anything in it you are afraid might offend me, take heart, for I pardon you in advance. So speak openly and without fear, as to someone who knows and loves you.”
The Caliph’s kindness put Sidi-Nouman at ease, and at last he began his story.

“Commander of the Faithful,” he said, “I am dazzled by the splendor of Your Highness’s presence, but I will do what I can to satisfy your wish. I am far from perfect, yet I am not cruel by nature, and I take no pleasure in breaking the law. I admit that the way I treated my horse may give Your Highness a poor opinion of me and set a bad example for others. Still, I did not punish it without cause, and I hope you will find me more deserving of pity than of punishment.”

“Commander of the Faithful, I won’t waste your time describing my birth. It is not distinguished enough to deserve Your Highness’s notice. My ancestors were careful people, and I inherited enough money to live comfortably, though not lavishly.

“With a modest fortune of my own, the only thing I still needed for happiness was a wife who would return my affection. But that blessing was not meant for me. The very day after the wedding, my bride started testing my patience in the hardest ways she could find.

“In our country, custom requires us to marry without ever seeing the person we will spend our lives with. So a man has no right to complain, as long as his wife is not truly repulsive or plainly deformed. And whatever flaws her body may have, charm and good conduct go a long way toward making up for them.

“When she had been brought to my house with the usual ceremonies, I saw my wife unveiled for the first time, and I was delighted to find that the reports of her beauty had not misled me. I began married life in high spirits, with every hope of happiness.

“The next day a grand dinner was served for the two of us, but my wife did not come, so I told a servant to fetch her. She still did not appear, and I waited impatiently for some time. Finally she came into the room, took her place at the table, and plates of rice were put in front of us.

“I ate mine with a spoon, as one naturally does. But I was amazed to see that my wife did nothing of the kind. She took a little case from her pocket, picked out a long pin, and used it to carry her rice to her mouth one grain at a time.

“‘Amina,’ I cried in astonishment, ‘is this how you eat rice at home? Do you do it because your appetite is so small, or are you counting the grains so that you never eat more than a certain number? If it is thrift, and you want to teach me not to be wasteful, you needn’t worry. We will never ruin ourselves that way! Our fortune is large enough for all our needs. So, dear Amina, don’t hold yourself back. Eat as much as you like, as I do!’

“After such affectionate words I expected a cheerful reply. But Amina said nothing at all. She went on picking at her rice as before, with longer and longer pauses between grains. She ignored the other dishes, and every now and then she simply put a bread crumb in her mouth, hardly enough to feed a sparrow.

“Her stubbornness annoyed me, but I tried to excuse her to myself. Perhaps she had never been used to eating with men, I thought, and her family had taught her to be modest and reserved in front of her husband. Or perhaps she had already eaten, or meant to eat later in her own rooms. So I paid no more attention, and when I had finished I left the room, privately very irritated by her strange behavior.

“The same thing happened at supper, and at every meal we shared for the whole next day. Clearly no woman could live on two or three crumbs of bread and a few grains of rice, and I decided to find out how and when she got her food. I pretended not to notice anything she did, hoping that she would gradually grow used to me and be friendlier. But I soon saw that this hope was completely in vain.

“One night I lay with my eyes shut, looking for all the world like a man fast asleep, when Amina got up softly and dressed without making the slightest sound. I couldn’t imagine where she was going, and my curiosity was so strong that I decided to follow her. As soon as she was dressed, she slipped quietly out of the room.

“The moment the curtain fell behind her, I threw a cloak over my shoulders and pushed my feet into a pair of slippers. Looking through a lattice that opened onto the courtyard, I saw her going out through the street door, which she carefully left open.

“The moon was bright, so I had no trouble keeping her in sight until she entered a cemetery not far from the house. There I hid in the shadow of the wall and crouched down carefully. I had hardly hidden myself when I saw my wife coming toward me with a ghoul. Your Highness knows these demons: they roam the country, make their lairs in abandoned buildings, and leap out at unwary travelers to eat their flesh. When no living person comes their way, they go to the cemeteries and feed on the dead.

“I was nearly struck dumb with horror at the sight of my wife with this hideous female ghoul. They passed right by me without noticing. They dug up a corpse that had been buried that very day, then sat on the edge of the grave to enjoy their dreadful meal, chatting quietly and cheerfully all the while, though I was too far away to hear what they said. When they had finished, they threw the body back into the grave and heaped the earth over it. I made no attempt to disturb them. I hurried back to the house, careful to leave the door open as I had found it, got back into bed and pretended to be sound asleep.
“A little while later Amina came in as quietly as she had gone out. She undressed and slipped into bed, apparently pleased with herself for how cleverly she had carried off her outing.

“As you can imagine, after such a scene I couldn’t sleep for a long time. At the first call to prayer I dressed and went to the mosque. But even prayer did not calm my troubled spirit, and I could not face my wife until I had decided what to do about her. So I spent the morning wandering from garden to garden, turning over different plans for forcing her to give up her horrible habits. I thought of using violence to make her submit, but I was reluctant to be unkind to her. And I had a feeling that gentle means were more likely to work. A little calmer, I turned for home and arrived about dinnertime.

“As soon as I came in, Amina ordered dinner, and we sat down together. As usual, she kept picking at a few grains of rice, and I resolved to speak to her at once about what weighed so heavily on my heart.

“‘Amina,’ I said, as calmly as I could, ‘you must have guessed how surprised I was when, the day after our wedding, you refused to eat anything but a few scraps of rice, and behaved in a way that would have deeply wounded most husbands. Still, I was patient with you. I only tried to tempt your appetite with the finest dishes I could think of, and it was all for nothing. And yet, Amina, it seems to me that there are some among them just as sweet to the taste as the flesh of a corpse?’”

“The words were hardly out of my mouth when Amina, who understood at once that I had followed her to the graveyard, flew into a rage worse than any I have ever seen. Her face turned purple, her eyes seemed about to burst from her head, and she actually foamed at the mouth.

“I watched her in terror, wondering what would come next, but never guessing where her fury would end. She seized a vessel of water that stood nearby, dipped her hand into it, and muttered some words I could not catch. Then she sprinkled the water on my face and screamed like a madwoman:
“‘Wretch, take the reward for your prying, and become a dog!’”

“The words had barely left her mouth when I knew, without feeling any change come over me, that I was no longer a man. The shock and surprise were so great, since I had no idea Amina was a sorceress, that I never thought of running. I stood rooted to the spot while Amina grabbed a stick and began to beat me. Her blows were so heavy that I only wonder they did not kill me on the spot. But they shook me out of my daze, and I bolted into the courtyard with Amina right behind me, lunging wildly at me, and I was not quick enough to dodge every blow. At last she grew tired of chasing me, or else some new trick occurred to her that would bring me a swift and painful death. She opened the gate to the street, meaning to crush me as I went through. Dog though I was, I saw what she intended, and the sheer danger sharpened my wits. I timed my dash so well that I got through, and only the tip of my tail was caught when she slammed the gate.

“I was safe, but my tail hurt terribly, and I yelped and howled so loudly all down the street that the other dogs came and attacked me, which made things no better. To get away from them, I ran into a cookshop that sold tongues and sheep’s heads.

“At first the owner was very kind. He drove off the other dogs that were still at my heels, while I crept into the darkest corner. But though I was safe for the moment, I was not meant to stay long under his protection. He was one of those people who think all dogs are unclean, and that all the washing in the world can hardly cleanse you after touching one. So once my enemies had gone off to hunt other prey, he tried to coax me out of my corner and force me into the street. But I refused to leave my hole, and I spent the night asleep, which I badly needed after the pain Amina had given me.

“I don’t want to tire Your Highness with the sad thoughts that filled me after my change of shape. But you may be interested to hear that the next morning my host went out early to do his marketing and came back loaded with the sheep’s heads, tongues and trotters he would sell that day. The smell of meat drew hungry dogs from all over the neighborhood, and they gathered at the door, begging for scraps. I crept out of my corner and stood with them.

“Though he disliked dogs as unclean animals, my protector was a kind-hearted man. Knowing I had eaten nothing since the day before, he threw me bigger and better pieces than the ones the other dogs got. When I had finished, I tried to go back into the shop, but he wouldn’t allow it. He stood so firmly in the doorway with a stout stick that I had to give up and look for another home.

“A few steps further on was a baker’s shop, and its master seemed to be a cheerful, good-humored man. He was eating his breakfast at that moment, and though I gave no sign of hunger, he threw me a piece of bread right away. Before gobbling it up, as most dogs do, I bowed my head and wagged my tail to thank him. He understood, and smiled warmly. I didn’t really want the bread at all, but I felt it would be rude to refuse, so I ate it slowly, to show him I was only doing it out of politeness. He understood that too, and seemed quite willing to let me stay in his shop. So I sat down facing the door, to show that I asked only for his protection. He gave it, and even encouraged me to come into the house itself, giving me a corner to sleep in where I would be out of everyone’s way.

“The kindness this excellent man heaped on me was far greater than anything I could ever have expected. He was always affectionate in the way he treated me, and I shared his breakfast, dinner and supper, while I gave him all the gratitude and devotion he deserved.

“I sat with my eyes fixed on him, and he never left the house without me at his heels. If I happened to be asleep when he was getting ready to go out, and didn’t notice, he would call, ‘Rufus, Rufus!’ since that was the name he had given me.

“Some weeks went by like this. Then one day a woman came in to buy bread. In paying, she put down several coins, and one of them was counterfeit. The baker noticed and refused to take it, asking for another in its place. The woman, for her part, refused to take it back, insisting it was perfectly good, but the baker would have nothing to do with it. ‘It’s such a poor imitation,’ he cried at last, ‘that even my dog wouldn’t be fooled. Here, Rufus! Rufus!’ At the sound of his voice I jumped onto the counter. The baker threw the coins down in front of me and said, ‘Find out if there is a bad coin.’ I looked at each in turn, then laid my paw on the false one, glancing at my master to point it out.

“The baker had only been joking, of course, and he was amazed at my cleverness. The woman, finally convinced that the man was telling the truth, handed over another coin in its place. After she left, my master was so pleased that he told all the neighbors what I had done, and made far more of it than there really was.
“The neighbors, quite naturally, refused to believe his story. They tested me several times with all the bad money they could gather, but I never failed the test.

“Soon the shop was full from morning till night with people who, on the pretext of buying bread, had come to see whether I was as clever as they had heard. The baker did a roaring trade, and admitted I was worth my weight in gold to him.

“Naturally, plenty of people were jealous of his thriving trade, and many traps were laid for me, so he never dared let me out of his sight. One day a woman I had never seen in the shop came in to buy bread like everyone else. As usual I was lying on the counter. She put down six coins in front of me, and one of them was counterfeit. I spotted it straight away and laid my paw on it, looking up at the woman as I did. ‘Yes,’ she said, nodding. ‘You’re right, that’s the one.’ She stood studying me for a long while, then paid for her bread and left the shop, signaling to me to follow her without being seen.

“My mind was always fixed on finding some way to throw off the spell that bound me, and the way this woman had looked at me made me think she might have guessed what had happened to me. I was not wrong. Still, I let her get a little way off and only stood at the door watching her. She turned around, and when she saw I hadn’t moved, she beckoned to me again.
“All this time the baker was busy at his oven and had forgotten about me, so I slipped out quietly and ran after the woman.

“Her house was a good distance away. When we got there she opened the door and said to me, ‘Come in, come in. You will never regret following me.’ Once I was inside she bolted the door and led me into a large room, where a beautiful young woman sat at her embroidery. ‘Daughter,’ my guide cried, ‘I’ve brought you the baker’s famous dog, the one that can tell good money from bad. When I first heard about him, remember, I told you he had to be a man, turned into a dog by magic. Today I went to the baker’s to test the story for myself, and I talked the dog into following me here. Now what do you say?’

“‘You’re right, mother,’ the girl answered. She got up and dipped her hand into a bowl of water, then sprinkled it over me and said, ‘If you were born a dog, stay a dog; but if you were born a man, let this water give you back your true shape.’ In an instant the spell was gone. The dog’s form vanished as if it had never existed, and a man stood in front of her.

“Overwhelmed with gratitude at being freed, I threw myself at her feet and kissed the hem of her dress. ‘How can I thank you for your kindness to a stranger, and for what you have done for me? From now on I am your slave. Do with me as you wish!’
“Then, to explain how I had come to be turned into a dog, I told her my whole story. I ended by thanking the mother for the happiness she had given me.

“‘Sidi-Nouman,’ the daughter replied, ‘don’t speak any more of what you owe us. Knowing we have helped you is payment enough. Let’s talk about Amina, your wife. I knew her before she married. I knew she was a magician, and she knew I had studied the same art under the same teacher. We often met at the same baths, but we disliked each other and never tried to be friends. As for you, it isn’t enough that your spell has been broken. She must be punished for her wickedness. Please wait a moment here with my mother,’ she added quickly. ‘I’ll be back soon.’
“Left alone with the mother, I told her again how grateful I was, to her as well as to her daughter.

“‘My daughter,’ she told me, ‘is as skilled a magician as Amina herself, as you can see, but you would be amazed at how much good she does with her knowledge. That is why I have never stood in her way; otherwise I would have put a stop to it long ago.’ As she was speaking, her daughter came back in, holding a small bottle.

“‘Sidi-Nouman,’ she said, ‘the books I’ve just looked in tell me that Amina is out at the moment but will be back at any time. They also show me that in front of the servants she is pretending to be very worried about your absence. She has put about a story that while you were at dinner with her, you suddenly remembered some urgent business and rushed out of the house without closing the door. A dog wandered in through it, she says, and she had to drive it out with a stick. So go home at once and wait in your room for Amina to come back. When she arrives, go down and meet her, and in her shock she will try to run off. Then have this bottle ready and throw the water in it over her, saying boldly, “Receive the reward of your crimes.” That is all I have to tell you.’

“Everything happened just as the young magician had said it would. I had been in my house only a few minutes when Amina came back, and as she came toward me I stepped in front of her with the water in my hand. She gave a loud cry and turned for the door, but it was too late. I had already thrown the water in her face and spoken the magic words. Amina vanished, and in her place stood the horse you saw me beating yesterday.
“That, Commander of the Faithful, is my story. Now that you have heard my reasons for what I did, may I hope that your Highness will not think this wicked woman has been treated too harshly?”

“Sidi-Nouman,” the Caliph answered, “your story is certainly a strange one, and nothing can be said in your wife’s defense. But without condemning how you have treated her, I ask you to think how much she must suffer from being turned into an animal, and I hope you will let that be punishment enough. I will not order you to make the young magician find a way to give your wife back her human form, because I know that once women like her start doing evil they never stop, and I would only call down on your head a revenge far worse than the one you have already suffered.”

chapters.title: The Story of Ali Cogia, Merchant of Baghdad
paragraphs: In the reign of Haroun-al-Raschid there lived in Baghdad a merchant named Ali Cogia. He had no wife or children and was content with the modest profit his trade brought in. He had spent several years quite happily in the house his father had left him, when three nights in a row he dreamed of an old man who came to him and scolded him for neglecting the duty of a good Muslim by putting off his pilgrimage to Mecca for so long.

The dream troubled Ali Cogia greatly, since he did not want to give up his shop and lose all his customers. For some time he had closed his eyes to the need to make this pilgrimage, and had tried to ease his conscience with extra good works. But the dream felt to him like a direct warning, and he decided not to delay the journey any longer.

First he sold his furniture and the goods in his shop, keeping back only what he could trade with on the road. He sold the shop too, and had no trouble finding a tenant for his house. The one matter he could not settle to his satisfaction was how to keep safe the thousand pieces of gold he wanted to leave behind.

After thinking it over, Ali Cogia came up with a plan that seemed secure. He took a large jar, put the money at the bottom, and filled the rest with olives. He corked the jar tightly, carried it to a friend of his, a merchant like himself, and said:
“My brother, you have probably heard that I leave with a caravan for Mecca in a few days. I’ve come to ask whether you would do me the favor of keeping this jar of olives for me until I return.”
The merchant answered at once, “Here, this is the key to my shop. Take it and put the jar wherever you like. I promise you will find it in the same place when you get back.”

A few days later Ali Cogia climbed onto the camel he had loaded with goods, joined the caravan, and reached Mecca in good time. Like the other pilgrims he visited the sacred Mosque, and when his religious duties were done, he displayed his goods as attractively as he could, hoping to find buyers among the people passing by.
Before long two merchants stopped in front of the display, and after going through the goods, one said to the other:
“If this man were smart, he would take these wares to Cairo. He’d get a much better price there than he is likely to get here.”

Ali Cogia heard this and wasted no time acting on the advice. He packed up his goods, and instead of going back to Baghdad he joined a caravan bound for Cairo. The trip delighted him. He sold nearly everything at once and bought a stock of Egyptian curiosities to sell in Damascus. But the caravan he would have to travel with was not leaving for another six weeks, so he used the wait to see the Pyramids and some of the cities along the Nile.

Now Damascus charmed the good Ali so much that he could hardly bring himself to leave. At last he remembered that he had a home in Baghdad. He planned to go back by way of Aleppo, and after crossing the Euphrates, to follow the Tigris.

But when he reached Mossoul, he had become such good friends with some Persian merchants that they talked him into going with them to their own country, and even as far as India. So it happened that seven years went by after he left Baghdad, and in all that time the friend who had the jar of olives never once thought of him or of it. In fact the matter only crossed his mind a month before Ali Cogia actually came home, when his wife remarked one day that it was a long time since she had eaten olives and she would like some.

“That reminds me,” said the husband, “that before Ali Cogia went to Mecca seven years ago, he left a jar of olives with me. But by now he must surely be dead, and there’s no reason we shouldn’t eat the olives if we like. Give me a light and I’ll go and get them and see how they taste.”

“Husband,” the wife answered, “please, don’t do anything so shameful! Even if seven years have gone by with no word of Ali Cogia, that doesn’t mean he’s dead, and he could return any day. How disgraceful it would be to have to admit that you had betrayed his trust and broken the seal on his jar! Pay no attention to what I said, I don’t really want olives now. And after all this time they’re probably spoiled anyway. I have a feeling that Ali Cogia will come back, and what will he think of you? Let it go, I beg you.”
But the merchant refused to listen to her, sensible as her advice was. He took a light and a dish and went into his shop.
“If you’re going to be so stubborn,” said his wife, “I can’t stop you. But don’t blame me if it turns out badly.”

When the merchant opened the jar, he found the olives on top were rotten. To see whether the ones underneath were in better shape, he shook some out into the dish. As they tumbled out, a few gold pieces tumbled out with them.
The sight of the gold woke all the merchant’s greed. He looked into the jar and saw that the whole bottom was full of gold. Then he put the olives back and went to his wife.
“Wife,” he said as he came into the room, “you were quite right. The olives are rotten, but I’ve closed the jar up so well that Ali Cogia will never know anyone touched it.”
“You would have done better to believe me,” the wife replied. “I hope no harm comes of it.”

These words had no more effect on the merchant than the earlier ones, and he spent the whole night wondering how he could keep the gold if Ali Cogia came back and asked for his jar. Very early the next morning he went out and bought fresh olives. He threw the old ones away, took out the gold and hid it, and filled the jar with the new olives. Then he corked it again and put it back where Ali Cogia had left it.

A month later Ali Cogia came back into Baghdad. His house was still rented out, so he took a room at an inn, and the next day he set out to see his friend the merchant, who welcomed him with open arms and many cries of surprise. After a few minutes of questions, Ali Cogia asked the merchant to give him the jar he had looked after for so long.
“Of course,” said the merchant. “I’m only glad I could be of use to you. Here is the key to my shop. You’ll find the jar where you put it.”

Ali Cogia fetched his jar and carried it to his room at the inn, where he opened it. He pushed his hand down but felt no money, though he was still sure it must be there. So he took some plates and bowls from his traveling kit and emptied the olives out. It was no use. The gold was not there. The poor man was struck dumb with horror. Then he raised his hands and cried, “Can my old friend really have committed such a crime?”

In great haste he went back to the merchant’s house. “My friend,” he cried, “you’ll be surprised to see me again, but I can’t find the thousand pieces of gold I put at the bottom of this jar, under the olives. Perhaps you borrowed them for your business. If so, you are welcome to them. I only ask you to give me a receipt, and you can repay me whenever it suits you.”
The merchant had expected something like this and had his answer ready. “Ali Cogia,” he said, “when you brought me the jar of olives, did I ever touch it?”

“I gave you the key to my shop and you put the jar where you wanted yourself, and didn’t you find it in exactly the same spot and the same condition? If you put gold in it, it must still be there. I know nothing about that; you only told me there were olives. Believe me or not as you please, but I have not laid a finger on the jar.”

Ali Cogia kept trying every means to make the merchant admit the truth. “I love peace,” he said, “and I would deeply regret having to turn to harsh measures. Once more, think of your reputation. I will be in despair if you force me to call in the law.”

“Ali Cogia,” the merchant answered, “you admit that what you left with me was a jar of olives. You came and took it away yourself, and now you say it held a thousand pieces of gold and that I have to hand them over! Did you ever mention any gold before? I didn’t even know there were olives in the jar! You never showed me what was inside. You may as well demand pearls or diamonds while you’re at it. Now go away, please, before a crowd gathers outside my shop.”

By now a number of people had stopped to listen to the quarrel, not just passers-by but the merchants from the neighboring shops, who kept trying to make peace between the two men. But when the merchant had spoken his last words, Ali Cogia decided to lay the whole matter before them, and he told them the whole story. They heard him out, and then asked the merchant what he had to say for himself.

The merchant agreed that he had kept Ali Cogia’s jar in his shop, but he insisted he had never touched it. As for what was inside, he swore that he knew only what Ali Cogia himself had told him, and he called on everyone there to witness the insult he was being made to suffer.
“You’ve brought this on yourself,” said Ali Cogia, seizing him by the arm. “Since you want the law, you will have the law! We’ll see whether you dare to tell your story again in front of the Cadi.”

As a good Muslim, the merchant could not refuse to be taken before a judge, so he accepted the challenge. “Very well,” he told Ali Cogia, “nothing would please me more. We’ll soon see which of us is in the right.”

The two men then appeared before the Cadi, and Ali Cogia told his story once more. The Cadi asked him who his witnesses were. Ali Cogia answered that he had taken no such precaution, since he had thought of the man as a friend and had always found him honest until then.

The merchant for his part held to his version. He offered to swear a solemn oath that he had never stolen the thousand gold pieces, and that he had not even known they were there. The Cadi let him take the oath and declared him innocent.

Ali Cogia was furious at being left with such a loss. He protested against the verdict and announced that he would take his case to the Caliph, Haroun-al-Raschid, in person. The Cadi took no notice of these threats, entirely satisfied that he had done the right thing.

With the judgment given, the merchant went home in triumph, while Ali Cogia returned to his inn to write out a petition to the Caliph. Next morning he stood along the road the Caliph would take after the midday prayer, and held out his petition to the officer who walked ahead of the Caliph. It was this officer’s duty to gather such papers and, once inside the palace, pass them on to his master. There Haroun-al-Raschid went through them carefully.

Ali Cogia knew this custom, so he followed the Caliph into the public hall of the palace and waited to see what would come of it. After a while the officer came out and told him that the Caliph had read his petition and had set a time for hearing him the following morning. The officer also asked for the merchant’s address, so that he could be summoned as well.
That same evening the Caliph went out to walk through the town, as he liked to do, with his grand vizier Giafar and Mesrour, the chief of the eunuchs. All three were in disguise.

As they went down one street, a noise caught the Caliph’s attention. He looked through a doorway that opened onto a courtyard and saw ten or twelve children playing in the moonlight. He hid in a dark corner and watched them.
“Let’s play at being the Cadi,” said the brightest and quickest of the children. “I’ll be the Cadi. Bring Ali Cogia before me, and the merchant who robbed him of the thousand pieces of gold.”
The boy’s words reminded the Caliph of the petition he had read that morning, and he waited, interested to see what the children would do.

The other children welcomed the idea gladly, since they had heard a great deal of talk about the affair, and they quickly agreed on who would play which part. The Cadi sat down solemnly in his seat, and an officer brought in Ali Cogia first, as the plaintiff, and then the merchant, as the defendant.
Ali Cogia bowed low and argued his case point by point. He ended by begging the Cadi not to make him bear so heavy a loss.
When the Cadi had heard him, he turned to the merchant and asked why he had not paid Ali Cogia back the money in question.
The pretend merchant repeated the reasons the real merchant had given the Cadi of Baghdad, and he too offered to swear that he was telling the truth.

“Wait a moment!” said the little Cadi. “Before we get to oaths, I’d like to look at the jar of olives. Ali Cogia,” he went on, “do you have the jar with you?” When he learned that Ali Cogia did not, he said, “Go and fetch it and bring it to me.”

Ali Cogia went off for a moment, then came back and made a show of setting a jar down at the Cadi’s feet. He declared that it was his jar, the one he had given the accused to look after. To be thorough, the Cadi asked the merchant whether he recognized it as the same jar. The merchant’s silence admitted that it was, and the Cadi ordered the jar opened. Ali Cogia made the motion of lifting off a lid, and the little Cadi in turn pretended to peer into a jar.
“What beautiful olives!” he said. “I’d like to taste one.” Pretending to put one in his mouth, he added, “They’re really excellent!
“But,” he went on, “I find it strange that olives seven years old should be as good as that! Send for some olive dealers and let’s hear what they say!”
Two children were brought forward as olive merchants, and the Cadi spoke to them. “Tell me,” he said, “how long can olives be kept and still be pleasant to eat?”
“My lord,” the merchants answered, “no matter how carefully they are kept, olives never last past the third year. They lose their flavour and their color, and are good for nothing but throwing away.”
“If that’s so,” said the little Cadi, “then examine this jar and tell me how long the olives in it have been there.”
The olive merchants made a show of inspecting the olives and tasting them. Then they reported to the Cadi that the olives were fresh and good.
“You’re wrong,” he said. “Ali Cogia states that he put them in this jar seven years ago.”
“My lord,” the olive merchants replied, “we assure you these olives are from this year’s harvest. And if you asked every merchant in Baghdad, you wouldn’t find one who would say otherwise.”

The accused merchant opened his mouth as if to protest, but the Cadi gave him no chance. “Be quiet,” he said. “You are a thief. Take him away and hang him.” With that the game ended, and the children clapped their hands and led the criminal off to be hanged.

Haroun-al-Raschid was astonished at the wisdom of the child, who had judged so wisely the very case he himself was to hear the next day. “Could there be any other verdict?” he asked the grand vizier, who was just as impressed as he was. “I can’t imagine a better judgment.”
“If things really are as we have been told,” the grand vizier answered, “then it seems to me that Your Highness can only follow this boy’s example, both in how he reasoned and in what he concluded.”

“Then mark this house carefully,” said the Caliph, “and bring me the boy tomorrow, so that he can try the case in my presence. Summon the Cadi too, so he can learn his duty from a child. Tell Ali Cogia to bring his jar of olives, and make sure two olive dealers are here.” With that, the Caliph went back to the palace.

Early the next morning the grand vizier returned to the house where they had seen the children at play and asked to see the lady of the house and her children. Three boys came out, and the grand vizier asked which of them had played the Cadi in the game the evening before. The eldest and tallest, turning pale, admitted that it was he. To his mother’s great alarm, the grand vizier said he had strict orders to take him into the Caliph’s presence.

“Does he mean to take my son away from me?” cried the poor woman. But the grand vizier hurried to calm her. He assured her that she would have the boy back within the hour, and that once she knew why he was wanted she would be perfectly content. So she dressed the boy in his best clothes, and the two of them left the house.

When the grand vizier brought the child before the Caliph, the boy was somewhat overawed and confused, and the Caliph set about explaining why he had sent for him. “Come closer, my son,” he said kindly. “I believe it was you who judged the case of Ali Cogia and the merchant last night? I happened to overhear you, and I was very pleased with how you handled it. Today you will see the real Ali Cogia and the real merchant. Sit down right here beside me.”

The Caliph took his seat on the throne with the boy beside him, and the two parties to the case were shown in. One after the other they threw themselves down and touched their foreheads to the carpet at the foot of the throne. When they stood up, the Caliph said, “Now speak. This child will give you justice, and if more is needed, I will see to it myself.”

Ali Cogia and the merchant argued their sides one after the other. But when the merchant offered to swear the same oath he had sworn before the Cadi, the child stopped him and said that first he must see the jar of olives.

At this, Ali Cogia brought the jar to the Caliph and took off the cover. The Caliph picked out an olive, tasted it, and told the expert merchants to do the same. They declared the olives good, and from this year’s crop. The boy told them that Ali Cogia said he had put the olives in the jar seven years earlier, and they gave the same answer the children had given.

By now the accused merchant could see that he was certain to be condemned, and he tried to offer some excuse in his defense. The boy had too much sense to order him hanged. He looked at the Caliph and said, “Commander of the Faithful, this is no game now. It is for Your Highness to sentence him to death, not for me.”

Then the Caliph, convinced that the man was a thief, ordered him taken away and hanged. This was done, but not before the man had confessed his guilt and told where he had hidden Ali Cogia’s money. The Caliph told the Cadi to go and learn how to dispense justice from a child, and he sent the boy home with a purse of a hundred pieces of gold as a sign of his favor.

chapters.title: The Enchanted Horse
paragraphs: It was the Feast of the New Year, the oldest and grandest of all the feasts in the Kingdom of Persia. The king had spent the day in the city of Schiraz, taking part in the magnificent displays his subjects had prepared in honor of the festival. The sun was going down, and the king was just about to signal his court to withdraw, when an Indian suddenly appeared before his throne. He was leading a horse in rich trappings, which looked exactly like a living one.

“Sire,” he said, bowing to the ground as he spoke, “I know I come before Your Highness very late, but I can promise you that none of the wonders you have seen today can compare with this horse, if you will only be good enough to look at him.”
“All I see,” the king replied, “is a clever copy of a real horse, and any skilled craftsman could make as much.”

“Sire,” the Indian answered, “I am not speaking of how he looks, but of what I can do with him. I need only mount him and wish myself in some particular place, and however far away it is, I will be there in a few moments. That, Sire, is what makes this horse so marvelous, and if Your Highness permits, you can test it for yourself.”

The King of Persia was fascinated by anything out of the ordinary, and he had never met a horse with such powers. He told the Indian to mount the animal and show what it could do. In an instant the man had leapt onto its back and was asking where the king wanted to send him.
“Do you see that mountain?” asked the king, pointing to a huge mass rising into the sky about three leagues from Schiraz. “Go and bring me a leaf from the palm tree that grows at its foot.”

The words had barely left the king’s mouth when the Indian turned a screw set in the horse’s neck, close to the saddle. The horse shot up into the air like lightning and was soon out of sight even of the sharpest eyes. A quarter of an hour later the Indian was seen coming back with the palm leaf in his hand. He guided his horse to the foot of the throne, dismounted, and laid the leaf before the king.
As soon as the king had seen the astonishing speed the horse was capable of, he longed to own it himself. He felt so sure the Indian would gladly sell it that he already regarded it as his.
“I never guessed from his looks how valuable an animal he was,” he told the Indian, “and I’m grateful to you for showing me my mistake. If you will sell him, name your own price.”

“Sire,” the Indian replied, “I never doubted that a ruler as wise and accomplished as Your Highness would do my horse justice once he knew its power. I even thought it likely that you would want to own it. Much as I value it, I will give it up to Your Highness on one condition. I did not build this horse myself. The man who made it gave it to me in exchange for my only daughter, who made me swear a solemn oath that I would never part with it except for something of equal value.”

“Name whatever you like,” the king cried, cutting him short. “My kingdom is large and full of fine cities. You have only to choose the one you prefer, and you shall be its ruler for the rest of your life.”

“Sire,” answered the Indian, who did not find the offer nearly as generous as the king thought it, “I am most grateful for Your Highness’s princely offer. I beg you not to be offended if I say that I can give up my horse only in exchange for the hand of the princess, your daughter.”

The courtiers burst out laughing when they heard this, and Prince Firouz Schah, the heir to the throne, was filled with anger at the Indian’s presumption. The king, however, thought it would cost him little to part with the princess in return for such a wonderful toy. While he was still hesitating over his answer, the prince broke in.
“Sire,” he said, “you cannot possibly doubt for a moment what answer to give to such an insolent bargain. Think of what you owe to yourself and to the blood of your ancestors.”

“My son,” said the king, “those are noble words, but you don’t grasp what this horse is worth. If I turn down the Indian’s proposal, he will simply make it to some other monarch, and I could not bear the thought of anyone but me owning this Seventh Wonder of the World. I am not saying I will accept his terms, and he may yet be talked into reason. In the meantime, I want you to look the horse over and, with its owner’s permission, test what it can do.”

The Indian had overheard the king, and he took it as a sign that the king was giving way. He gladly agreed to what the king wished and stepped forward to help the prince into the saddle and show him how to steer. But before he could finish, the young man turned the screw and was gone from sight.

They waited a while, expecting to see him come back across the sky at any moment. At last the Indian grew afraid. He threw himself down before the throne and said to the king, “Sire, you must have seen that the prince was too impatient to let me tell him how to return to the place he left from. I beg you not to punish me for something that was not my fault, and not to make me pay for any misfortune that may follow.”
“Then why,” cried the king, in a rush of fear and anger, “didn’t you call him back when you saw him disappear?”

“Sire,” said the Indian, “he went so fast that I was stunned, and by the time I found my voice he was already out of earshot. But let us hope he will notice a second screw and turn it, which will bring the horse back down to earth.”
“And if he does?” the king replied. “What is to stop the horse from plunging straight into the sea, or smashing him against the rocks?”
“Don’t be afraid, your Highness,” said the Indian. “This horse can cross the seas, and it will carry its rider wherever he wants to go.”

“Well, your head will answer for it,” said the monarch. “If he is not safely back with me in three months, or at least has not sent word that he is safe, you will pay with your life.” With that he ordered his guards to seize the Indian and throw him in prison.

Meanwhile Prince Firouz Schah had risen merrily into the air. For an hour he kept climbing higher and higher, until the mountains could no longer be told apart from the plains. Then he thought it was time to descend, and assumed he only had to turn the screw the opposite way. To his surprise and horror, however he turned it, it made no difference at all. Then he remembered that he had never stopped to ask how to get back to the ground, and he understood the danger he was in. Luckily he kept his head. He began going carefully over the horse’s neck, and at last, to his great joy, he found a tiny peg, much smaller than the first, close to the right ear. He turned it and felt himself sinking toward the earth, though more slowly than he had left it.

By now it was dark and the prince could see nothing, so, feeling rather uneasy, he had to let the horse choose its own course. It was past midnight when Prince Firouz Schah finally touched the ground again, faint and exhausted from the long ride and from having eaten nothing since early morning.

As soon as he dismounted, he tried to work out where he was. As far as he could tell in the thick darkness, he was standing on the terraced roof of an enormous palace, with a marble balustrade running all around it. In one corner of the terrace was a small door that opened onto a staircase leading down into the palace.

Some men would have hesitated to explore any further, but the prince did not. “I mean no harm,” he said, “and whoever owns this place will not hurt me once he sees I carry no weapon.” Afraid of putting a foot wrong, he crept carefully down the stairs. On a landing he saw an open door, and beyond it a dimly lit hall.

Before going in, the prince stopped and listened, but all he heard was the sound of men snoring. By the light of a lantern hanging from the ceiling he saw a row of black guards asleep, each with a bare sword lying beside him. He realized that this hall must be the antechamber to the rooms of some queen or princess.

Prince Firouz Schah stood perfectly still and looked around until his eyes got used to the gloom. Then he noticed a bright light shining through a curtain in one corner. He crept softly toward it, drew the folds aside, and stepped into a magnificent chamber full of sleeping women. All of them lay on low couches except one, who lay on a sofa, and he knew this must be the princess.
